The sense “ray of light” apparently developed as a
literal translation of Latin columna lucis column or pil-
lar of light, found in Bede’s writing in Old English.
—v. Before 1425, from the noun.

## bean
bean n. Old English (about 1000) béan; cognate with
Old High German bona bean (modern German Bohne),
and Old Icelandic baun that point to Proto-Germanic
*bauno, with no further cognates.
The slang meaning “head” is first recorded in Ameri-
can English in 1905, perhaps from the phrase bean ball,
used in baseball, and the verb meaning “to hit someone
on the head” is first recorded in American English in
1910.
bear! n. large, heavy mammal. About 1150 bere (geni-
tive beran ), developed from Old English bera (before
893, in a translation of St. Gregory’s Dialogues ). Cog-
nates appear in Old High German bero (modern Ger-
man Bar), Middle Dutch bere (modern Dutch beer),
from Proto-Germanic *beron-, Old Icelandic bjorn, all
meaning “bear,” literally, “brown (animal)” (a designa-
tion shared with beaver ) going back to the Indo-Euro-
pean base *bher- light brown (Pok.136), which is
related to the source of Old English brian BROWN.
The actual name of the European brown bear consid-
ered “the brown animal” by the Germanic, Baltic, and
Slavic peoples goes back to the Indo-European base
that was the source of Latin ursus (see URSINE), Greek
arktos (see ARCTIC), and Old Irish art. Compare the
related words BRUIN and BEAVER! rodent.
Bear in the sense of a speculator who sells short,
hoping for a fall in stocks (from which we derived bear-
ish, 1881), was first recorded in 1709, in an article in the
Tatler by Steele, as a shortening of bearskin jobber,
supposed to be from the phrase “to sell the bearskin,”
in allusion to the proverb “sell the bear’s skin before
one has caught the bear” (recorded since the 1500’s);
see also BULL!.
bear? v. carry, bring forth. Before 1123 beren, devel-
oped from Old English beran (about 725, in Beowulf).
The word is cognate with Old Saxon beran, Old Frisian
bera, Old High German beran to carry, (from Proto-
Germanic *beranan ), giberan bring forth, give birth to
(modern German gebdren ), Old Icelandic bera to car-
ry, and Gothic bairan, all from the same Indo-European
base (*bher-, Pok.128) that is common to Latin ferre to
carry, bring, Greek phérein, Armenian berem J carry,
Old Irish berid, beirid, and Sanskrit bhérati (he) carries.
—bearable adj. About 1454, formed from
English bear + -able*. —bearer n. 1255, developed
from Old English, in phrases such as weeter-berere.
—bearing n. About 1250 bering behavior, conduct,
formed from Middle English beren, v. + -ing.1 —bear-
ings n.pl. 1711, formed from English bearing + -s!.

## beard
beard n. Old English beard (before 830, in the Vespa-
sian Psalter ). The correspondence in spelling between
Old English and modern English is accidental, as the
modern form developed from Middle English, first re-
corded as the surname Berd (1165). The word is cog-
nate with Old Frisian berd, Old High German bart
(modern German Bart ), Middle Dutch baert (modern
Dutch baard), late Old Icelandic bardh, from Proto-
Germanic *bardaz, and with Latin barba beard, Old
Slavic brada, and Lithuanian barzda, from Indo-Euro-
pean *bhardha (Pok.110).
—v. About 1303, berden to grow or have a beard, reach
the age of puberty, in Mannyng’s Handlyng Synne;
later, to face boldly, defy (1525), a meaning already

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:116 COLUMN:2 -->
known in the Middle English phrase rennen in ber«
oppose openly, and in the berd to one’s face, directly

## beast
beast n. Probably before 1200 beste, in Ancrene Riwk
(compare English bestial, which retained the Middl.
English spelling), borrowed from Old French beste
from Vulgar Latin *besta, from Latin béstia wild ani
mal, of uncertain origin. Middle English beste a livin;
being, an animal as distinct from “man,” was used t
translate the Latin word animal and took the place o
Old English déor deer (which became specialized), jus
as in this sense beast was replaced in the 1500’s by
animal. —beastly adj. Probably about 1200. Compar:
BESTIAL.

## beat
beat v. strike repeatedly. Probably before 1200 beter
in Ancrene Riwle, developed from Old English béata:
(about 725, in Beowulf). Though the word is not foun
in Gothic it is cognate with other Germanic forms, suc]
as Old High German bézan to beat, kick, and Old Ice
landic bauta, from Proto-Germanic *bautanan, fron
Indo-European *bhau-/bhu- (Pok.112). The past tens
beat developed in the 1500’s as a shortened form fron
Middle English beted. The old past participle beat i
still found in dead-beat all tired out. —n. About 1300
from the verb. —beater n. (1200) —beating n. (probabl;
about 1200).

## beatific
beatific (bé’atif ‘ik) adj. blissful, making blessed. 1639
borrowed from French béatifique, or perhaps directl
from Late Latin beatificus, derived from Latin beatu
happy, blessed; see BEATITUDE; for suffix see -FIC
—beatification n. 1502, borrowed from Middle Frencl
béatification, from Late Latin beatificare; for suffix sec
-ATION. —beatify v. make blessed. 1535, in a version o
Trevisa’s translation of De Proprietatibus Rerum, bor
rowed from Middle French béatifier, learned borrow
ing from Late Latin beatificare, from beatificu
beatific; for suffix see -FY.
The appearance of beatification about 130 year
before beatific suggests that beatific is possibly a bac!
formation of beatification.

## beatitude
beatitude (béat’atiid) n. bliss, blessing. Probably befor
1425, borrowed through Middle French béatitude, an
directly from Latin beatitid6 state of blessedness, fron
beatus happy, blessed, past participle of beare mak
happy; whether related to Latin bene well, and t
bonus good, is a matter of doubt; for suffix see -TUDE
The reference to the Beatitudes in the New Testa
ment books of Matthew and Luke is first recorded i
1526.

## beatnik
beatnik n. Bohemian, especially of the 1950’s. 1958
formed in English from beat generation (name coinet
by American novelist Jack Kerouac, 1922-1969, for th
post-World War II group of young artists and writer:
+ Yiddish suffix -nik, as in nudnik, from Russian -ni
agent suffix, as in sputnik (1957); for suffix see -NIK.

## beau
beau (b6) n. suitor, dandy. 1684, borrowed from Frenc!
beau, noun use of earlier adjective meaning “fine
handsome,” from Old French bel, from Latin bellu
handsome, fine, originally a diminutive form of bonu
good; see BONUS. The meaning “lover, sweetheart” i
not recorded in English before 1720. The original Mic
dle English beau became obsolete in the early 1500’
so that the current use is a reborrowing of moder
French. —beau geste, 1920, borrowed from French.

## beautility
beautility n. the qualities of fine design, combinin
usefulness and beauty or elegance. 1973, formed i

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:117 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: beauty | 85 | beer -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:117 COLUMN:1 -->
English as a blend of beauty and utility (coined by Ada
Louise Huxtable, American architectural critic).

## beauty
beauty n. Before 1325 bealte, beute, in Cursor Mundi,
borrowed from Old French biauté, beauté, belté (ear-
lier beltet), from Vulgar Latin *bellitatem state of
being handsome, from Latin bellus fine, handsome, see
BEAU; for suffix see -TY. —beautiful adj. About 1443,
formed from English beauty + -ful. —beautify v. 1526,
formed from English beauty + -fy. —beautician n.
1924, formed from English beauty + -ician (as in physi-
cian, optician ). —beauteous adj. About 1400, formed
from Middle English beaute (about 1330) + -ous.

## beaver
beaver n. amphibious mammal. Old English beofor
(about 1000, in A‘lfric’s Glossary ), earlier bebr (about
720). The word has cognates in Old High German bibar
beaver (modern German Biber ), Old Saxon bibar, Mid-
dle Dutch and modern Dutch bever, Old Icelandic
bjorr; from Proto-Germanic *bebrus; and outside Ger-
manic with Latin fiber, Old Slavic bebrui, Lithuanian
bebrus, and Sanskrit babhru-s large mongoose, all
meaning literally “brown (animal),” from Indo-Euro-
pean *bhe-bhrii-s (Pok.136), and ultimately derived
from the same root as Old English bran BROWN.

## bebop
bebop n. style of jazz. 1944 (but said to go back to the
1920's), originally imitative of the continually shifting
accents in the music of a group of jazz players.

## because
because conj. About 1375, in Chaucer’s Canterbury
Tales, Middle English by cause for the reason (that);
later bycause (1380), because (1425). —adv. Probably
about 1380, bi cause on account (of), for the sake (of);
later because (about 1385); see BY and CAUSE.

## beck
beck n. calling gesture, as in at one’s beck and call.
Before 1382 bek, in the Wycliffe Bible, noun use of
Middle English bekken, v., beckon to; see BECKON.
While the Middle English Dictionary derives beck
(Middle English bek) from bekken, which is not re-
corded in English before 1385, in Chaucer’s Troilus
and Criseyde, it is possible that formation of beck (Mid-
dle English bek) was influenced by Middle English
bekenen beckon, recorded in The Ormulum (probably
about 1200), which would account for the appearance
of beck, n. before bekken, v. However, a lapse of three
years in a record of such antiquity may be simply a
defect in the availability of source material.
beckon vy. signal by a gesture. Old English bécnian
(before 830, in the Vespasian Psalter), West Saxon
béacnian, developed from béacen, bécen a sign, BEA-
CON.
As alluded to at beck, n. Middle English had two
forms that meant “beckon”: 1) bekken (about 1385)
derived from 2) bekenen (before 1200), developed
from Old English; both related to beken a signal fire,
beacon.

## become
become v. Old English becuman happen, come about
(about 725, in Beowulf), formed from be-, bi- + cuman
come. This is a common Germanic compound cognate
with Old Frisian bikuma come about, Old High Ger-
man biqueman obtain, Gothic biqgiman come upon sud-
denly. —becoming adj. About 1475, developed from
English become, v.

## bed
bed n. Old English (about 700) bed. The Germanic
cognates include Old Frisian and Old Saxon bed, Old
High German betti bed, Middle High German bette,
bet (modern German Bett ), Old Icelandic bedhr, and
Gothic badi bed, from Proto-Germanic *badja-. As the
Germanic cognates derive from the same source as

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:117 COLUMN:2 -->
Latin fodere to dig, fossa ditch, Greek béthros pit,
Welsh bedd grave, and Lithuanian bedu dig, from
Indo-European *bhedh-/bhodh- to dig (Pok.113), the
semantic connection with “dig” is supposed to be ei-
ther a hole or ditch to lie in or soft ground to lie on;
however, that idea disappeared in Germanic, which
had only two senses: a sleeping place for man, and a
garden bed for plants.

## bedlam
bedlam n. scene of noisy confusion. 1667, figurative use
of an earlier sense of a lunatic asylum, madhouse
(1663), in allusion to Bedlam, the popular name of St.
Mary of Bethlehem, insane asylum in London, England
(founded 1247). Bethlehem appeared as Betleem (town
of Bethlehem in Judea) before 971, and, in reference to
the hospital, as Bedlem, in 1418.

## Bedouin
Bedouin (bed’tin) n. a wandering desert Arab. About
1400, Bedoyn, in Sir John Maundeville’s Travels; bor-
rowed from Old French bediin, from colloquial Arabic
badawin, plural of badawiy desert dweller. Later ap-
parently reborrowed (1603) from French bedouin, a
spelling which was fully established only in the late
1800’s. The transferred sense “a wanderer” is recorded
in 1863.

## bee
bee n. insect. Old English béo (before 900, in Alfred’s
translation of Boethius’ De Consolatione Philoso-
phiae ), earlier bio-wyrt bee wort, a plant (about 700)
and Béo-wulf Bee-wolf, a personal name (about 725, in
Beowulf).
The word is cognate with Old High German bia, bini
bee (modern German Biene ), Old Icelandic by (usually
in compounds), Middle Dutch bie (modern Dutch bj),
and is found in many other of the older European lan-
guages, such as Old Slavic bicela, Old Prussian bitte,
and Welsh bydaf nest of wild bees, from Indo-Euro-
pean *bhei-/bhi- (Pok.116).

## beech
beech n. tree. 1296 beche, developed from Old English
(about 700) baece, later béce (from Proto-Germanic
*bokjon ), a derivative form of older béc beech (from
Proto-Germanic *b6k6).
The fruit of the tree is an ancient food source for
agricultural animals so that the tree was widely known
in ancient Europe, and the word is therefore cognate
with many of the older Germanic languages, including
Old Icelandic bék beech, Old High German buohha,
Middle High German buoche (modern German
Buche ), Middle Dutch boeke. The Germanic forms are
cognate with Latin fagus and Greek phégos oak, from
Indo-European *bhago-s beech (Pok.107); see also
BOOK.

## beef
beef n. Probably before 1300 bef, in Kyng Alisaunder,
borrowed from Old French buef, boef beef, ox, from
Latin bovem, accusative of bés ox. The Latin bds (actu-
ally an Umbrian dialect form) is cognate with Greek
botis ox, Old Irish bd cow, Middle Welsh buw, and
Sanskrit gaui-s (go-) cow, which in turn is cognate with
Old English ci cow; thus cow is ultimately related to
beef. From Indo-European *gwou-s (Pok.482).

## beep
beep n. 1929, formed in English in imitation of the
sound of a horn, especially of an automobile; later ex-
tended to the sound emitted in radar tracking and
other signals. —v. 1936, from the noun. —beeper n.
1946, formed from English beep, n. + -er?.

## beer
beer n. Probably about 1225 ber, in King Horn, devel-
oped from Old English béor (about 725, in Beowulf).
Cognates include Old Frisian biar, bier beer, Old High
German bior, Middle High German bier and modern

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:118 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: beet | behin -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:118 COLUMN:1 -->
German Bier, Middle Dutch and modern Dutch bier,
and Old Icelandic bjorr (from West Germanic). The
native Scandinavian word, as seen in Old Icelandic ol,
is cognate with English ale.
Whether English beer and its West Germanic cog-
nates are connected with Latin bibere to drink, is a
matter of conjecture, but the phonology is difficult.

## beet
beet n. plant with edible root. Old English (about 1000)
béte, borrowed from Latin béta, a name adopted into
other Germanic languages such as Old Frisian bete,
Old High German bieza, Low German bete (modern
German Beete ) and Middle Dutch béte.
The possibility of Celtic origin of Latin béta is
remote, because the Irish is borrowed from Latin and
the Welsh from Middle English, and there is no Gaulish
or other word that is unquestionably the source of the
Latin.
beetle! n. insect. About 1440 bytylle, later betylle
(before 1500), developed from Old English (about 700)
bitula, later bitela, from bitan to bite, and bita a bite,
morsel; see BITE.
beetle? v. project, overhang. 1602, in Shakespeare’s
Hamlet, apparently a back formation by Shakespeare
from earlier beetyl-browde beetle-browed, having
prominent, overhanging brows (1562), from_bitel-
brouwed, betilbrowed (before 1376), (Middle English
bitel sharp-edged, sharp, probably Old English *bitol
sharp, biting + browed).

## befall
befall v. About 1225 bifallen to fall out in the course of
events, to happen, developed from Old English befeal-
Jan to fall (probably about 875, in a version of Genesis ),
formed from be- by, about + feallan to FALL. The word
is cognate with Old Saxon and Old High German bifal-
Jan (modern German befallen ), and Old Frisian bifalla.

## before
before prep., adv., conj. About 1175 beforen, devel-
oped from Old English beforan (about 725, in Beowulf )
and biforan (about 750, in poetry of Cynewulf), both
Old English forms meaning “in front, ahead” (be-, bi-
by, about + foran before, from fora FORE).
This is a Common Germanic compound cognate
with Old Frisian bifara, Old Saxon biforan, Old High
German bifora, Middle High German bevor (modern
German bevor, conj.).

## beg
beg v. Probably before 1200 beggen ask as charity, in
Ancrene Riwle; probably related to or formed from
BEGGAR.
The Anglo-French begger to beg, is first recorded
somewhat later than the Middle English verb. It may
be a borrowing from Middle English, but we cannot
exclude the possibility that Middle English beggen was
from Anglo-French.

## beget
beget v. bring forth, produce. About 1250 begeten, al-
teration of earlier biyeten (before 1121) through influ-
ence of geten to GET. Middle English biyeten
developed from Old English begietan, bigeotan to get
(by effort), acquire. A similar form is found in Gothic
bigitan.

## beggar
beggar n. Probably before 1200, in Ancrene Riwle, per-
son who lives by begging; borrowed perhaps from Old
French begart, begard, originally, a member of the
Beghards, lay brotherhoods of mendicants that arose in
the Low Countries in the early 1200’s, from Middle
Dutch beggaert mendicant; for the suffix -aert see
-ARD. It is a matter of conjecture whether the Middle
Dutch stem beg- was derived from begine a member
of the Beguines lay sisterhoods devoted to religious life.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:118 COLUMN:2 -->

## begin
begin v. Old English (about 1000, in A®lfric’s version «
Genesis ) beginnan (be- by, about + -ginnan to begit
recorded only in compounds, such as Old English o1
ginnan and aginnan to begin.).
The Old English is cognate with Old Frisian biginn
to begin, Old Saxon and Old High German biginna
(modern German beginnen), and Gothic duginnai
further connections are uncertain.

## begonia
begonia (bigdn’ya) n. tropical plant. 1751, probabl
borrowed through French (1706), from New Lati
formed on the name of Michel Bégon, 1638-171
French governor of Haiti and patron of botany +4 -i
New Latin suffix used in taxonomy.

## behalf
behalf n. on (or in) behalf of, in the interest of. Abot
1303 behalve, in Mannyng’s Handlyng Synne; late
behalf, literally meaning “beside” (about 1386, i
Chaucer’s Legend of Good Women ); fusion of Old En;
lish (him) be healfe by (his) side, and on (his) healfe o
(his) side, from healfe side, HALF. From the latter pai
of the 1400’s onward, the form behalve gave way t
behalf, paralleling the displacement of the singulé
halve by half.
Comparable development appears in Germa
meinethalben on my behalf, developed from Middl
High German von minen halben on my half or sid
where halbe means “side” as in Middle English.

## behave
behave v. About 1410, formed from be- thoroughly -
have to have or bear oneself (in a specified way).
Old English behabban to encompass, contain (be- -
habban have, hold) is only coincidentally similar i
form and no direct connection exists between Ol]
English behabban and the form behave of the 1400’
—behavior n. Probably before 1425 behaver, in a tran
lation of Higden’s Polychronicon, later behavour (prol
ably before 1475), influenced by the synonymot
haver, havour (about 1450); developed from behave -
-our -or!.The spelling behavior with i appeared in 153
influenced by the synonymous havior (1478), earlic
havour, haver (about 1450), an alteration (by associ:
tion with Middle English haven to have) of Midd
French and Old French avoir, aveir, noun use of ver
meaning to have, from Latin habére (see HABIT).
—behaviorism n. 1913, coined by John B. Watso1
1878-1958, American psychologist, founder of th
school of psychology.

## behemoth
behemoth (bihé’moth) n. large, powerful animal «
thing. Before 1382 bemoth an animal mentioned i
Job, in the Wycliffe Bible, later behemot (1388, in
second version of the Wycliffe Bible); borrowed fro
Latin behéméth, from Hebrew bahémoth beasts «
beast.

## behest
behest (bihest’) n. command, bidding. Probably befo1
1200 biheste promise, command, request, in Lay
mon’s Chronicle of Britain, alteration of Old Englis
beh&s promise, from behatan to promise (be- by, abot
+ hatan to call, command). Old English beh@s repr
sents Proto-Germanic bi-Haissiz, and the Old Englis
hatan is cognate with Old High German heizan an
Gothic haitan to order, command, from Proto-Germal
ic *Haitanan, Indo-European *kai-, root kéi- (Pok.53&
The addition in Middle English of -t to Old Englis
beh#s was influenced by the -t of the synonymot
word behight, on a pattern also seen in such words :
amongst.

## behind
behind prep., adv., adj. Old English (about 725, in
version of Exodus ) behindan (be-, bi- by + hindan |

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:119 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: behold | bellicose | 87 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:119 COLUMN:1 -->
back, behind; see HIND! back). The word is identical
with Old Saxon bihindan, and cognate with Old High
German hintana (modern German hinten ), and Gothic
hindana back of, behind of, from the root hind- in
hinder and hindmost.

## behold
behold v. Before 1200 biholden, in Ancrene Riwle, de-
veloped from Old English bihaldan (before 830, in the
Vespasian Psalter), corresponding to West Saxon be-
healdan give regard to, hold in view, watch (be-, bi- by
+ haldan, healdan HOLD). The word is identical with
Old Saxon bihaldan hold, keep, Old Frisian bihalda,
Old High German bihaltan (modern German behal-
ten).
The meaning “indebted” as in beholden to is first
recorded in Middle English probably about 1390, in Sir
Gawain and the Green Knight.

## behoove
behoove (bihtiv’) v. be necessary (or proper) for. Prob-
ably before 1200 bihoven, in Layamon’s Chronicle
of Britain and Ancrene Riwle; developed from Old
English behofian have use for (about 725, in Beowulf),
from *behof advantage, use, (only recorded in deriva-
tives such as behdflic useful). The Old English is cog-
nate with Old Frisian behof advantage, and Middle
High German behuof useful thing, beheben take, hold
(related to Old English hebban raise, as seen in its past
tense hdf; see HEAVE).

## beige
beige (bazh) adj., n. pale-brown. 1858, borrowed from
French beige, earlier baige, from Old French bege of
the natural color (of cotton and wool), of uncertain ori-
gin. Several dictionaries suggest a borrowing of Old
French from Italian bambagia cotton, from Medieval
Latin bambax (genitive bambacis ), but this raises the
problem of the disappearance of the first syllable bam-.
Another suggestion is that the first syllable, bam-, bom-,
in Old French bambais, and particularly bombace cot-
ton, was taken to be bon good, and that the syllable
was easily eliminated because of its weak meaning
(compare, for instance, bonhomme —homme fellow,
boneurté — eureté happiness, bonaventure — aven-
ture lucky).

## being
being n. person, thing that exists. 1380, in Chaucer’s
Canterbury Tales, from earlier use meaning “exist-
ence” (1340, in Ayenbite of Inwyt), developed from
verbal noun of be, v.

## belay
belay (bila’) v. fasten (a rope) by winding. 1549, devel-
oped from Middle English beleggen encircle, surround
(before 1250, in The Owl and the Nightingale ); devel-
oped from Old English belecgan to lay over (about 725,
in a version of Genesis ), from be-, bi- by, over, against
+ lecgan to LAY! put down.

## belch
belch v. An altered form belchen (1483) of earlier belk-
en (about 1350), both variants of Middle English bolken
to belch, vomit, overflow; developed from Old English
bilkettan (about 950), later bealcan, balcettan, bylcet-
tan to belch, vomit, utter (words) vehemently (about
1025).
The word is cognate with Middle Dutch belken bel-
low, roar, cry out, and possibly related to Old English
bellan to roar (see BELLOW), but is almost certainly
imitative in origin.
The phonetic alteration of belken to modern English
belch came about by palatalization.
—n. 1513, from the verb.

## beleaguer
beleaguer (bilé’gor) v. surround, besiege. 1589, prob-
ably from Low German belegeren (be- around + Jeger
camp). The word is cognate with Swedish belagra to

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:119 COLUMN:2 -->
besiege, German Belagerung siege, and belagern
beleaguer, and Dutch belegeren besiege, of which the
Dutch Jeger encamping army, lair, bed, is related to
English LAIR.

## belfry
belfry n. bell tower. 1272 belfrey bell tower; probably
before 1300, berefrei movable tower for besieging for-
tifications, in Kyng Alisaunder; borrowed through An-
glo-French berefrei, berfret, Old North French berfroi,
belfroy, belefroy, probably from Middle High German
bercfrit portable shelter, originally used to protect a
besieging force, from Proto-Germanic *bergzan protect,
and *frithuz peace, shelter, meaning a protective shel-
ter.
According to Bloch and Wartburg, “The loan cannot
go back to the period of the Frankish invasion [of
France] because at that time siege warfare was hardly
practiced.” Therefore, the often cited hypothetical
Frankish source is probably not relevant.

## belief
belief n. Before 1400 belyefe, earlier bileve (before
1225) and bileave (probably before 1200, in Ancrene
Riwle ); all forms replacing Old English geléafa by in-
fluence of later Old English belyfan (about 1000, in
works of A‘lfric), beléfan believe. The Old English ge-
léafa is cognate with Old Saxon gilobo belief, Old High
German giloubo (modern German Glaube ), and Goth-
ic galaubeins belief, galaubjan to believe; see BELIEVE.
Old High German giloubo is from Proto-Germanic *3a-
lauben.
By the 1400’s the distinction in the final consonant
was developing to differentiate belief and believe, as
seen in the pattern proof — prove and grief — grieve.

## believe
believe v. Before 1393 believen, in Gower’s Confessio
Amantis, earlier beleven (about 1386, in Chaucer’s
Legend of Good Women) and bileven (1225, in King
Horn ). The Middle English forms developed from Old
English belyfan (about 1000, in works of A¢lfric) and
beléfan believe, which replaced a variety of Old
English dialectal forms including Mercian geléfan,
Northumbrian geléfa, and West Saxon gelyfan believe.
These Old English words are cognate with Old Saxon
gildbian believe, Old High German gilouben (modern
German glauben), and Gothic galaubjan to believe,
literally, to make palatable to oneself, accept, approve,
from Proto-Germanic *3a-laubjanan, from Indo-Euro-
pean *Jeubh-/loubh- (Pok.683).

## belittle
belittle v. 1781, American English, in writings of
Thomas Jefferson, formed from be- + little.

## bell
bell n. Old English belle (before 900, in works of Al-
fred); cognate with Middle Low German and Middle
Dutch belle bell; perhaps related to Old English bellan
to roar, BELLOW.

## belladonna
belladonna (bel’adon’s) n. poisonous plant or the drug
made from it. 1597, as an Italian term introduced into
an English work on plants, literally, fair lady. According
to one source (1757), the plant got its name because
women made a cosmetic from its juice.

## belle
belle (bel) n. beautiful girl or woman. 1622, in Fletch-
er’s The Beggars Bush, borrowed from French belle, as
a noun use of belle, adj., beautiful, from Old French
belle (feminine of bel fine, handsome); see BEAU.

## belles-lettres
belles-lettres (bellet’ra) n.pl. finer forms of literature.
1665, borrowed from French belles lettres literary
studies, literally, fine letters, being parallel to beaux
arts fine arts.

## bellicose
bellicose adj. warlike, belligerent. Probably before

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:120 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: belligerent | benig -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:120 COLUMN:1 -->
1425, in a translation of Higden’s Polychronicon, bor-
rowed perhaps through influence of Italian bellicoso
(1363), from Latin bellicdsus, from bellicus of war, from
bellum war; see DUEL; for suffix see -OSE.!

## belligerent
belligerent adj. fond of fighting, warlike. 1577 belliger-
ant, borrowed perhaps through influence of Italian bel-
ligerante (1480) from Latin belligerantem (nominative
belligerans), from belligerare wage war, from belliger
waging war (bellum war + gerere to conduct). —n.
1811, from the adjective. —belligerence n. 1814,
formed from English belliger(ent) + -ence.

## bellow
bellow v. roar. About 1300 belewen be enraged, roar,
developed from Old English (about 750) belgan
become angry; cognate with Old Icelandic belgja to
swell up, Old High German belgan swell up, be angry,
Oid Saxon belgan become angry; related to Anglian
belg (compare blzstbzlg a bellows, béanbzelg bean
pod) and West Saxon bylg bag; see BELLOWS, BELLY.
—n. 1779, from the verb.

## bellows
bellows n. sing. or pl. instrument for producing air
current. 1372-74 belowes, earlier beliges (about 1125),
plural of beli (about 1200) and bali (about 1250), both
meaning “stomach, abdomen, BELLY.” The Old
English word for bellows was bléstbzlg, literally, blow-
ing bag.

## belly
belly n. About 1200 beli abdomen, bowels, developed
from Old English (about 700) baelg (with dialect vari-
ants belg, bylg) bag; cognate with Old High German
balg bag, skin, Old Icelandic belgr, Gothic balgs wine-
skin, (from Proto-Germanic *balziz), Old Irish bolg
bag, and Welsh bola, boly belly, bag, from Indo-Euro-
pean *bhelgh-/bholgh- to swell (Pok.125). Related to
BILLOW, BELLOW. —v. 1606, in Shakespeare’s Troylus
and Cressida, from the noun.
belong y. 1340 belongen, in Ayenbite of Inwit, formed
from bi- thoroughly + longen go along with, be appro-
priate to, from Jong, adj., dependent (on), belonging
(to); formed after Old English gelang, gelong (about
725, in Beowulf), from ge- (prefix expressing comple-
tion of action) + *lang of uncertain meaning. Old
English gelang is cognate with Old High German and
Old Saxon gilang nearby, at hand, but no trace can be
found in Old English of a form corresponding to Old
High German bilangen, Middle Dutch belanghen
(modern German and Dutch belangen ), all meaning
“to concern, interest, belong to.” —belongings, n.pi.
1603, in Shakespeare’s Measure for Measure, formed
from English belonging, verbal noun, + plural suffix
-s},

## below
below adv. About 1325, Middle English bilooghe (bi-,
variant of be- by, about + Jooghe, variant of lou, lowe
LOW!, adj.). Below was very rare in Middle English and
only appeared as an adverb; it began apparently as a
variant of the earlier a-lowe, the parallel form to an-
high (now on high ); the synonymous forms a-low, be-
low were analogous to a-fore, be-fore. Below gained
currency in the 1500’s, and is frequent in Shakespeare.
—prep. 1575, from the adverb.

## belt
belt n. Old English (about 1000) belt, found also in Old
High German balz and Old Icelandic belti, all bor-
rowed ultimately from Latin balteus girdle, belt, per-
haps of Etruscan origin.

## bench
bench n. Before 1200, developed from Old English
benc (about 725, in Beowulf), and cognate with Old
Frisian bank, benk bench, Old High German bank, and

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:120 COLUMN:2 -->
Old Icelandic bekkr, in which -kk- is the North Ge
manic correspondence of -nk-.

## bend
bend v. Probably before 1300, in Arthour and Merli
developed from Old English (probably about 1001
bendan tighten (a bow); originally, constrain; causativ
of Old English bindan to BIND. Old English benda
developed from Proto-Germanic *bandjanan. —
About 1434, from the verb.

## beneath
beneath adv., prep. 1125 benethan, developed fro1
Old English (854) beneothan (be-, bi- by, about + ne
than below; cognate with Old Saxon nithana belov
Old High German nidana, and Old Icelandic nethai
related to Old English nithera, niothera lower, NET!
ER).

## benediction
benediction n. blessing. Probably before 1400 benedi
cioun, in Sir Ferumbras; borrowed, perhaps by infli
ence of rare Old French benedicion, from Lat
benedictidnem (nominative benedictio ), from bened
cere to bless; literally, speak well of (bene well + dice:
to say); for suffix see -TION. Doublet of BENISON.

## benefactor
benefactor n. one who gives help or money. 1451, :
The Paston Letters, borrowed, probably by influenc
of Middle French bienfacteur, from Late Latin ben
factor, from the Latin phrase bene facere do well -
-tor the agent suffix. —benefaction n. Before 166
from Late Latin benefactidnem (nominative benefa
tid ), from benefacere, in Classical Latin always writte
as two words; for suffix see -TION.

## benefice
benefice n. office or position in the church, fief. Abo
1300, borrowed through Old French benefice, and d
rectly as a learned borrowing from Latin beneficiu:
kindness, promotion, from beneficus obliging, kin
from bene well + the root of facere do. —beneficent
n. kindness, gift. About 1454, from Latin beneficent
from a variant stem of beneficus kind; for suffix s¢
-ENCE. —beneficent adj. 1616, probably formed |
English from beneficence, on the pattern of earlie
English benevolent, magnificent; for suffix see -ENT

## benefit
benefit n. advantage. Before 1376 benfet good deed, :
Piers Plowman, borrowed through Anglo-French be:
fet, benfait, from Old French bienfait, and direct
from Latin benefactum good deed (bene well + fa
tum, neuter past participle of facere to do). —v. 147
from the noun. —beneficial adj. 1464, borrowe
through Middle French bénéficial and directly fro
Latin beneficialis, from beneficium a benefit, kindne:s
for suffix see -AL!. —beneficiary n. 1611, borrowe
probably from French bénéficiaire, from Lat
beneficiarius, from beneficium; for suffix see -ARY.

## benevolent
benevolent adj. kindly, charitable. About 1443, bo
rowed from Middle French benivolent, and direct
from Latin benevolentem (bene well + volente
(nominative voléns), present participle of velle |
wish); for suffix see -ENT. —benevolence n. Probab
about 1400, borrowed from Old French benivolenc
and directly from Latin benevolentia well-wishin
from benevolentem.

## benign
benign adj. kindly. Probably before 1325, borrowe
from Old French benigne, a learned borrowing fro!
Latin benignus good-natured (bene good, well + -gnu
from gignere to bear, beget; see KIN). —benignant ac
Before 1782, formed in English from Latin benignu
on the pattern of earlier malignant. —benignity .
About 1380 benignite, in Chaucer’s Canterbury Tale
borrowed from Old French benignité, learned borrov

ing from Latin benignitatem (nominative benignitas ),
from benignus; for suffix see -ITY.

## benison
benison (ben’ezen) n. blessing. Probably before 1300
benisoun, borrowed from Old French beneicon, benei-
son, a learned borrowing from Latin benedictidnem;
see the doublet BENEDICTION.
bent! adj. not straight, crooked. Probably before 1300
ibent, in Arthour and Merlin; \ater bent (about 1370, in
Chaucer’s An A.B.C. ), developed from bent, past par-
ticiple of BEND. —n. inclination, tendency. 1586, devel-
oped from earlier bent, adj., being turned or inclined
in some direction (1534, in writings of Sir Thomas
More), probably asa translation of Latin inclinatio incli-
nation.
bent? n. stiff grass. 1364; an earlier meaning, “grassy
place,” is attested in 1327; an earlier form Benet- (1136
and after, in place names), developed from Old English
Beonet- (851), as in Beonet-léah Bentley, and is cognate
with Old Saxon binet and Old High German binuz
(early modern German Bintze, German Binse ) mean-
ing “rush, marshy grass,” from Proto-Germanic
*binut-, of unknown origin.

## benzene or benzine
benzene or benzine n. volatile chemical compounds
obtained from hydrocarbons. 1835 benzine, borrowed
from German Benzin (coined in 1833 by E. Mitscher-
lich, German chemist), from Benz(oesaure ) benzoic
acid (1791, in English) the acid obtained from benzoin
(from Benzoe benzoin + Sdaure acid), + -in -ine?,
chemical suffix. The form benzene is attested since
1872.

## benzoin
benzoin (ben’zdin) n. resin used in cosmetics, incense,
ete. 1562 benzoin, earlier (1558) bengewine, which
probably gave rise to the alteration benjamin (a variant
name current from the late 1500’s to the 1800's); also
English benjoin (1601), borrowed from Middle French
benjoin and Italian benzoi, from which English as-
similated the z. The source of the word in European
languages is Arabic Juban jawi incense of Jawa (Java); lu
of the first element in Arabic, being mistaken as the
definite article in Arabic, was omitted in the borrowing
process.

## bequeath
bequeath v. leave or give in a will. Probably before
1200 biquethen, in Layamon’s Chronicle of Britain, de-
veloped from Old English becwethan give by will (800-
885, in Alfred’s Will); earlier, to say, speak (probably
about 750, in Andreas), a compound of be-, bi- by,
about + cwethan say, from Proto-Germanic *kwetha-
nan.

## bequest
bequest n. legacy, bequeathing. Before 1338 biqueste,
in Mannyng’s Chronicle of England; later occasionally
biquyst, as in the 1378 version of Piers Plowman (be-.,
bi- be- + quiste, about 1300; later quest, between 1330
and 1350, with the -e- spelling by analogy with Middle
English biquethen; Middle English quiste, quest devel-
oped from Old English *cwis, *cwiss something said,
utterance —compare Old English andcwis an answer,
uncwisse speechless, forms cognate with Gothic ana-
quiss slander, missaquiss dispute —all from the Indo-
European base *gwet- (Pok. 480) of Old English cwide
saying, speech + a suffix beginning with t-; the tt be-
coming ss (from Proto-Germanic *kwessis, Indo-Euro-
pean gwet-tis). The new t in Middle English is
probably due to analogy between biquethen— bi-
quiste, quiste and pairs such as give—gift, freeze—
frost, etc.).

## berate
berate (birat’) v. scold sharply. 1548, formed from

## English
English prefix be- thoroughly + rate to scold (about
1390, in Chaucer’s Canterbury Tales), perhaps bor-
rowed from a Scandinavian source (compare Norwe-
gian dialect and Swedish rata reject, find fault).

## bereave
bereave (birév’) v. leave desolate and alone, rob. About
1175 bireaven, developed from Old English beréafian,
about 725, in a version of Genesis (be-, bi- thoroughly
+ réafian rob, about 725, in Beowulf); cognate with
Old Frisian birava despoil, Old Saxon biroban, Old
High German biroubén (modern German berauben ),
and Gothic biraubén, from Proto-Germanic *rauboja-
nan, cognate with Sanskrit ropayati breaks off from
Indo-European *reup-/roup- (Pok.870). —bereave-
ment n. 1731, in Bailey’s Dictionary, formed from
English bereave + -ment. —bereft adj. About 1375, in
Chaucer’s Canterbury Tales, developed from _be-
reaved, bireved, later bereft, past participle of Middle
English bireaven.
The two forms bereaved and bereft have existed side
by side since the latter 1300’s, bereaved being the ear-
lier form; however, the usage is not now interchangea-
ble: bereaved is applied to loss of a beloved one, bereft
is applied to circumstances, especially in such phrases
as bereft of hope.

## beret
beret (bara’) n. cap with no visor. 1827, borrowed from
French béret, earlier berret, Old Gascon berret, from
Medieval Latin birretum, from Vulgar Latin *birrittum
(diminutive form of Late Latin birrus cape with a
hood), perhaps of Gaulish origin.

## beriberi
beriberi (ber’éber’é) n. disease affecting nerves. 1703,
borrowed from Singhalese beriberi (reduplication of
beri weakness).

## berkelium
berkelium (bérké’léam) n. radioactive metallic chemi-
cal element. 1950, New Latin berkelium, formed from
Berkeley, California, site of University of California,
where it was first produced + New Latin -ium (suffix
of chemical elements).

## berm
berm n. bank of a canal; side of a road; later, terrace
along a river bank or beach (1891). 1729, borrowed
from French berme, from Dutch berm and German
Berme; see BRIM.

## berry
berry n. Old English berie (about 1000, in A#lfric’s
translation of Deuteronomy ). Though the early history
of this word is uncertain, it is found in various forms in
all Germanic languages, and is cognate with Old Saxon
-beri in winberi grape, and Old High German beri
berry (modern German Beere ), Middle High German
and Middle Dutch bere, Old Icelandic ber, Danish ber,
Swedish bar, and Gothic -basi in weinabasi grape.
The form with s, seen in Gothic, is preserved in mod-
ern Dutch bes, and through the Proto-Germanic *bas-
ja-, *bazja- may possibly be connected with a root form
represented by Sanskrit bhas- to eat, in babhasti chews
thoroughly, from Indo-European *bhes-/bhos-
(Pok.145). —v. berrying vbi.n. the producing or gather-
ing of berries. 1845, American English, in writings of
James Fenimore Cooper.

## berserk
berserk (bérsérk’) adj. violently angry, mad. 1851, de-
veloped in English either as a shortening of earlier
berserker (1822, in Scott’s The Pirate ) or more prob-
ably a back formation of berserker, from a misunder-
standing of the function of the final -r in the
Scandinavian berserkr where the -r is a case ending of
the masculine singular, rather than an agent noun suf-
fix for one who goes berserk.
The word is of uncertain etymology, though its refer-

and frenzied fury is undisputed. Berserker is borrowed

## berth
berth n. 1622, safe room or space necessary to keep
ships from running afoul of each other, of uncertain
origin; perhaps related to BEAR? in the sense “bearing-
off room,” that is “room or way made by keeping a safe
distance from the shore.” The extended sense of “a
sleeping place” is first recorded for a ship’s passenger
(1796) and a railroad passenger (1806). —v. 1667, in
Pepys’ Diary, from the noun.

## beryl
beryl (ber’al) n. hard blue-green mineral used as a gem.
Before 1300, borrowed from Old French beril, and
from Latin béryllus, from Greek béryllos.
According to the Greek scholar Frisk, béryllos is a
back formation from béryllion, from Prakrit veruliya,
variant of Pali veluriya (formed in Sanskrit as vaidurya-
m lapis lazuli), from Dravidian, and probably formed
on Vélar (now Bélir ) the name of a town in southern
India.

## beryllium
beryllium (beril’6éam) n. metallic chemical element.
1863, New Latin beryllium, formed from Latin béryllus
BERYL + New Latin -ium (suffix of chemical elements).

## beseech
beseech v. beg. Probably before 1200 bisechen, in An-
crene Riwle and Layamon’s Chronicle of Britain;
formed from Middle English be-, bi- about, or perhaps
meaning “thoroughly” + sechen seek, developed from
Old English sécan (about 725, in Beowulf); earlier
sodhte (about 700, in early glossaries, past tense only).
The word is cognate with Old Frisian biséka and mod-
ern German besuchen to seek out, visit; see SEEK.

## beset
beset v. set upon, attack. Old English besettan sur-
round, about 725, in Beowulf (be-, bi- about + settan
SET); cognate with Old Frisian bisetta surround, Old
Saxon bisettjan, Old High German bisezzan, Middle
High German besetzen (modern German besetzen oc-
cupy, settle), and Gothic bisatjan, from Proto-German-
ic *bi-satjanan. The meaning “to assail, attack”
appeared in Middle English before 1200.

## beside
beside prep., adv. Probably before 1200 bisiden, biside,
in Layamon’s Chronicle of Britain, formed from Old
English bi sidan by the side; earlier, besidan, probably
about 725 (be, bi by + sidan, dative case of side SIDE).
The adverbial use is now generally replaced by be-
sides.

## besides
besides adv., prep. Probably before 1200 bisides, in
Layamon’s Chronicle of Britain, but generally of later
use about 1390 and after, formed of Middle English
bisiden beside + -s, variant form of the adverbial geni-
tive ending -es.

## besom
besom (bé’zam) n. broom of twigs. Old English (about
800) besma, later besema bundle of twigs (used as a
broom or as a flail); cognate with Old Frisian besma,
Old Saxon besmo, Middle Dutch besem, bessem (mod-
ern Dutch bezem ) and Old High German besmo, besa-
mo (modern German Besen ), from Proto-Germanic
*besmon.

## best
best adj., adv. superlative of good and well. Probably
before 1200 beste or best, in Ancrene Riwle, earlier
betste (before 1121); found in Old English betst, betsta
(about 725, in Beowulf). Forms of best are common in
Germanic as seen in the variety of cognates, such as
Old Frisian, Old Saxon, and Middle Dutch best, Old
High German bezzist best (modern German best ), Old

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:122 COLUMN:2 -->
Icelandic beztr, and Gothic batists—all ultimatel
from the Germanic base *bat- (see also BETTER) + th
superlative suffix represented by Old English -st -est
Old English betst was reduced to best by assimilatio.
of the t to the following s (and similarly in German ani
other modern Germanic languages).
The relationship of best and better with good an
well developed outside of Old English.
—n. Probably before 1200 best, in Layamon’s Chron:
cle of Britain, earlier beste, betste (probably befor
1175); from the adjective. —v. 1863, verb use of besi
n.

## bestial
bestial (bes’chal) adj. Before 1393, in Gower’s Con
fessio Amantis; borrowed from Old French bestial an:
from Latin béstialis like a beast, from béstia BEAST; fo
suffix see -AL}.

## bestow
bestow v. Before 1375 bestowen, bistowen give (alm:
etc.), mete out, from be-, bi- be- + stowen to place
spend, STOW. —bestowal n. 1773, act of bestowing
formed from English bestow + -al?.

## bet
bet v. to wager. The origin of this word is uncertair
The verb is first recorded in 1597, in Shakespeare’s .
Henry IV, and it is suggested that it derived from bee
v., to make good, developed from Middle Englis
beten to mend, remedy; improve, make better; kindl
or replenish (a fire); arouse (emotion), stimulate (ac
tion), Old English b#tan, cognate with Old Saxo
bétian, Old High German beizen and Old Icelandi
beita, from Proto-Germanic *baitjanan.
The shortened e of bet is due to the presence of shor
-e forms in Middle English beten, as signaled by rime
and by tt- spellings. Betting (1599, in Shakespeare
Henry V) was very likely thought of as “improving
game or contest, stimulating action, etc.” The means o
material with which to beet is frequently indicated i
a phrase with mid or with, but Shakespeare’s turnin
the means (i.e. money) into the direct object of the ver
seems to be without precedent.
—n. 1592, probably from the verb. The later date fo
the verb (1597) may be a defect in the record o
English.
With similarity of form, it is tempting to draw a cor
nection between modern English bet and Middl
English bet advantage (noun use of bet, adv., the earlie
form of BETTER). However, no accepted connectio:
has been established.

## beta
beta (ba’to) n. second letter of the Greek alphabe
Before 1325, in Cursor Mundi, borrowed from Lati
béta, from Greek béta, from Semitic; compare Hebre\
béth the second letter of the Hebrew alphabet, literall
meaning a house, originally formed from the hierc
glyph of a house.

## betel
betel (bé’tal) n. East Indian pepper plant whose leave
are wrapped around a nut (betel nut) and chewed as:
stimulant. 1553, borrowed from Portuguese betel
vitele, from Malayalam vettila, or Tamil vettilei, _
béte noire (bat’ nwar’) thing dreaded or detested, bu;

eray’s Barry Lyndon; French béte noire, literally, blac
beast.

## betray
betray v. be disloyal to. About 1280 bitrayen mislea:
deceive, betray, formed from Middle English bi- be
thoroughly + trayen betray, borrowed from O)
French trair, from Latin tradere hand over (tran
across + dare give; see DATE! period). —betrayal .

ral.

## yetroth
yetroth v. promise in marriage. About 1303 betrou-
hen, variant of bitreuthen, in Mannyng’s Handlyng
syynne (be-, bi- by + treuth a pledge, TROTH). —be-
rothal n. 1844, formed from English betroth +4 -al?.

## yetter
yetter adj., adv. comparative of good and well. Probably
9efore 1300 better, earlier bettre (about 1250) and
etre (1131); developed from Old English bettra
before 900, in writings of Alfred), earlier betra (about
(50, in Cynewulf’s Elene) and betera (about 725, in
Beowulf). The word was used as the comparative of
zood in older Germanic languages and is cognate with
1d Frisian betera, Old Saxon betiro, Old High German
ezziro better (modern German besser ), Old Icelandic
»etri, and Gothic batiza —all from Proto-Germanic
‘batizon, containing the comparative suffix represent-
sd by Old English -ra -er.
The Proto-Germanic base *bat- is represented by the
Did and Middle English adverb bet better, which is
sognate with Old Frisian bet, Old High German baz,
Id Icelandic betr, from Proto-Germanic batiz, and is
yossibly related to Old English bot remedy, compensa-
ion; modern English BOOT? (now used only in to boot ).
—n. About 1175, but developed in Old English from
he adjective in such phrases as the better and the
worse. —v. Before 1400, from the adjective, and analo-
sous to Old English beterian, gebeterian be or make
etter; cognate with Old Frisian beteria, Old High Ger-
man bezziron, Middle High German bezzern, and
nodern German bessern.

## yetween
yetween prep., adv. 1225 bitwene, earlier bitwenen
probably before 1200, in Layamon’s Chronicle of Brit-
2in ) and betwenen (about 1200); developed from Old
!nglish betwéonum (about 750, in Cynewulfs Elene );
‘ormed from bi-, be- by + twéonum two each (about
(25, in Beowulf).
Between combines two earlier forms in Old English:
petweonum (Mercian betwinum) and _ betwéon,
betwin. The elements twéonum and twéon partially
correspond through *tweohnum and *tweohn (Proto-
Germanic *twiHn ) to Gothic tweihnaim and tweihna,
Jrammatical cases of tweihnai two each, a derivative of
‘wa TWO, cognate with Sanskrit dvikd-s double, from
indo-European *dwei-k-/dwi-k- (Pok.231).

## setwixt
setwixt (bitwikst’) prep., adv. between. Before 1333
bytwixte, earlier betwix (1127); developed from Old
English betweox (before 899, in writings of Alfred),
ormed from bi-, be- by + tweox for two. Old English
betweox is probably a shortened form of *betweoxum
wofold, the element *-tweoxum from *twiscum, da-
ive plural of *twisc, cognate with Old Frisian twiska,
Nid Saxon twisc, and Old High German zwiski two
2ach, from Proto-Germanic *twiska-, formed from the
adverb *twis twice (compare Old High German zwis,
Sanskrit dvis, Greek dis and Latin bis, from Indo-Euro-
pean *dwis); see TWO.
The final t in betwixt developed in Old English but
was infrequently used until after 1500 when it gradual-
y became the regular spelling.

## bevel
bevel n. edge, angle. 1677 bevil, earlier bevile, adj.
1562), possibly borrowed from Old French *bevel, a
‘orm implied by French biveau, béveau (in which Mid-
die and modern French -eau come from Old French
el). The supposed Old French *bevel may have devel-
sped from baif gaping (beér, baér to open, gape, from
Medieval Latin batare + -if -ive; see BAY® space).

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:123 COLUMN:2 -->
The problem here lies in the dates of borrowing.
Since the word is first recorded in English (1562), there
appears to be a gap of about 150 years between the
assumed borrowing from Old French (a period ending
in 1400) and the appearance of bevile in English.
—v. 1677, probably from the noun.

## beverage
beverage n. liquid for drinking. About 1300, earlier as
a surname (1237); borrowed from Old French bevrage,
from bevre to drink, variant of boivre, from Latin
bibere, see IMBIBE; for suffix see -AGE.

## bevy
bevy (bev’é) n. group, flock. About 1425, applied to
quails; before 1450, applied to a group of ladies; bor-
rowed from Anglo-French bevée, of unknown origin. It
has been conjectured that the word corresponds to Old
French bevee, buvee drink, drinking, and thence to
Italian bevuta drinking bout or party, “but of this there
is no known evidence” —OED.

## beware
beware v. Developed from the imperative phrase be
ware (probably about 1200, in the plural beth warre ),
from be, v., and ware, adj., careful; see AWARE.
Old English had the compound bewarian to defend,
not found in Middle English, and the verb warian to
guard, keep clear of, which survived only in certain
specialized phrases in modern English, such as “ware
holes,” in the sense of “keep clear of the holes,” and a
use commonly mistaken as a contraction of beware.
Old English also had wer on one’s guard, from Proto-
Germanic *wards, Indo-European *wor6s (Pok.1164),
and Middle English war, ware appeared regularly in
the phrase to be ware to be on one’s guard. From such
constructions be ware soon began to be treated as a
single word.

## bewilder
bewilder v. perplex, confuse. 1684, first occurring in
the past participial form bewildered (be- thoroughly +
now archaic wilder lead astray or into the wilds, prob-
ably back formation from wilderness, on the analogy of
wander ).

## beyond
beyond prep., adv. Before 1325 biyond, in Cursor Mun-
di, earlier beionde (1154), developed from Old English
begeondan (probably about 885, in the Anglo-Saxon
Chronicle ), from bi-, be- by + geond yonder, prep. +
-an from or at (a place, position, direction), compare
Old Icelandic -an, Old High German and Gothic -ana;
see YONDER.
bi-, prefix meaning: 1a twice, as in bimonthly = twice
each month. b once every two, as in bimonthly = once
every two months. 2 having two, or doubly, as in bipo-
lar = having two poles, biconvex = doubly convex. 3
two, as in bisect = section or divide in two. About 1250,
borrowed through Old French bi-, or directly from
Latin bi-, from Old Latin dvi- (dui-); cognate with
Greek di- twice, two; see DI-. Bi-, though once confined
largely to adjective and verb stems of Latin origin, is
today a free-forming prefix added to nouns, adjectives,
verbs, and adverbs as the situation suits.

## bias
bias n. slant, prejudice. 1530, in Palsgrave’s Lesclar-
cissement, borrowed from Middle French biais slant,
from Old Provencal biais, of uncertain origin.
According to Bloch and Wartburg, the Old Proven-
eal form is possibly from Greek epikarsios oblique,
which may have come into Provencal through the
Greek colonies on the coast of France through a form
*bigassius, *ebigassius (compare Marseilles and Nice,
names of Greek origin).
—v. 1622, from the noun. —biased adj. 1649, prej-
udiced, earlier (1611) as a participial of bias, v. Note the

participial adjective is recorded before the verb, sug-
gesting that the earlier use of biased was influenced by
the French verb biaiser (1402).

## bib
bib n. cloth worn under the chin to protect clothing.
1580, developed from earlier verb bibben to drink
(probably about 1380), perhaps borrowed from Latin
bibere; see IMBIBE.

## Bible
Bible n. Before 1325, in Cursor Mundi, borrowed in
part through Anglo-Latin biblia (replacing Old English
bibliothece the Scriptures, after use in Jerome) from
Medieval Latin Biblia, and in part from Old French
bible, a learned borrowing from Medieval Latin Biblia,
neuter plural, though interpreted as feminine singular
of Late Latin biblia (usually biblia sacra holy books),
probably from the habit of considering the Scriptures
as one work. Biblia was the popular name as evidenced
by the wide variety of its use in European languages:
Provencal bibla, Spanish and Portuguese biblia, Italian
bibbia; Middle High German bibel (modern German
Bibel), Dutch bijbel, and Old Icelandic bibla (later,
biblia ).
Late Latin biblia was borrowed from Greek biblia,
plural of biblion (often byblion ) originally, little book,
but later the ordinary word for “book,” and so diminu-
tive of byblos book, writing, scroll (literally meaning
“paper” and the same as byblos Egyptian papyrus, the
inner bark of which paper was made; compare similar
processes of formation in Latin liber book, also derived
from liber the inner bark of a tree, and English book,
from Old English boc, related to bdc beech tree).
The general meaning “book or treatise, especially a
lengthy one” is recorded 1387, in a version of Piers
Plowman.
—biblical adj. 1790, replacing earlier Biblic (1684),
from which it was formed + -al?.
biblio- combining form meaning: 1 book or books, as in
bibliophile = lover of books. 2 the Bible, as in bibliola-
try = excessive reverence for the Bible.
Biblio- has been an element of a few English words
since about 1000 in the Old English period. As a natu-
ralized combining form in English it began to appear
with some frequency in the 1800’s, in imitation of the
Greek element biblio- from biblion book; see BIBLE and
BIBLIOGRAPHY for further explanation.

## bibliography
bibliography n. list of books. 1678, borrowed perhaps
through influence of French bibliographie (1633), from
Greek bibliographia the writing of books (biblion book
+ -graphia record, account, from graéphein write).
—bibliographer n. 1656, formed in English from Greek
bibliographia + English suffix -er !. —bibliographical
adj. 1679, formed possibly from English bibliography
+ -ical.
The form biblio- was already known in English
through earlier bibliotheke library (1549), and biblio-
theca the Scriptures (about 1000, in writings of A¢lfric)
and other forms so that it is quite possible biblio- was
a natural formation from established Greek elements
in the great literary flowering of England during the
period after the mid-1500’s, and became a naturalized
combining form in English by the early 1800’s when
most words in biblio- are first recorded in English. It is
also possible that the utility of bibliography and bibliog-
rapher were largely responsible for promoting biblio-
as a combining form in modern English.

## bicameral
bicameral (bikam/osral) adj. having two legislative
chambers. Before 1832, in writings of Jeremy Ben-

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:124 COLUMN:2 -->
tham, formed in English from bi- two + Late Latir
camera chamber + English suffix -al!; see CAMERA.

## biceps
biceps (bi’seps) n. muscle having two heads or origins
especially the large muscle in the upper part of the
arm. 1634, borrowed probably from French bicep:
(1562), and from Latin biceps (genitive bicipitis ) two
headed (bi- two + -ceps, -cipit-, caput HEAD ).

## bicker
bicker v. to quarrel. Probably before 1300 bikeren (bik
ering, in Arthour and Merlin) to attack; formed ir
English perhaps from Middle Dutch bicken to slash
stab, attack + English suffix -er 4 frequently, again anc
again. The suggested Middle Dutch bicken is support
ed by Middle English biker, n.; see noun below. Middle
Dutch bicken to slash, attack has cognates in Old Hig
German bicchan to thrust, attack, Middle Low Germar
bicken, Old English becca pickax, Gaulish beccus beak
see BEAK). —n. Probably before 1300 biker battle, at
tack, in Arthour and Merlin; later, quarrel (1350), prob
ably developed from bikeren, v.

## bicycle
bicycle n. 1868 (perhaps 1866, in U.S. Patents), prob
ably formed in English from bi- two + -cycle wheel, or
the pattern of earlier tricycle, applied to carriage:
(1828).
According to most sources bicycle is borrowed from
French; however, it is not recorded in French unti
1869 and is held by French scholars to be a borrowings
from English (see Petit Robert, 1978). The confusior
apparently comes from the fact that it was a workman
Lallement, in a French carriage works who, in 1865
made the improvements in Macmillan’s version (1839
of the pedal velocipede and went to America with hi
invention.
—v. 1869, from the noun.

## bid
bid v. command, offer, proclaim. Before 1121 bidder
beg, request, influenced by and often confused i
meaning with beden offer, announce, command, bu
developed from Old English biddan ask for, demanc
(about 725, in Beowulf). Of the two forms, Middle
English bidden (Old English biddan ) is cognate with
Old Frisian bidda, Old High German bitten ask for
beseech (modern German bitten ), Old Icelandic bidh
ja, and Old Saxon and Gothic bidjan, from Proto-Ger
manic *bidjanan, cognate with Sanskrit jfu-badh
bending the knees, from Indo-European *bhedh- benc
(Pok.114); and beden (Old English béodan ) is cognat
with Old Frisian biada, Old High German biotan ti
offer (modern German bieten ), Old Icelandic bjédha
Old Saxon biodan, and Gothic anabiudan to command
from Proto-Germanic *biudanan, cognate with Gree!
petithesthai inquire, from Indo-European *bheudh- bi
awake, be aware (Pok.150). —n. offer. 1788, in corre
spondence of Thomas Jefferson, from the verb.

## bide
bide v. wait, abide. Old English bidan stay, wait (abou:
725, in a version of Genesis ). Old English bidan is cog,
nate with Old Saxon bidan, Middle Dutch biden, Oli
High German bitan to wait, Old Frisian bida, Old Ice
landic bidha, and Gothic beidan to wait. Except in suc:
use as bide one’s time, the word has been largely di
placed by abide. The Germanic meaning “to wait” he
grown from an earlier one “to trust.” Compare th!
cognate Greek peithesthai obey and Latin fidere trus
from Indo-European *bheidh- convince (Pok.117).

## biennial
biennial (bien’éal) adj. requiring or occurring (ever
two years. 1621, borrowed perhaps from French bie
nal (1550), or formed in English from Latin biennim

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:125 COLUMN:1 -->
two-year period (bi- two + annus year) + English suffix
al}.

## bier
bier (bir) n. stand for a coffin or corpse. Probably before
1200 bere, in Layamon’s Chronicle of Britain, devel-
oped from Old English (before 900) West Saxon bér
jitter or stretcher; earlier, Anglian bér, formed from
the stem of beran to bear; see BEAR? carry.
Since about 1600 the modern spelling bier has devel-
oped, apparently influenced by French *biére coffin,
from Old French biere litter, bier, ultimately from
Frankish *béra (compare Old High German bara bier,
a cognate of Old English bér, bér), from Proto-Ger-
manic *b#rd, Indo-European *bhéra (Pok.131).

## bifocal
bifocal adj. 1888, formed from English bi- + focal.
—bifocals n. pl. 1888 or 1889, formed from noun use
of bifocal, adj. + -s in such phrases as perfection bifo-
cals. Though bifocals were conceived by Benjamin
Franklin who used the term double spectacles (1784),
the name bifocals did not appear until over 100 years
later.

## big
big adj. About 1300, strong or sturdy (in reference to
persons and animals); of obscure origin, perhaps bor-
rowed from a Scandinavian source (compare Norwe-
gian dialect bugge strong man).
Its use much before 1400 is rare, the general sense
“of great size, large” appearing earlier (about 1380) in
Patience, and Pearl, slightly later in Chaucer’s Troilus
and Criseyde (about 1385).
—adv. 1563, from the adjective.

## bigamy
bigamy (big’omé) n. practice of having two spouses at
the same time. About 1250, borrowed from Old French
bigamie and from Medieval Latin bigamia, from Late
Latin bigamus twice married (forming a hybrid of
Latin bi- two, twice + Greek gamos marriage, a form
equivalent to Greek digamos twice-married person).
The Greek gamos is related to gamein to marry, and to
gambros relative by marriage, in-law; cognate with
such forms as Latin gener son-in-law, and Sanskrit jami-
s blood-brother (or -sister), and thus to the Indo-Euro-
pean base *Zem/(a)- marry (Pok.369). —bigamous adj.
1864, formed from English bigamy + -ous, after Medi-
eval Latin bigamus.

## bight
bight n. curve or bend in coastline. 1278, in a place
name ( Syde biht in Lancashire), developed from Old
English (825) byht a bend, related to bugan to bend,
bow; see BOW! bend. Old English byht (from Proto-
Germanic *buHtis, Indo-European *bhugh-tis, (Pok.
153) is cognate with Middle Low German bucht (mod-
ern German Bucht ), Middle Dutch and modern Dutch
bocht bend, bight.

## bigot
bigot (big’at) n. prejudiced person. 1598, hypocrite, es-
pecially a hypocritical professor of religion; borrowed
from Middle French bigot hypocrite, of uncertain ori-
gin. Possibly a term of Germanic origin (compare Old
High German bi got by God), and originally in Old
French (1155) a proper name among the Normans and
also a term of disparagement for Normans and some
others. According to the French scholar Gamillscheg,
and others, the name may have been inspired by an
excessive use of profanity adopted by the Norman sol-
diers from the English oath, and it is suggested that a
comparison exists with Middle French godon an Eng-
lishman, again probably inspired by the English fond-
ness for God damn.
The sense of a prejudiced person first appeared in
1661, but the development of this sense and the earlier

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:125 COLUMN:2 -->
meaning “hypocrite,” in French or in English, have
never been successfully accounted for.
—bigoted adj. 1645, formed from English bigot + -ed 2.
—bigotry n. Before 1674, borrowed from French bigo-
terie, from bigot; for suffix see -RY.

## bijou
bijou (bé’zhii) n. jewel, trinket. 1668, borrowed from
French bijou, from Breton bizou, earlier besou finger
ring, from biz finger (like other native Breton words, it
is common in Celtic; compare Cornish bis, bes, and
Welsh bys finger), cognate with Old Icelandic kvistr
twig, from Indo-European *gwistis finger (Pok.481).

## bike
bike n. 1882, American English, shortened and altered
form of bicycle.

## bikini
bikini (biké’né) n. women’s very brief two-piece bath-
ing suit. 1948, borrowed from French bikini, named
after Bikini atoll in the Marshall Islands of the Pacific,
where several atomic bomb tests were carried out after
1946.
The name of the bathing suit, once a registered trade
name of Louis Reard, has been attributed to an analogy
with the shape of the mushroom cloud of an atomic
explosion and to the “explosive” effect of the skimpy
suit on men, but no concrete evidence is available.

## bile
bile n. bitter secretion, gall. 1665, borrowed from
French bile, a learned borrowing from Latin bilis bile,
anger; cognate with Welsh bustl, Old Cornish bistel,
and Breton bestl, all meaning bile, from Indo-Euro-
pean *bistli-s (Pok.102). —bilious adj. 1541, of or having
to do with bile, in a translation of Galen’s Terapeutyke;
later, ill-tempered (1561); borrowed from Middle
French bilieux, a learned borrowing of Latin bilidsus
full of bile, from bilis bile; for suffix see -oUS. Note that
in the record of English the adjective preceded the
noun by some 120 years.

## bilge
bilge n. bottom of a ship’s hull. 1513, probably variant
of earlier bulge a ship’s hull, a leather bag (about 1200);
borrowed from Old North French boulge, originally
meaning “leather sack,” from Late Latin bulga leather
sack, apparently from Gaulish bulga, from Indo-Euro-
pean *bholgha, root *bhelgh- to swell (Pok.125).

## bilk
bilk v. defraud, cheat. 1672, in Andrew Marvell’s The
Rehearsal Transposed, developed as an extended sense
of the earlier meaning “‘to balk or spoil one’s score in
the game of cribbage” (1651, in a collection of Cleve-
land’s poetry), perhaps as a verb use of bilk, n. (1633,
in Ben Jonson’s A Tale of a Tub ), either the verb or the
noun possibly being an alteration in the pronunciation
of the verb BALK.
bill! n. written statement. About 1370 bille, in Chau-
cer’s An A.B.C.,, a formal plea or charge in law, and
about 1378, in a version of Piers Plowman, a petition or
legislative measure; borrowed from Anglo-French bille
list, schedule, account (blend of Old French bille stick
of wood, with bulle a decree) and Anglo-Latin billa
(similar blend of Medieval Latin billia tree trunk, with
bulla seal, document with a seal attached); both bille
and billa ultimately derive from Gaulish (compare Old
Irish bile tree, tree trunk); see BILLET!,? and BULL?
decree. It has been suggested that the English may
originally have applied bille and billa to a wooden tally.
The meaning “account or invoice” is first recorded in
1404, the meaning “paper money, note” from paper
bill (1670), curiously before dollar bill (1774), is first
recorded in American English in 1682. The meaning
“broadside,” as in the phrase post no bills, is first re-
corded about 1426, in The Paston Letters.

bill? n. beak. Probably before 1200, in Ancrene Riwle,

of sword (about 725, in Beowulf) and earlier in the

billet! (bil’/it) n. written order for soldier’s food and
lodging. 1644; earlier meaning “an official record or
register” (probably before 1425, in a translation of Hig-
den’s Polychronicon ); borrowed from Anglo-French
billette list, schedule (a diminutive form of bille; see
BILL’), perhaps influenced by Middle French billette,
variant of Old French bullette certificate (a diminutive
form of bulle document, learned borrowing from Medi-
eval Latin bulla document, seal; see BULL? decree).
billet? (bil’it) n. thick stick of wood. 1437, in Proceed-
ings of the Privy Council, borrowed from Middle
French billette, a diminutive form of bille stick of
wood, from Medieval Latin billia tree trunk, possibly of
Gaulish origin (compare Old Irish bile sacred tree,
trunk of a tree, from Indo-European *bhelyom, root
*bhel- swell, Pok.122); see BLADE.

## billiards
billiards n. 1591, earlier used as an adjective in billiard
stick (1588); borrowed from Middle French billard cue
stick (a diminutive form of bille stick of wood; see BIL-
LET?). The -s added to the English word parallels use in
the names of other games, such as checkers, skittles,
and bowls.

## billion
billion n. 1690, (in Great Britain) second power of a
million, in Locke’s Essay Concerning Human Under-
standing, borrowed from French billion, formed from
bi- two + (miillion, from Old French millon MILLION.
The difference between British and German use
(one million millions) and American, Canadian and
modern French use (one thousand millions) comes
from British and German use of the original meaning
in French, while the later meaning, that resulted from
change by French mathematicians to dividing the nu-
merals of long numbers in groups of threes rather than
groups of sixes, was adopted elsewhere.
—billionaire n. 1860, American English, in Oliver Wen-
dell Holmes’ Elsie Venner, patterned on millionaire.

## billow
billow n. great wave, surge of the sea. 1552, probably
borrowed from a Scandinavian source (compare Old
Icelandic bylgja billow, Danish bglge, and Swedish bél-
ja). The Scandinavian words are cognate with Old
Dutch bolghe, bulghe, Middle Dutch bulge bubble,
blister, Middle High German bulge billow, probably
related to Old High German bulga (modern German
Bulge leather bag), from Proto-Germanic *bul3-, Indo-
European *bhilgh-, root *bhelgh- to swell (Pok.125).
The connections with bellow (except as a roaring of
the sea) and belly are not substantiated by semantic
links in Middle English.
—v. surge, swell. 1597, from the noun. —billowy adj.
About 1615, formed from English billow + -y!.

## billy
billy n. club or stick. 1848, American English (burglar’s
slang), a crowbar; 1856, a policeman’s club; probably
from Billy nickname of William. Like the names Jack
and Jenny, Billy was used to name various implements
and machines as early as 1795, and is recorded as a
common appellation about 1500.
billy goat Informal. male goat. 1861; earlier Billy
(1849), an application of the male name Billy (nick-
name of William), after the earlier nanny goat (1788).

## bin
bin n. box. Old English binne manger (about 750, in

European *bhendh-na, root *bhendh- BIND (Pok.127)

## binary
binary adj. consisting of two parts, dual. Before 1464
borrowed through Anglo-Latin binarius, from Lat
Latin binarius (from Latin bini two at a time; related t
bis twice, from Old Latin dvis and thence to Latin duc
TWO); for suffix see -ARY. —binary digit (1946) —binar
number (before 1796) —binary system (1835, of biologi
cal classification; 1802, of a binary star).

## bind
bind v. Old English bindan (about 725, in a translatio1
of Exodus ). The word was pronounced with a shor
vowel in Old and Middle English, as it is in its cognates
Old Saxon bindan to bind, Old Frisian and Old Icelan
dic binda, Old High German bintan (modern Germat
binden ), and Gothic bindan. The Sanskrit cognat
badhnati (he) binds, is of the same Indo-European bas
*bhendbh- to bind (Pok.127), which probably appears i1
-fend- of Latin offendix knot, band, and Greek peism
cable, rope. Bind is thereby ultimately related to BAND
fasten. —n. 1295, developed from Old English bind
band (about 1000), probably from the verb. The twé
modern English forms band and bind were probabl;
confused at first; until Middle English band (1126) sup
planted bind except in specialized usages and in th
curious modern popular usage to be in a bind (1950
and later), both forms may have had some interchange
able usage or been differentiated by dialect use rathe
than semantic applications. —binder n. 1218, in su1
names, earlier bindere (before 1000), formed from Oli
English bindan, v. + -ere -er!. —bindery n. 181(
American English, formed from bind +4 -ery.

## binge
binge n. spree (of drinking, eating, etc.). 1854, Englis.
dialect, apparently a special use of dialectal binge t
soak (a wooden vessel); and so by extension “to drin
heavily” in allusion to soaking up alcohol, perhaps rem
iniscent of a popular and long-established connectio;
between alcoholic drink and soak with reference t
drink in such phrases as an old soak for a drunk.

## bingo
bingo n. 1929, game developed from lotto, probabl
from earlier use as an exclamation indicating the suc
denness with which something happens (1927). Befor
that, it is possible only to guess at various connection!
such as bingo a slang term for brandy, in Hughes’ Top
Brown (1861).

## binnacle
binnacle (bin’akal) n. box or stand for ship’s compas:
1762, alteration of earlier bittacle (1622), borrowe
from French bitacle binnacle, from Old French habit)
cle dwelling, later, binnacle, from Latin habitacului)

tional sources, the Spanish scholar Corominas finds thi
the Spanish term bitécula (now bitaécora) is derive’
from French.

## binocular
binocular (banok’yalar) adj. of, for, or using both eye
1738, perhaps developed from the earlier meanir
having two eyes (1713); borrowed from French binoe.
laire, ultimately from Latin bini two at a time + oct
eyes; for suffix see -AR. —binoculars n. pl. 1877, fro

adj.

## binomial
binomial (bind’méel) n. expression consisting of tv)
terms or names. 1557, borrowed from New Lat}
binomialis, from Medieval Latin binomius having tv}

names, alteration of Latin binéminis (bi- two + ndémen,
genitive nOminis NAME); for suffix see -AL!. —adj. con-
sisting of two terms or names. 1570, from the noun.
bio- a combining form meaning: 1 life, living things, as
in biology = science of life or living things. 2 biological,
as in biochemistry = biological chemistry. The combin-
ing form probably entered English through New Latin
bio- as a borrowing of Greek bio-, combining form of
bios life, way of living, which is cognate with Latin
vivus living, and with Old English ewic, cwicu quick, in
the archaic sense “living,” and Gothic qius. The Indo-
European root has the various stems *gwiy(9)-, gwi-wo-,

## biography
biography n. account of a person’s life. 1683, in Dry-
den’s translation of Plutarch’s Lives, borrowed perhaps
through New Latin biographia, from Late Greek bio-
graphia (from Greek bio- life + -graphia record, ac-
count, from graphein write). —biographer n. 1715, in
writings of Addison, probably formed from English bi-
ography + -er', perhaps by influence of Medieval
Greek biographos writer of lives——biographical adj.
1738, formed from English biography + -ical.

## biology
biology n. study of living things. 1819; borrowed from
German Biologie, also used by Lamarck, 1802, from
bio- (from Greek bios life, way of living) + -logie study
of, from Greek -logia, from -/6gos one who treats of).
The word appears earlier in English with the meaning
“study of human life and character” (1813, and now
obsolete), perhaps as an independent borrowing of
Greek elements cited above. —biological adj. 1859,
formed from English biology + -ical. —biologist n.
1874, formed from English biology + -ist, perhaps by
influence of earlier French biologiste (1836), and ear-
lier English biologist (1813) but in reference to the
study of human life and character.

## bionics
bionics (bion‘iks) n. the making of electronic devices
modeled on biological systems. 1959, formed from
English bio- living, life, biological + -onics, as in elec-
tronics. —bionic adj. (1970)

## biopsy
biopsy (bi’opsé) n. medical examination of living tissue.
1895, borrowed from French biopsie (bio- living, life +
Greek 6psis a viewing). —v. perform a biopsy on. 1964,
from the noun.

## biotic
biotic adj. 1600, borrowed from Late Latin biéticus,
from Greek bidtikés related to life, lively, from biénai,
a form of biotin to live, from bios life; for suffix see -IC.

## biped
biped (bi’ped) n. animal having two feet. 1646, bor-
rowed, perhaps through French bipéde, or ‘directly
from Latin bipedem two-footed (bi- two + pedem,
nominative pés FOOT).

## birch
birch n. About 1385, in Chaucer’s Canterbury Tales,
developed from Old English (about 700) birce; cognate
with Old Saxon birka, berka, Middle Low German and
Middle Dutch berke (modern Dutch berk ), Old High
German biricha, birca (modern German Birke), from
Proto-Germanic *berkjon, Old Icelandic bjork, from
Proto-Germanic *berk6, all meaning “birch”; also cog-
nate with Old Prussian berse, Lithuanian bérZas, Latvi-
an berzs, Russian beréza, Serbian breza, Old Slavic
bréza birch, and Sanskrit bhurj4-s a species of birch,
from Indo-European *bherag-/bhyg- (Pok.139).
Latin farnus, fraxinus, meaning ash tree, have been
associated by some with the word for birch, although
the phonology is not clear.
—birchbark n. (1643, American English).

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:127 COLUMN:2 -->

## bird
bird n. 1353 bird, variant of brid (before 1200, in An-
crene Riwle, the form predominating until the later
1400’s); found in Old English brid young fowl (probably
about 750, in Phoenix ); of uncertain origin, with no
corresponding form in any other Germanic language.

## birth
birth n. About 1250 birthe, in a translation of The Story
of Genesis and Exodus; earlier burthe, burde (probably
before 1200, in Ancrene Riwle ) and birde (probably
about 1200, in The Ormulum ). The Middle English
forms were influenced by, and perhaps borrowed from,
a Scandinavian source (compare Old Icelandic burthr,
Old Swedish byrth birth), that affected the previously
Old English gebyrd birth (cognate with Old High Ger-
man giburt, modern German Geburt, and Gothic ga-
baurths), from Proto-Germanic *(3a)burdis, cognate
with Sanskrit bhrtis, from Indo-European *bhr-tis
(Pok.131).
The early spellings with d, found up to the mid-
1200’s, show how the Old English -byrd was displaced
by the Scandinavian forms with th.
—v. About 1250, from the noun. —birthday n. About
1384, in the Wycliffe Bible; earlier Old English byrd-
dzg.

## biscuit
biscuit n. hard cookie or cracker (now only in British
use). A spelling reborrowed from French in the 1800’s
to replace English bisket, developed in the 1500’s from
besquite (before 1338, in Mannyng’s Chronicle of
England ). Middle English besquite was borrowed from
Old French bescuit, literally meaning “‘twice-cooked”
in reference to how it was prepared (bes- twice, from
Latin bis + Old French cuit, past participle of cuire to
cook, from Vulgar Latin *cocere, from Latin coquere;

## bisect

## bishop

## bismuth
bismuth (biz’moth) n. reddish-white metallic chemical

## bison

## bland
bland adj. 1667, soft, mild, gentle, in Milton’s Paradise

## blank

roys, or mars,” is first recorded before 1661. —v. af-
ct with blight. 1695, from the noun. The figurative
nse of the verb first appeared in 1712, in Addison’s
ritings in The Spectator.

om (British) Type B-limp, a designation for “limp diri-
ible,” without a rigid internal structure, in early ex-
eriments, as opposed to the Type A-rigid lighter-

## blind
blind adj. Old English blind (about 725, in an early
version of Genesis). The word had both literal and
figurative meanings even in Old English. Its cognates
include Old Frisian and Old Saxon blind, Old High

pean *bhlendh-o-s (Pok.157). By some sources also re-
lated to Old English and Gothic blandan to mix; see
BLEND. —n. About 1200, in The Ormulum, from the
adjective. The meaning “covering for a window” is first
recorded in 1730. —v. Middle English blinden (about
1225, in Ancrene Riwle ); gradually, probably by influ-
ence of blind, adj., replacing earlier blenden (before
1200, in Layamon’s Chronicle of Britain ), developed
from Old English blendan. Middle English blinden is
cognate with Old Frisian blindia, modern Dutch ver-
blinden, Danish forblinde, Gothic gablindjan; also cog-
nate outside Germanic with Lettish b/éndu I see dimly,
and Old Slavic bledo go blindly. —blinder n. 1809,
American English, formed from blind, v. + -er', re-
placing earlier blind halter (1711).

## blindfold
blindfold v. 1526, in Tyndale’s translation of the Bible,
alteration (influenced by fold! wrap) of earlier blind-
feld, blindfelled (1483), past participle of blindfellen to
strike blind, to blindfold (probably before 1200, in An-
crene Riwle), developed from Old English (about
1000) geblindfellian (blind + gefeollan to strike down,
FELL!; an Anglian form corresponding to West Saxon
gefyllan ). —n. 1880, in Wallace’s Ben Hur, from the
