## dogma
dogma n. 1638, authoritative opinion, doctrine; used
earlier in the plural form dogmata (before 1600, in
Richard Hooker’s Ecclesiastical Polity); borrowed,
probably by influence of Middle French dogme, from
Latin dogma philosophical tenet, from Greek dogma
(genitive dégmatos) opinion, tenet, from dokein to
seem good, think; see DECENT. —dogmatic adj. 1678;
earlier dogmatical (1604); borrowed probably through
French dogmatique, from Latin dogmaticus, from
Greek dogmatikés, from dogma (genitive dogmatos )

—dogmatism n. 1603, borrowed from French dog-
matisme teaching of new doctrine, from Medieval
Latin dogmatismus, modeled after Late Greek dog-
matismos; from dogma (genitive dogmatos ); for suffix
see -ISM.

## doily

er), supposedly from Doiley surname of a dry goods

—vV. give out alms, charity. 1465, from the noun.

adj. mournful, sorrowful. Probably before 1300 diolful,

## donation

## donjon
donjon (dun’jan) n. Before 1325 dunjon large tower of

Don Juan (don win’) libertine, rake. 1854, in Thack-
eray’s The Newcomes, in allusion to Don Juan, name of
a legendary Spanish nobleman famous for his many
love affairs, popularized by Tirso de Molina, Spanish
dramatist (1571-1648), in E] Burlador de Sevilla The

## Donnybrook or donnybrook
Donnybrook or donnybrook n. 1852, scene of uproar
and disorder or great commotion; in allusion to Donny-
brook, the name of a suburb of Dublin, Ireland, once
famous for its annual fair, suppressed in 1855 for its
wild brawls.

## doom
doom n. Before 1325 dome, in Cursor Mundi, devel-
oped from Old English (about 725) dom law, judgment,
trial, sentence, condemnation; cognate with Old Fri-
sian and Old Saxon dom statute, law, judgment, Old
High German tuom, Old Icelandic domr judgment, de-

cognate with Greek thdmés heap, and Sanskrit dhaman
site, dwelling place, domain, rule. All of the various
forms of doom are from an Indo-European base *dhé-/
*dho-/dha- (Pok. 235) meaning that which is put or set
up, statute, ordinance.
The extended meaning of final fate, destruction,
ruin, death is first recorded in English about 1600, in
Shakespeare’s Sonnets.
—v. 1382 domen pronounce judgment on, from the
noun.
—doomsday n. Before 1200 domes dai, developed from

## door

developed from Old English duru (feminine) door (first

ic stem *dur-. The Old English forms are cognate with
Old Saxon dor gate, duri, pl., door, Old High German
tor gate (modern German Tor ), turi, p|., door (modern
German Tir ), Old Icelandic dyrr (feminine pl.) door,
and Gothic daur gate, from Proto-Germanic *duran;
and outside Germanic, cognate with Latin forés, pl.,

dviri, Lithuanian durys (nominative pl.), and Sanskrit
dvaras (nominative pl.), diras (accusative pl.) dvarau
(dual), from Indo-European *dhwor-/dhwor-/dhur-
(Pok. 278). The numerous cognates of door in the plural
suggest that doors consisted of two parts that slid or
pivoted together. —doorbell n. (about 1815, in Jane
Austen’s Persuasion )—doorknob n. (1846, in American
English) —doorway n. (1799, in Southey’s works)
—dooryard n. (about 1764, in American English)

## dope
dope n. 1807, American English, sauce, gravy, in Wash-

um, a thick, viscous substance when used for smoking
(1889). In the 1890’s the latter sense was extended to

tives dope fiend (1896), dope addict (1933), and a
preparation of drugs designed to influence a race-
horse’s performance (1900). Perhaps because the

## doubt
doubt v. Probably before 1200 duten, in Ancrene

1280); borrowed from Old French douter doubt, fear,
from Latin dubitare hesitate, waver in opinion, related

## douche
douche (diish) n. jet of water applied to any part of the

ian doccia shower, conduit, from docciare to spray,
make jet forth, probably from doccione conduit, from
Latin ductidnem (nominative ductio ) a leading, from
duc-, stem of dicere to lead; see TOW! pull. —v. admin-
ister a douche. 1838, probably borrowed from French

## dough
dough n. About 1150 doh dough for bread or pastry;
later dogh, 1303, in Mannyng’s Handlyng Synne; devel-
oped from Old English (about 1000) dag. Old English
dag is cognate with Middle Low German déch dough,
Middle Dutch deech (modern Dutch deeg ), Old High
German teic (modern German Teig), Old Icelandic
deig (Swedish deg, Danish dej), and Gothic daigs
dough, from Proto-Germanic *daizaz, which is cognate

Oscan feihtiss (accusative plural) walls, Armenian déz
heap, and Sanskrit deha-s body; all from the Indo-Euro-
pean base *dheigh-/dhoigh- (Pok. 244), meaning to
knead dough or work clay.
Though the spelling with g appeared by the 1300’s,
dow was acommon spelling up to the late 1500’s when
the modern spelling is first recorded in 1596, in Shake-
speare’s The Taming of the Shrew.
The slang meaning of money is first recorded in
American English in 1851.
—doughnut n. 1809, American English, in Washington
Irving’s Knickerbocker’s History of New York.

## doughty
doughty (dou’té) adj. Probably before 1200 duhti brave,
strong, in Layamon’s Chronicle of Britain; later douhti
(probably before 1300); developed from Old English
(1030) dohtig and dyhtig able, strong, valiant (about
725, in Beowulf). The later dohtig is probably an alter-

worthy) of earlier dyhtig, cognate with Middle Low
German and Middle Dutch duchtich doughty (modern
Dutch duchtig ), Middle High German tuhtec able, use-
ful (modern German ttichtig capable), from Proto-Ger-
manic *duHtiz4s, adjective to the noun *duHtiz (Old

are found in Old High German tugan be worthy, Old

The spelling with g began to appear in the 1300’s and

## dour
dour adj. Before 1350 (in northern dialect) severe;
later, 1375 (Scottish), in John Barbour’s The Bruce,

related to ENDURE. Dour meaning stubborn, gloomy,
sullen, is first recorded in English about 1470.

## douse

over; perhaps from an earlier verb douse to strike,
punch (1559). The word is probably related to Middle
Dutch dossen or early modern Dutch doessen beat
with force and noise.

## dove
dove n. Probably before 1200 duve (also in the place
name Duvebrigge, 1150); probably developed from
Old English dife-, in dufe-doppa dabchick, a water
bird; cognate with Old Saxon duba dove, Middle Dutch
dave (modern Dutch duif), Old High German tuba
(modern German Taube dove, pigeon), Old Icelandic
dufa (Swedish duva, Danish due ), and Gothic -dubd (in
hraiwa-dabo turtledove), from Proto-Germanic
*dubon, from Indo-European *dheubh-/dhubbh- dark,
(Pok. 264). —dovecote n. (1200) —dovetail n. 1565-73,
a joint in carpentry. —v. 1657, to fit together.

## dowager
dowager n. widow who holds title or property from her
husband. 1530 douagier, in letters of Palsgrave, later
dowager (1542); borrowed from Middle French doua-
gere, douagiere, from douage dower, from douer en-
dow, from Latin dotare, from dos (genitive dotis)
DOWRY; for suffix see -ER!. The meaning of an elderly,
dignified lady is first recorded in English in Dickens’

## dowdy
dowdy n. poorly dressed woman. 1581, probably a
diminutive form of earlier doue poorly dressed woman
(about 1338); of uncertain origin. —adj. poorly dressed,

## dowel

(of a cask), related to Old High German tubili plug
(modern German Dobel, Dibel peg, plug, dowel), cog-
nate with Greek typhoi wedges, from Indo-European

or bolt of wood is first recorded in English in 1794.
down! adv. to a lower place. Before 1275 doun, devel-
oped from an Old English word element -dtine- (before

sor ). —downcast adj. (about 1303, in Mannyng’s Hand-
lyng Synne) —downer n. depressant drug. (1968,

## down’
down’ n. rolling, grassy land. About 1300 doune hil
Layamon’s Chronicle of Britain (earlier 1254, in ;
name); developed from Old English dan hill (661
the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle), cognate with Old I
dan citadel, fortress, Old Welsh din fortress, hill fe
from Indo-European *dhano- (Pok. 263). English te
(Old English tun fort, enclosure, town, with t for Ce
d) and related words are based on very early borr
ing from this Celtic group.
In other Germanic languages Old English dan is<
nate with a group of words whose meaning is restric
to dune or sandbank, including Old Frisian dane, |
Saxon duna, Middle Dutch dunen (modern Du
duin ), Middle Low German dune, and Old Icelar
dunn DOWN?. Doublet of DUNE.

## dowry
dowry n. Before 1338 dowarye widow’s share of
husband’s property, in Mannyng’s Chronicle
England; later, dowarie property a bride brings to
marriage (before 1387, in Trevisa’s translation of I
den’s Polychronicon ); borrowed from Anglo-Fre
dowarie, Old French douaire, from Medieval Li
dotarium, from Latin dds (genitive dotis ) dowry,
lated to donum a giving, gift; see DONATION; for su
see -RY. —dower n. Before 1387, widow’s share of
husband’s property, and property a bride brings to
marviage, in Trevisa’s translation of Higden’s P
chronicon; borrowed from Old French douaire,
DOWRY. The original distinction in meaning, if th
was one intended, was soon lost, and is only rece!
maintained in English.

## dowse
dowse v. use a divining rod to locate water, etc., unt
ground. 1691 deusing rod, in Locke’s correspondet
later dowse (1838), of uncertain origin; perhaps a.
lect term, possibly from south England.

## doxology
doxology (doksol’ajé) n. hymn or statement prai
God. 1649, borrowed through French doxologie, o1
rectly from Medieval Latin doxologia, from Greek ¢
ologia, from doxolégos praising, glorifying, from a
glory, praise, from dokein to seem good, seem, th
see DECENT; for suffix see -LOGY.

## doyen
doyen (doi’en) n. 1422, leader of ten; borrowed fi
Middle French doyen, from Old French deien; see
doublet DEAN. The modern meaning of the sei
member of a group is first recorded in 1670 and 1
have been a reborrowing from French. —doye
(doi’en) n. 1905, female doyen, borrowed from Fre:
doyenne (feminine of doyen), from Middle Frer
from Old French deien.

## doze
doze v. sleep lightly. 1693; earlier, make drowsy, stu
fy, bewilder (1647); probably borrowed from a S
dinavian source (compare Old Icelandic disa be qu
doze, also Middle High German doésen be quiet, sh
ber, daesen to scatter); see DIZZY. —n. 1731, from
verb.

## pn
pn n. Probably before 1300 doseyn group of twelve,
yng Alisaunder; borrowed from Old French do-
le, dozaine a dozen, twelve (douze, doze twelve +
from Latin -anus). Old French douze (pro-
inced diidza ) is from Latin duodecim, altered from
ler duodicem by influence of decem, (duo TWO +
pm TEN).
» adj. colorless, dull. 1775, dull brown; earlier drab-
lur’d (1768), and drapp-colour (1686), the color of
> or drab cloth (1541); borrowed from Middle

).

## thma
thma (drak’mo) n. 1 principal silver coin of the an-
t Greeks. 1579-80, in Thomas North’s translation of
jarch’s Lives. 2 a small ancient Greek weight, 1527.
h senses in modern English were borrowed from
n drachma, from Greek drachmé and both re-

he Wycliffe Bible; 2) the ancient weight, before
8, in Trevisa’s translation of Bartholomew’s De Pro-

gma, drama, from Latin drachma, from Greek

## ft
ft n. 1552, possibly 1543, a privy; later, extract of
illation (1576), and plan, sketch (1579); spelling vari-
‘of earlier draught from drahte (probably before
0, in Layamon’s Chronicle of Britain ); developed
bably from Old English *dreaht, *draeht (compare
English dragan, v., to DRAW, and the cognates, Old
h German traht a carrying, Old Icelandic drattr a
ing, a drawing, and Middle Dutch dracht, from

ulling is first recorded probably before 1200 in ref-
nce to drawing in of nets for fishing or catching
. The sense of the act of drinking in one swallow
so first recorded probably before 1200. Later mean-
s include a rough copy of a writing (before 1382) and
flow of a current of air (1768-74). —v. 1714, select
some special purpose; from the noun. The sense of
ting a rough copy of a letter, etc., is first recorded
'828. —draftee n. military conscript. 1866, Ameri-
English, formed from English draft + -ee.
he form draft is a spelling reflecting the shift in

## B
B v. 1440 draggen draw or pull, in Promptorium
vulorum; borrowed from a Scandinavian source
mpare Old Icelandic draga ) or perhaps a dialectal
lant of drawen (Old English dragan ) to DRAW. —n.
9-40, heavy harrow; earlier, a dragnet (1300-01);
rowed from a Scandinavian source (compare Swed-
dragg grapnel, Icelandic drag-net dragnet), or per-
s developed from Old English (about 1000) draege
gnet; related to dragan DRAW. The slang sense of an
oying, boring person or thing, is first recorded in
3, probably an extension of the earlier meaning of
ething heavy or unmoving acting as an impedi-
at (1708). —dragnet n. Old English dreg-net, about
Oin 4"Ifric’s Glossary (drege drag, dragnet, related
lragan DRAW + net).

## ggle
ggle v. 1513, make or become wet or dirty, as by

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:331 COLUMN:2 -->
dragging through mud or water; apparently a frequen-
tative form of DRAG; for suffix see -LE°. The meaning
of lag behind, straggle, is first recorded in 1577.

## dragon
dragon n. Before 1250 dragun huge serpent; later,
mythical fire-breathing monster (about 1250), and as a
surname Dragun (1165-66); borrowed from Old
French dragon, learned borrowing from Latin draco-
nem (nominative draco ) serpent, dragon, from Greek
drakon (genitive drakontos ) serpent, seafish, literally,
the one with the (deadly) glance, from a lost noun *drak
glance (later -dra ), cognate with Sanskrit drs- glance,
and related to Greek dérkesthai to flash or gleam (like
the eye), see clearly, look at or on, from Indo-European
derk-/drk- (Pok. 213). —dragonfly n. (1626, in Francis
Bacon’s Sylva Sylvarum )

## dragoon
dragoon (dragiin’) n. 1622, mounted soldier armed with
a kind of carbine or musket; borrowed from French
dragon carbine or musket, dragoon, literally, dragon,
from Old French; see DRAGON; for suffix see -OON. The
soldier was so called because the carbine or musket he
carried “breathed fire” like a dragon. —v. to force or
drive to something or some end. 1689, from the noun.

## drain
drain v. Before 1398 dreynen, strain or filter (a liquid),
in Trevisa’s translation of De Proprietatibus Rerum ;
later dreyn to draw off a liquid (1440); developed from
Old English (about 1000) dréahnian, from Proto-Ger-
manic *drauzndjanan, apparently from the root
*drau3- related to dryge DRY. The word seems to have
disappeared from use shortly after the Old English pe-
riod, reappearing later in the 1500’s. The figurative
sense of to exhaust is recorded about 1660. —n. 1372,
from the verb (compare the compound dreinhole );
earlier as a surname Drene (1327). —drainage n. 1652,
formed from English drain + -age.

## drake
drake n. About 1300, male duck, in Havelok the Dane,
corresponding to Low German drake male duck, Ger-
man dialect drache, and the second element in Old
High German anutrehho (from *anut-trahho ), Middle
High German antrech (modern German Enterich ).
The first element anut-, ant-, -ent derives from Old
High German anut, enit duck (modern German Ente),
which is cognate with Middle Dutch aent (modern
Dutch eend ), and Old English zenid, ened duck, from
Proto-Germanic anidis; and outside Germanic with
Sanskrit 4ti-s aquatic bird, Greek nétta (earlier *natya )
duck, Latin anas, genitive anatis, Lithuanian 4ntis, Old
Slavic ati, from Indo-European *anat-/ant-/pt- (Pok.
41). The origin of the element -trehho in Old High
German anutrehho is apparently a West Germanic
*drako, of uncertain meaning. The full forms *en-
drake, *andrake expected in Old English are not found
there or in Middle English.

## dram
dram n. About 1373 dram and before 1398 dragme
small weight of apothecary’s measure; borrowed
through Anglo-Latin dragma, drama, and from Middle
French drame, dragme, both Anglo-Latin and Middle
French from Late Latin dragma, from Latin drachma
drachma, from Greek drachmé; see the doublet
DRACHMA.
The figurative sense of a small amount, especially of
talent, is first recorded in English about 1425.

## drama
drama n. 1515 drame; later drama, in Ben Jonson’s
Epigrams (1616); borrowed from Late Latin drama
play, drama, from Greek drama (genitive dramatos )
play, action, deed, from dran to do, act, perform, cog-
nate with Lithuanian daryti to do, from Indo-European

*dera-/dra- to work (Pok. 212). —dramatic adj. 1589
drammatick, in Puttenham’s The Arte of English Poesi;
borrowed through Middle French dramatique, or di-
rectly from Late Latin dramaticus, from Greek
dramatikés of or pertaining to plays, from draéma (geni-
tive dramatos ) drama; for suffix see -IC. —dramatis per-
sonae (dram/atis perso’né) 1730, the characters of the
drama or play, in Henry Fielding’s The Temple Beau;
borrowed from New Latin dramatis personae, literally,
persons of the drama. —dramatist n. 1678, formed in
English from Greek dra4ma (genitive dramatos) +
English -ist. —dramatize y. 1780-83, formed in English
from Greek drama (genitive dramatos ) + English -ize.

## drape
drape v. Probably before 1400 draperen to decorate
with cloth hangings; 1436 drapen to weave into cloth;
borrowed from Old French draper, from drap cloth.
—n. 1665, cloth or hangings, drapery; in some instances
borrowed from French drap cloth from Old French
drap, from Late Latin drappus cloth, possibly from
Gaulish, and in other instances, from the English drape,
v. The Gaulish word, found in the proper name Drap-
pus, is perhaps a variant of *drapus, cognate with San-
skrit drapi-s mantle, garment, from Indo-European
*drop-, root *drep- (Pok. 211). —drapery n. Probably
before 1325 draperie cloth, textile fabric; borrowed
from Old French draperie, from drap cloth; for suffix
see -ERY.

## drastic
drastic adj. Before 1691, (of medicines) acting with
force, in writings of Robert Boyle; borrowed from
Greek drastikés effective, from drastéon (thing) to be
done, from drdan to do, act, see DRAMA; for suffix see -IC.
The meaning of extreme, severe, is first recorded in
English in 1808, in Jeremy Bentham’s writings, possibly
suggested by the earlier English noun meaning of a
drastic medicine or severe purgative (1783), or bor-
rowed from the French meaning of drastique (1741).

## draw
draw v. pull, tug. Probably before 1200 drawen, in
Layamon’s Chronicle of Britain, and drahen, in An-
crene Riwle; developed from Old English dragan
(before 900, in Alfred’s translation of St. Gregory’s Pas-
toral Care), Old English dragan is cognate with Old
Saxon dragan, Old Frisian draga, drega, Old High Ger-
man tragan (modern German tragen ) to carry, bear,
with Old Icelandic draga to pull, draw, Gothic gadra-
gan to pull or carry together, from Proto-Germanic
*drazanan, and with Russian doréga and Polish droga
road or way, from Indo-European *dhragh- (root *dhe-
ragh-), Pok. 257. Though there are many constructions
and uses that reflect Latin trahere to pull or draw,
there is no etymological connection in form between
the Latin and Old English.
The meaning to trace (a line or figure) by drawing a
pencil or pen across a surface, is first recorded in Mid-
dle English probably about 1200.
The spelling change in Middle English from g to w
occurred because the sound represented by a + g of
the Old English dragan (in the stem drag-) developed
into the diphthong represented by the spelling aw in
Middle and modern English.
—n. Probably before 1300, in the compound drawe-
brigge; earlier, as a surname Draespere (1255); from
the verb. The meaning of the action of drawing, as in
shooting a bow, is first recorded about 1400-25, and
that of a tie in a game or contest, in the phrase draw
game, in 1825, in American English.
—drawbridge n. Probably before 1300 drawebrigge, in
Kyng Alisaunder; formed from Middle English draw,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:332 COLUMN:2 -->
drauht, etc. + brigge, brugge, etc. —drawer n. About
1385, person who draws (a sword); earlier, as a surname
Drahere (1327); formed from English drawen to draw
+ -er!. The sense of a box that can be drawn out of a
cabinet, desk, etc., is first recorded in 1580. The plural
drawers an undergarment, is first recorded in 1567.
—drawing n. Probably before 1300, the pulling of a
sword or bowstring, in Kyng Alisaunder; the meaning
of the act of making pictures, sketches, etc , is first
recorded in 1467, and of the picture itself, in 1688-89,
in Pepys’ Diary. —drawing room 1642, private room to
withdraw to; earlier drauht chambre (1435) and prob-
ably Anglo-French drawyng chaumbre (1410). Tradi-
tionally drawing room is given as a shortening of
withdrawing room (1591 with-drawing roem ); earlier
withdrawyng chambre (1392-93); however, withdraw-
ing room and drawing room seem to be parallel terms
into the late 1800’s when drawing room displaced the
other term.

## drawl
drawl v. 1597, craw] or draw along; 1598, speak slowly,
draw out words, in Shakespeare’s Merry Wives of
Windsor; borrowed probably from Middle Dutch dral-
en to linger, delay (also formed in Low German and
East Frisian dralen, in the same sense), apparently an
intensive form derived from the root of DRAW, v. —n.
1760, from the verb.

## dray
dray n. cart for hauling heavy loads. 1370 dreye wheel-
less sled for logs; later drey a little cart (1565-73); a
derivative form of Old English dragan to DRAW; re-
lated to Old English draege dragnet, and cognate with
Old Icelandic draga (pl. drogur ) timber trailed along
the ground. —drayman n. 1581, formed from English
dray + man.

## dread
dread v. Probably before 1200 dreden fear greatly, in
Ancrene Riwle and Layamon’s Chronicle of Britain;
shortened form of adreden; developed from Old
English (about 1000) adr&dan, a contraction of earlier
ondrédan counsel or advise against, fear (900, in a ver-
sion of Beowulf); and cognate with Old Saxon antdra-
dan and Old High German intratan fear, dread. Old
English ondr#dan was misconstrued in late Old
English as on + *dré@dan (of unknown origin), but is
properly analyzed as ond-, and-, cognate with Greek
anti against, ANTI + r@dan advise, cognate with Old
High German ratan to advise, counsel, Gothic garédan
reflect upon.
—n. Probably before 1200 dred, in Layamon’s Chroni-
cle of Britain, from dreden, v.

## dream
dream n. About 1250 drem, in The Story of Genesis and
Exodus; probably developed from Old English dréam
joy, music (influenced in meaning by Old Icelandic
draumr dream); cognate with Old Saxon drom merri-
ment, noise, Old Frisian dram dream, Old High Ger-
man troum (modern German Traum), Old Icelandic
draumr dream, from Proto-Germanic *draumaz, ear-
lier *drauzmas, and possibly with Old Saxon bidriogan
deceive, gidrog phantom, ghost, Old High German tri-
ogan deceive (modern German ftriigen ), Old High Ger-
man gitrog phantom, ghost, Old Icelandic draugr,
Middle Irish aurddrach phantom, ghost, Avestan druj-
lie, deception, druZaiti he lies, deceives, and Sanskrit
drihyati he seeks to damage, he hurts, from Indo-Euro-
pean *dhreugh-/dhrough-/dhrugh- (Pok. 270).
Though dream is not recorded in Old English with
the meaning of a vision, the number of Germanic cog-
nates of the same meaning strongly suggests that the
meaning existed in Old English, but that perhaps the

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:333 -->
