dered antimony. 1799 kohhel, borrowed from Arabic
koh, kuhl metallic powder, especially antimony. See
also ALCOHOL and ANTIMONY.

## kohlrabi
kohlrabi (k6l’ra’bé) n. vegetable with a stem shaped
like a turnip. 1807, borrowing of German Kohlrabi,
alteration of Italian cavoli rape, plural of cavolo rapa
kohlrabi (cavolo cabbage, from Latin caulis cabbage,
stalk of a plant and rapa turnip, from Latin rapa, see
RAPE? plant). Latin caulis is cognate with Greek kaulos
stem, from Indo-European *kaul-/kul- (Pok.537). The
alteration of Italian cavoli, cavolo to kohl- occurred
through translation of “cabbage” from Italian to Ger-
man.

## koine
koine (koi’na or koi’né) n. standard language or dialect
of a region in which different languages or dialects
exist. 1926, extended sense of earlier Koine the Greek
language commonly used during the Hellenistic period
(a modified Attic dialect, found in the Septuagint and
the New Testament); borrowed from Greek koiné in hé
koiné dialektos the common dialect, from koiné, femi-
nine singular of koinds common, earlier *komyé6s, cog-
nate with Latin cum with (and prefix com-), from
Indo-European adverb *kom near, along (Pok.612).

## kola or cola
kola or cola (k6’la) n. bitter brownish nut of an African
tree, used to give flavor to soft drinks. 1830, variant of
earlier cola (1795); of African origin (compare Temne
kola, Mandingo kolo).

## kolkhoz
kolkhoz (kolkoz’) n. collective farm in the Soviet Union.
1921, borrowing of Russian kolkhéz, acronym formed
from kol(lektivnoe) khoz(yaistvo) collective economy.
—kolkhoznik n. member of a kolkhoz. 1955, borrowing
of Russian kolkhéznik; formed from kolkhéz + -nik
personal suffix, -NIK.

## kook
kook (kik) n. Slang. odd, cranky, or crazy person. 1959,
American English; possibly a shortened and altered
form of CUCKOO. —kooky adj. Slang. odd, cranky, or
crazy. 1959, American English; formed from English
kook + -y'.

## kopeck or kopek
kopeck or kopek (k6’pek) n. Russian coin. 1698 copec,
1716 copeck, borrowed from Russian kopéika, diminu-
tive of kop’yé lance, spear; so called because kopecks
minted from 1535 to 1719 bore a figure of Czar Ivan
IV with a lance in his hand.

## Koran
Koran (koran’) n. sacred book of the Moslems. 1625
Core, 1735 Koran; borrowed from Arabic gor’an, qur-

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:602 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: kosher | 570 | kung | fu -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:602 COLUMN:1 -->
‘an a reading, recitation, book, from the root of qgara’a
he read, recited.

## kosher
kosher adj. right or fit according to Jewish law. 1851,
borrowing of Yiddish kosher, from Hebrew kasher fit,
proper, lawful. The informal meaning of legitimate,
correct, proper, was first recorded in Farmer and Hen-
ley’s Slang and Its Analogues (1896, though perhaps
earlier as this extended sense has been known in Ger-
man student slang since 1737). —v. prepare (food) ac-
cording to Jewish law. 1892 in Zangwill’s Children of
the Ghetto; from the noun (influenced by Yiddish kash-
ern make kosher, from Hebrew kashér).

## kowtow
kowtow (kou’tou’) n. act of slavish submission. 1804
koo-too Chinese custom of touching the ground with
the forehead to show respect or submission, borrowing
of Chinese k‘o-t‘ou, literally, knock the head. The
meaning of an act of slavish submission is first recorded
in 1834. The current spelling is found in 1864. —v.
show slavish submission to, fawn, truckle. 1826, in Ben-
jamin Disraeli’s Vivian Grey; from the noun.

## Kremlin
Kremlin n. citadel of Moscow, the seat of the Soviet
government. 1662 Cremelena, borrowed from Old
Russian kremlini; later Kremelin (1796), borrowed
from earlier German Kremelin (now Kreml after mod-
ern Russian kreml’ ). The Old Russian kremlini, adj.,
derived from kremii citadel, fortress, related to kréma
slice, kremén’ flint.
The spelling Kremlin (without second medial e) ap-
peared in 1833, probably influenced by French Krem-
lin. The application of the name to the Soviet
government, is first recorded in H. G. Wells’ The Shape
of Things to Come (1933).
—Kremlinology n. study of the Soviet government and
its policies. 1958, formed from English Kremlin +
-ology study of, variant of -logy.

## krill
krill n. small shrimplike crustacean. 1907, borrowed
from Norwegian kril small fry of fish.
Kriss Kringle (kris’ kring’gal) Santa Claus. 1830, Ameri-
can English; borrowed from dialectal German Christ-
kind] Christmas gift (1792); literally, little Christ child,
diminutive of Christkind Christ child; see KINDERGAR-
TEN.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:602 COLUMN:2 -->

## krypton
krypton (krip’ton) n. inert gaseous element. 1898, bor-
rowing of Greek kryptén, neuter of kryptés hidden; see
CRYPT; so called from its being a rare gas, forming a
minute part of the atmosphere. The term was coined
by its discoverers, the British chemists Sir William
Ramsay, 1852-1916, and M.W. Travers.

## kudos
kudos (kii’dos) n. praise, accolade. 1831 (implied earlier
in kudos“d praised, used by Southey in 1799); borrowed
from Greek kydos glory, fame, renown, cognate with
koein notice, hear, Sanskrit kavi-s wise, and Latin cav-
ére watch out for, from Indo-European * keu-/kowa-/
ku- (Pok.587).
Kudos was originally a singular noun in English, as it
was in Greek, but because of the final -s it came to be
construed as a plural, which led to the appearance in
1941 of the singular form kudo, derived by back forma-
tion from kudos.
Ku Klux Klan (ki’ kluks’ klan’) secret society of militant
white supremacists that arose in the southern United
States after the Civil War. 1867 Kuklux Klan, American
English; formed in English supposedly from alteration
of Greek kyklos circle + English clan.

## kulak
kulak (kiilak’ or kii/lak) n. well-to-do Russian peasant
farmer or trader. 1886, borrowing of Russian kulak,
literally, fist, (figuratively) rich peasant, from Turkic
kulak fist (kol hand + diminutive suffix -ak). After the
Russian revolution kulak referred to peasant farmers
who were generally landowners opposed to Soviet col-
lectivization.

## kumiss
kumiss (kii’mis) n. fermented mare’s or camel’s milk.
1607, borrowed from Russian kumys, from Turkic
kumyz, kymys; related to kymmak to mix.

## kumquat
kumquat (kum’kwot) n. yellow fruit somewhat like a
small orange. 1699 camquit, from Chinese (Cantonese)
kamkwat (kam golden + kwat orange). The current
spelling is first recorded in 1870.
kung fu (kung’ fii’) Chinese method of fighting without
weapons, similar to karate. 1966, borrowing of dialectal
Chinese kung fu, literally, boxing method.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:603 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: 571 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:603 COLUMN:1 -->

## la
la n. sixth note of the musical scale. Before 1300, bor-
rowed, probably through Italian, from Medieval Latin
la, from the initial syllable of Latin Jabii of the lip, the
word sung to this note in the Hymn for St. John the
Baptist’s day; see GAMUT.

## laager
laager (li’gar) n. camp or encampment, especially one
protected by a circle of wagons. 1850 Jager, in R.G.
Cumming’s Hunter’s Life in South Africa; borrowed
from earlier Afrikaans Jager, probably from German
Lager camp, bed, couch, LAIR. Compare STALAG.
In modern Afrikaans the word is Jaer, corresponding
to modern Dutch Jeger. The spelling Jaager (probably
influenced by Afrikaans and Dutch Jaag layer) ap-
peared in English in 1881. The transferred military
sense of any defensive position protected by a circle of
armored vehicles, is first recorded in 1941.
—v. encamp in a laager. 1879, from the noun.

## lab
lab n. Informal. 1895, short for LABORATORY.

## label
label n. Probably about 1300 Jable narrow band with
pendants on a coat of arms, in Sir Bevis of Hamtoun;
borrowed from Old French Jabel ribbon, fillet, fringe,
possibly from Frankish (compare Old High German
lappa flap; see LAP! part of a garment). The meaning
of a strip of material attached to a document to hold an
appended seal is first recorded in Wycliffe’s writings
before 1400; the more generalized meaning of a tag or
sticker is found as early as 1679. —v. put or write a label
on. 1601, in Shakespeare’s Twelfth Night; from the
noun.

## labial
labial adj. of the lips. 1594, borrowed from Medieval
Latin Jabialis having to do with the lips, from Latin
labium Lip. —n. Phonetics. sound made by nearly clos-
ing or rounding the lips. 1668, from the adjective.

## labile
labile (1a’bal) adj. changeable, unstable. 1447 labyl (of
the mind) wandering, forgetful; borrowed from Middle
French Jabile, or directly from Latin Jabilis slipping,
fleeting, transient, from /4bi to slip, glide, fall; see LAP!
flap. The meaning of unstable appeared in Florio’s
translation of Montaigne’s Essays (1603). —lability n.
changeableness, instability. 1646, formed from English
labile + -ity.

## labium
labium (la’béam) n. Biology. lip or liplike part. 1597
(plural Jabia ); borrowing of Latin Jabium LIP.

## labor
labor n. Before 1325 Jabour task, project; later, exer-
tion, toil, work (before 1375); borrowed from Old
French Jabour, learned borrowing from Latin labor
toil, pain, possibly related to /abi to slip, glide, fall; see
LAP!. The spelling Jabor is found in Middle English as
early as 1377. The sense of physical exertions of child-
birth, was introduced from Latin in Spenser’s Epi-
thalamion (1595). —v. to work, toil. Before 1376
labouren; also laboren (1387, in a version of Piers Plow-
man); borrowed from Old French labourer, laborer,
learned borrowing from Latin Jabdrare to work, toil,
suffer, be in distress, from Jabor toil, pain. —labored
adj. (1579, in Spenser’s The Shepheardes Calender )
—laborer n. (probably before 1350) —laborious adj.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:603 COLUMN:2 -->
Before 1393, diligent or industrious, in Gower’s Con-
fessio Amantis; later, requiring hard work, burdensome
(about 1415, in Chaucer’s Canterbury Tales); bor-
rowed through Old French Jaborieux, and directly
from Latin Jaboridsus full of labor, toilsome, from Jabor
toil, pain; for suffix see -IOUS. —labor-saving adj. (about
1776, in Adam Smith’s writings) —labor union (1866,
American English)

## laboratory
laboratory n. 1605, borrowed from Medieval Latin
laboratorium a place for labor or work, from Latin Jab-
Orare to work, LABOR; for suffix see -ORY.

## labyrinth
labyrinth (lab’arinth) n. maze. 1548, in the figurative
sense of a confusing, complicated state of affairs; earlier
laberynthe maze (1408) and Jaboryntus (about 1380, in
Chaucer’s House of Fame ); both forms in allusion to
the labyrinth of Greek mythology built to contain the
Minotaur; borrowed from Latin Jabyrinthus, from
Greek Jabyrinthos, a word of the pre-Greek culture
designating a structure that was Egyptian, Cretan, or of
Asia Minor. Some have compared the Greek word to
Lydian (an Anatolian language related to Hittite) /4b-
rys, meaning a double-edged axe, symbol of royal
power; hence a labyrinth may have been a royal struc-
ture or palace. —labyrinthine adj. 1747, formed from
English labyrinth + -inel.

## lac
lac (lak) n. resinous substance deposited on trees by
certain insects. 1618, perhaps borrowed from Middle
French lJacce, but found also in Middle English as lacca
(probably about 1425, in a translation of Chauliac’s
Grande Chirurgie ); borrowed from Hindi Jakh, from
Sanskrit /aksa, perhaps originally so called from the
color of salmon (Indo-European *laksos, Pok.653). Re-
lated to LACQUER and LAKE?. See also SHELLAC.

## lace
lace n. Before 1325 Jace cord for tying, in Cursor Mun-
di; also laas (before 1382, in the Wycliffe Bible), devel-
oped from earlier Jaz (about 1230, in Ancrene Riwle );
borrowed from Old French Jas, Jaz a net, noose, string,
from Latin Jaqueus, a trapping and hunting term
meaning noose, snare; from Indo-European *lak-w-,
root */ék- a sprig or string (Pok. 673). Doublet of LASso.
The sense of a net of thread in an ornamental pattern
is first recorded in English in 1555. The earlier sense of
a thread or cord for tying is now retained chiefly in
reference to shoe or boot laces and string or cord to
draw clothing together.
—v. Probably before 1200 Jacen fasten with a lace, in
Ancrene Riwle; borrowed from Old French Jacier,
from Latin Jaqueare ensnare, from Jaqueus noose or
snare. Though the verb appears in the record of
English slightly before the noun, it is assumed that both
noun and verb were probably simultaneous borrowings
from Old French, though it is curious that the spelling
with c in the verb was so late in appearing in the noun.
—lacy adj. 1804, formed from English lace + -y’.

## lacerate
lacerate v. tear roughly, mangle. Probably before 1425
laceraten, in a translation of Chauliac’s Grande Chirur-
gie; borrowed from Latin laceratus, past participle of

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:604 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: laches | lad | 572 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:604 COLUMN:1 -->
lacerare tear to pieces, mangle, from /Jacer torn, man-
gled, of uncertain origin; for suffix see -ATE!. —lacera-
tion n. 1597, borrowed perhaps through Middle French
lacération, from Latin Jacerationem (nominative Jacer-
atio ), from Jacerare lacerate; for suffix see -ATION.

## laches
laches (lach’iz) n. Law. negligence in the performance
of a duty. Before 1376 laches, lachesse laziness, negli-
gence, in a version of Piers Plowman; borrowed
through Anglo-French lachesse, Old French laschesse,
from lasche lax, lazy, from laschier let go, loosen; see
LUSH!, adj. The specific legal sense of negligence in
performing a duty is first recorded in English in 1574.
A transferred sense of inexcusable negligence is found
in Disraeli’s Coningsby (1844).

## lachrymal or lacrimal
lachrymal or lacrimal (lak’ramol) adj. of or producing
tears. Probably before 1425 lacrimal, in a translation of
Chauliac’s Grande Chirurgie; borrowed from Medieval
Latin Jacrimalis, from Latin lacrima tear (earlier Ja-
cruma ), Old Latin dacruma TEAR’, n.; for suffix see
-AL!. It is also probable that Jachrymal was borrowed,
in some instances, through Middle French Jachrymal,
lacrymal, the spelling ch arising from the practice of
substituting it for c before r in Latin words, such as in
anchor.

## lachrymose
lachrymose (lak’ramés) adj. tearful, mournful. 1661,
tearlike; later, tearful, sorrowful (1727, in Bailey’s Dic-
tionary ); borrowed from Latin Jacrimosus tearful, dole-
ful, from Jacrima tear, see LACHRYMAL; for suffix see
-OSE!.

## lack
lack n. shortage, need. Before 1300 lac, lakke; later lak
(about 1300); perhaps developed from an Old English
*lac; cognate with Middle Low German Jak lack, fault,
slack, loose, Old Frisian Jek disadvantage, damage,
lakia to oppose, dispute, and Old Icelandic Jakr lacking,
from Proto-Germanic */aka-; possibly also cognate with
Latin Jaxus loose, LAX, and Greek Jagaros slack, loose,
thin, and /égein leave off, cease, from Indo-European
*(s\lég-/(s)lag- (Pok. 959). If the word did not exist in
Old English, it was probably borrowed from Middle
Dutch Jac deficiency, fault, which may have reinforced
the Middle English form regardless of the existence of
an Old English */ac. —v. to want, need. Before 1225
lacen; later laken (about 1250), and Jacken (about 1325);
probably from the noun. —lackluster adj. dull and
drab. 1600, in Shakespeare’s As You Like It, formed
from English lack, v. + luster.

## lackadaisical
lackadaisical (lak’oda’zokal) adj. languid, lethargic, list-
less. 1768, affectedly languishing, in Sterne’s Sentimen-
tal Journey through France and Italy; formed from
English lackadaisy, interj., alas, alack (1748, in Smol-
lett’s works) + suffix -ical. Lackadaisy is an alteration of
the earlier lack-a-day (1695, in Congreve’s Love for
Love ), a shortened and altered form of the phrase
alack the day, first found in Shakespeare’s Romeo and
Juliet (1592). It has been suggested that perhaps the
shift in meaning to that of languid or lethargic was
influenced by words such as Jax and Jassitude.

## lackey
lackey n. male servant, footman. 1529, borrowed from
Middle French Jaquais, of uncertain origin. Middle
French Jaquais was probably borrowed from Old Pro-
vencal lacai, which must have come from Jecar glutton,
covetous, from Jecar to lick. The later Spanish lacayo,
alacayo mercenary, according to the scholar Coromi-
nas, probably derived from Basque alakairu, alokairu,
alokari salary, wages, income, from Latin Jocarium
rent, payment, and also possibly from Basque lekaio

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:604 COLUMN:2 -->
lackey, popular musician who plays for money, also
from Latin locarium.
The figurative sense of servile follower, toady, ap-
peared in English in 1588.
—v. serve as a lackey. 1568, from the noun.

## laconic
laconic (lakon’ik) adj. using few words, concise. 1583, of
or pertaining to Laconia or its inhabitants; 1589, in the
Laconian manner, brief, concise; a shortened form of
earlier laconical (1576), and possibly influenced by
Middle French Jaconique. Both the English and French
forms were borrowed, probably through Latin Laco-
nicus Laconian, from Greek Lakdénik6és, from Lak6én a
Laconian (person from the ancient district of Laconia
in southern Greece whose capital was Sparta); for suffix
SCE IG
Reference to the brevity of speech thought charac-
teristic of Laconians appears in the record of English as
early as 1570 in the form Laconism the habit or prac-
tice of imitating the Laconians in brevity of speech.

## lacquer
lacquer n. kind of varnish. 1673 lacker, in Marvell’s The
Rehearsal Transposed; borrowed from obsolete French
lacre a kind of sealing wax, from Portuguese Jacre, from
lacca resinous substance, lac, from Arabic lakk, from
Persian Jak, from Sanskrit /aksa; see LAC. The spelling
lacquer, appearing as Jaquer (1697), and both in-
fluenced by French Jaque lake? (a deep-red coloring
matter), is first recorded in the verb (1688). An earlier
meaning of Jacquer, in the sense of dye obtained from
lac, is recorded in Hakluyt’s Voyages (1579). Related to
LAC, LAKE?, and SHELLAC. —v. to coat with lacquer.
1687 lackered, participial adjective; 1688 Jacquer; from
the noun.

## lacrosse
lacrosse (lakrés’) n. game played with a ball and long-
handled rackets. 1718, in American English; borrowed
from Canadian French Ja crosse the game of lacrosse;
originally, the racket used in the game; literally, the
hooked stick, the crosier.

## lact-
lact- a form of Jacto- before vowels, as in Jactiferous.

## lactation
lactation n. 1668, act of suckling a baby; later, secretion
of milk (1857); borrowed perhaps through French lac-
tation, from Late Latin lactationem (nominative lacta-
tid ), from Latin Jactare suckle, from Jac (genitive lactis )
milk; for suffix see -ATION. —lactate v. to secrete milk.
1889, probably a back formation from lactation; for
suffix see -ATE!.

## lacteal
lacteal (lak’téal) adj. of or like milk, milky. 1658, in
Phillips’ Dictionary, formed in English as if borrowed
from Latin Jacteus, from lac (genitive lactis ) milk, see
GALAXY; for suffix see -AL!.

## lactic
lactic adj. of or from milk. 1790 lactic acid an acid
obtained from sour milk; borrowed from French lac-
tique, formed from Latin lactis (genitive of Jac milk) +
French -ique -ic.
lacto- a combining form meaning milk, as in lacto-
globulin, or lactic acid, as in lactobacillus. Borrowed
from Latin Jac (genitive Jactis ) milk; see GALAXY.

## lactose
lactose n. milk sugar. 1858, formed in English from
Latin Jactis (genitive of lac milk) + English suffix -ose?.

## lacuna
lacuna (lakyii’na) n. empty space, gap, blank. 1663, bor-
rowed from Latin Jacina hole or pit, from Jacus (geni-
tive lacus ) pond, LAKE!. Doublet of LAGOON.

## lad
lad n. Probably before 1300 Jadde foot soldier, in Kyng
Alisaunder; later, young male servant, man of low social
position, vagabond (about 1300, in Havelok the Dane );
and boy or youth (before 1338, in Mannyng’s Chronicle

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:605 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: ladder | 573 | lam -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:605 COLUMN:1 -->
of England ); possibly borrowed from a Scandinavian
source (compare Danish and Norwegian askeladd, liter-
ally, ash lad, referring to the youngest son in a folk tale
who pokes in the ashes, and Norwegian tusseladd pale,
insignificant-looking person, weakling; literally, fairy
lad,
In Old English Ladda is found as a surname, also in
early Middle English Laddedale Ladde’s dale (about
1160), but whether the Old English form is identical
with the Middle English form is unknown.
—laddie n. young lad, lad. 1546, formed from English
lad + -ie.

## ladder
ladder n. About 1175 Izddre; later laddere (probably
before 1300); developed from Old English hl#der
(971). The Old English form is cognate with Old Frisian
hlédere, hladder ladder, Middle Dutch Jéder (modern
Dutch leer, also ladder, from Frisian), Middle Low Ger-
man ledder, Old High German leitara (modern Ger-
man Leiter), and dialectal Danish lejre ladder, from
Proto-Germanic *Hlaidr-. Outside Germanic cognates
are found in Old Lithuanian Slité ladder, Greek klimax
(genitive klimakos ) ladder, klinein to incline, and San-
skrit Srayate leans on, from Indo-European *klei-/kloi-/
kli-/kli- (Pok.601). Compare UDDER.

## lade
lade v. to load. Probably about 1200 laden to draw
water, in The Ormulum; later, to load (about 1250);
developed from Old English hladan to load, heap, draw
water (about 725, in Beowulf). The Old English form
is cognate with Old Frisian hlada to load, Old Saxon
hladan, Middle Dutch and modern Dutch Jaden, and
Old Icelandic hladha, from Proto-Germanic *Hlad-;
also with Old High German hladan, ladan (modern
German laden ), and Gothic afhlathan, from Proto-Ger-
manic *H]ath-, from Indo-European *klo-t-, root *kla-
lay out, pile up (Pok.599). —laden adj. burdened, load-
ed. 1595, from Jaden, past participle of Jade to load.

## ladle
ladle n. About 1300 Jadel, developed from Old English
(before 1000) hizedel, from hladan to load, LADE; the
suffix -le expresses the sense of an appliance or tool, as
in thimble. The Old English hlzdel is ultimately from
Proto-Germanic *Hladl4s. —v. dip out. About 1532,
from the noun.

## lady
lady n. Before 1121 Jafdige female ruler; later lavedi,
levedi (about 1300), and J/adi (probably about 1350);
developed from Old English hlafdie mistress of a
household, wife of a lord; literally, one who kneads a
loaf or loaves (before 830); earlier hlz#fdige (about 750,
in Cynewulf’s Elene ), a compound of hlaf bread, LOAF!
+ -dige, related to d#ge breadmaker, maker of dough,
from dag DOUGH. —ladies’ man (1784, in Cowper’s
Tirocinium ) —ladies’ room (1880) —ladybird n. 1592,
sweetheart, in Shakespeare’s Romeo and Juliet; 1704, a
ladybug. —ladybug n. (1699) —ladylike adj. (1586)
—ladyship n. Probably before 1200 JIzefdischipe; later
ladyschip (probably about 1380); formed from Middle
English lafdige, lavedi, ladi lady + -schip(e) -ship.

## lag
lag v. 1530 move too slowly, fall behind, in Palsgrave’s
Lesclarcissement; developed from earlier Jag, n. the
last or hindmost person (1514), found in the Middle
English compound Jag-mon last man (probably about
1390, in Sir Gawain and the Green Knight ). The Mid-
dle English form was possibly borrowed from a Scan-
dinavian source (compare Norwegian dialect lagga go
slowly). —n. a lagging or falling behind. 1837, from the
verb. —laggard adj. lagging, falling behind. 1702, in
‘Nicholas Rowe’s Tamerlane; formed from English Jag,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:605 COLUMN:2 -->
v. + -ard; n. laggard person. 1808, in Scott’s Marmion;
from the adjective.

## lager
lager (la’gar) n. stored beer. 1855, American English,
short for Jager beer (1854), half translation of German
Lagerbier (Lager storehouse, bed, LAIR + Bier BEER).

## lagniappe or lagnappe
lagniappe or lagnappe (lan’yap) n. small gift given to a
customer with a purchase. 1849, American English;
borrowed from Louisiana French or directly from Hai-
tian Creole Jagniappe, from American Spanish Ja fiapa,
or la yapa the gift; fapa, yapa, from Quechua yapa
something given into the bargain, an extra.

## lagoon
lagoon n. 1612 Jaguna, later Lagune (1673), both forms
in reference to Italian places, especially around Venice;
borrowed through French Jagune, and directly from
Italian Jaguna pond, lake, from Latin lacuna pond, hole,
from lacus (genitive Jacus) pond, LAKE?; for suffixal
ending see -OON. Doublet of LACUNA. The spelling Ja-
goon is first recorded in 1750, in American English, and
its use was probably influenced by Spanish laguna.

## lair
lair n. About 1410 leire place where an animal takes
shelter, from earlier Jeir bed, couch (probably before
1200); developed from Old English Jeger act or place
of lying down (about 725, in Beowulf). The Old English
leger is cognate with Old Frisian Jeger situation, Old
Saxon Jegar bed, Middle Dutch Jégher, léghere act or
place of lying down (modern Dutch Jeger bed, camp),
Old High German Jegar bed, a lying down (modern
German Lager bed, lair, camp, storehouse), Old Icelan-
dic legr grave, nuptials (as a lying down together), from
Proto-Germanic */ezran, and Gothic ligrs bed, related
to Old English licgan to repose, LIE?. Outside German-
ic cognates are found in Latin Jectus and Greek léchos
bed, from Indo-European *legh- lie (Pok.658).

## laird
laird (lard) n. Scottish. landowner. Before 1325, north-
ern Middle English Javered; later, Scottish Jard (about
1450), northern variants of Jord, loverd LORD.
laissez faire (les‘afar’) | absence of regulation and in-
terference by government. 1825, borrowing of French
laissez faire let do (as one pleases), the slogan of French
economists of the 1700’s who opposed government
regulation of trade and industry (laissez, imperative
form of Jaisser to let, from Latin Jaxare to slacken, from
Jaxus slack or lax, and faire to do, from Latin facere to
do).

## laity
laity (la’até) n. the lay or ordinary class of people.
Before 1415 laite, in Wycliffe’s The Lantern of Light,
formed in Middle English from Jay? + -ity.

## lake’
lake’ n. body of water surrounded by land. Before 1121
lac; later lake (probably before 1300, in Cursor Mundi ),
in part developed from Old English lacu body of water
(944, in original charter of King Edmund J), and in part
borrowed from Old French Jac. Both Old English Jacu
and Old French Jac were borrowed from Latin lacus
(genitive Jacus ) pond or lake, a word cognate with Old
Irish loch lake, Greek /akkos pond, cistern, pit, and Old
Slavic Joky, from Indo-European *laku- (Pok.653). Cog-
nates in Germanic are found in Old Icelandic Jogr sea,
water, Old Saxon Jagu, and Old English Jagu, from
Proto-Germanic *lazus.
lake? n. deep-red or purplish-red coloring matter ob-
tained from lac. 1616, probably borrowed through
French Jaque, from Old Provengal Jaca, from Arabic
lakk; see LACQUER.

## lam
lam n. Slang. on the run, hurried escape, as in take it
on the lam or on the lam. 1897, from the verb meaning

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:606 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: lama | 574 | lamprey -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:606 COLUMN:1 -->
of run away; of unknown origin, sometimes compared
with Jam to beat (1589 in Jamback and 1637 in LAM-
BASTE), but no apparent connection can be established
semantically with the current sense of Jam hurried es-
cape.

## lama
lama (la’ma) n. Buddhist priest or monk in Tibet and
Mongolia. 1654, borrowed from Tibetan blama (with
unsounded b ). —lamasery (la’maser’é) n. monastery of
lamas. 1867, borrowed from French lamaserie (lama,
from Tibetan blama + -serie, probably from Persian
sarai inn, as found in the irregular formation of earlier
French caravanserai (1686).

## lamb
lamb n. Old English (about 858) Jamb; earlier lomb
(about 725; also found in Middle English before 1200).
The Old English forms are cognate with Old Frisian
lamb lamb, Old Saxon lamb, Middle Low German Jam,
Middle Dutch and modern Dutch Jam, Old High Ger-
man lamb (modern German Lamm), Old Icelandic
lamb (Swedish lamm, Danish Jam ), and Gothic lamb,
from Proto-Germanic *lambaz, without cognates out-
side Germanic. —v. give birth to a lamb. 1611, in Cot-
grave’s Dictionary; from the noun. —lambkin n. 1579,
little lamb, in Spenser’s The Shepheardes Calender;
later, young or dear person, in Shakespeare’s 2 Henry
IV (1597); formed from English Jamb + -kin. As a sur-
name, Lambkin appeared in Middle English as early as
1257. —lambskin n. (before 1400, in Lanfranc’s Science
of Surgery ).
lambaste (lambast’) y. Informal. to beat, thrash. 1637,
probably formed from English lam (1596, probably
borrowed from a Scandinavian source; compare Icelan-
dic Jama bruise, and Old Icelandic Jemja to beat, lame)
+ BASTE’ to thrash. The figurative meaning of scold or
denounce, appeared in 1886.

## lambda
lambda (lam‘doa) n. eleventh letter of the Greek alpha-
bet. About 1400, in Maundeville’s Travels, borrowing
of Greek lambda, from a Semitic source (compare He-
brew lamedh the twelfth letter of the Hebrew alpha-
bet, probably originally meaning ox-goad and formed
from the hieroglyph of such an instrument). Mostly
appearing in English in scientific usage, lambda is
found in such terms as Jambda point (physics, 1932),
lambda hyperon (nuclear physics, 1954), Jambda virus
(genetics, 1965), and as the symbol for a millionth of a
liter (chemistry, 1934).

## lambent
lambent adj. moving lightly over a surface, flickering,
shimmering. 1647, borrowed from Latin Jambentem
(nominative lambéns ), present participle of Jambere to
lick, see LAP’; for suffix see -ENT. The sense of shining
with a soft, clear light, is first recorded in Pope’s Elvira
to Abelard (1717), and that of playing lightly and bril-
liantly over a subject, in 1871.

## lame
lame adj. About 1175 Jame; developed from Old
English (about 750) Jama; cognate with Old Frisian Jam,
lom lame, Old Saxon Jamo, Middle Dutch and modern
Dutch lam, Old High German Jam (modern German
lahm ), Old Icelandic Jami, modern Scandinavian Jam
from Proto-Germanic */amon. Outside Germanic cog-
nates are found in Middle Irish Jem foolish, insipid,
Lithuanian Jimti break down, Old Slavic lomiti to
break, Russian Jom fragments, and possibly also in
Greek ndélemés without pause, unceasingly, from Indo-
European */em-/Jom-/Im- break; soft (Pok.674). —v.
make lame, cripple. About 1300 lamen to injure,
wound, disable, in Havelok the Dane; from the adjec-
tive. The sense of to disable in the foot or leg, to cripple,

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:606 COLUMN:2 -->
is first recorded in 1460. —lame duck 1761, disabled
person or thing, in Walpole’s letters; later, in American
English, a public official who has been defeated for
reelection and is serving the last part of his term, in
Congressional Globe (1863).
lamé (lama’) n. rich fabric made of metal threads, espe-
cially ones of gold or silver. 1922, borrowing of French
lamé a fabric, type of thread; literally, laminated, from
lame metal leaf, from Latin Jamina LAMINA.

## lamella
lamella (lomel’s) n. thin plate, scale, or layer, especially
of flesh or bone. 1678, borrowing of Latin Jamella,
diminutive of /amina thin plate, LAMINA.

## lament
lament v. express grief, mourn. Before 1450 Jementen
to regret, be sorry for; later Jament express grief (1530,
in Palsgrave’s Lesclarcissement ); borrowed from Mid-
dle French Jamenter to moan, bewail, and probably
directly from Latin /Jamentari, from Jamentum a wail-
ing, related to Jatrare to bark or cry, and cognate with
Lithuanian /6ti to bark, and Greek Jéros chatter, from
Indo-European */a- a crying sound (Pok. 650). It is also
possible that in some instances Jament is a back forma-
tion from earlier Jamentation. —n. 1591, in Shake-
speare’s 1 Henry VI; borrowing of Middle French
lament, and probably borrowed directly from Latin
Jamentum. Also possibly a noun use of the verb in
English. —lamentable adj. Before 1420, in Lydgate’s
Troy Book; borrowing of Middle French Jamentable,
and borrowed directly from Latin Jamentabilis, from
Jamentari to lament; for suffix see -ABLE. —lamentation
n. Before 1382 lamentacioun, in the Wycliffe Bible,
borrowing of Old French lamentation, and borrowed
directly from Latin /amentatiOnem (nominative lamen-
tatio ), from Jamentari to jament; for suffix see -ATION.
The earliest recorded use in Middle English is in refer-
ence to the Lamentations of Jeremiah.

## lamina
lamina (lam‘ono) n. thin plate, scale, or layer. 1656, in
Blount’s Glossographia; borrowing of Latin /Jamina thin
piece of metal or wood, plate, leaf, layer; of uncertain
origin. —laminate v. 1665, to beat or roll into a succes-
sion of bonded plates or layers; formed from English
lamina + -ate!. Laminated is first recorded in 1931,
and laminated plastic in 1938. —lamination n. 1676,
formed from English Jaminate + -ion.

## lamp
lamp n. About 1200 Jampe oil lamp, light; borrowing of
Old French Jampe, from Latin Jampas, from Greek
Jampas torch, lamp, beacon, meteor, light, from ]4m-
pein to shine; cognate with Old Irish Jassair flame, Old
Prussian Jopis flame, Lithuanian /6pé light, Hittite Jap-
to glow, be hot, and in Germanic with Old Icelandic
leiptr lightning, from Indo-European */4 (1)p-/laip-/
lap- shine, burn (Pok.652). —lamplight n. (probably
about 1380) —lamppost n. (1790)

## lampoon
lampoon n. piece of satirical writing, speech, etc. in-
tended to ridicule or mock. 1645, in John Evelyn’s
Memoirs; borrowed from French lampon, of uncertain
origin; possibly from lamponner, see the verb. It has
also been suggested that the word in French may de-
rive from Jampons let us drink (a popular refrain of
satirical drinking songs of the 1600’s), from Jamper to
drink or guzzle, a nasalized form of Japer to lap, of
imitative origin. —v. ridicule or mock in a lampoon.
Before 1657, in Lovelace’s Poems, either from the
noun in English, or borrowed from French Jamponner
scoff or jeer at, from Middle French Jamponner (used
by the French chronicler Brantéme).

## lamprey
lamprey n. eel-like water animal with a large, round

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:607 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: lanai | languor | 575 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:607 COLUMN:1 -->
mouth. About 1300 Jaumprei, in Havelok the Dane;
earlier as a surname Lampre (1199); borrowed from
Old French Jampreie, from Medieval Latin Jampreda.
The Medieval Latin word may be an alteration (in-
fluenced by Latin Jambere to lick) of Late Latin nau-
preda, nauprida lamprey, perhaps a Gaulish
borrowing; or it may have an uncertain relationship to
Late Latin Jampetra lamprey; literally, lick rock, from
Latin Jambere to lick + petra (from Greek pétra ) rock,
as is traditionally explained in reference to their habit
of attaching themselves to rocks by their suckerlike
mouths. Doublet of LIMPET.

## lanai
lanai (lani’) n. porch, veranda. Before 1869, borrowing
of Hawaiian /anai shed, shelter, booth, porch. An ear-
lier spelling, ranai, is recorded in 1823 and 1826.

## lance
lance n. Probably before 1300 Jaunce horseman’s spear,
in Arthour and Merlin; earlier as surname Lance (1198-
99); borrowed from Old French Jance, from Latin Jan-
cea light spear, possibly of Celtic origin. —v. pierce
with a lance. Probably about 1300 Jauncen to throw,
thrust, pierce, in The Romance of Guy of Warwick;
later Jancen (before 1338, in Mannyng’s Chronicle of
England ); borrowed from Old French lancier, from
Late Latin Janceare wield a lance, pierce with a lance,
from Latin Jancea spear. Doublet of LAUNCH! throw
forward. —lancer n. 1590, in Marlowe’s Tamburlane
the Great; formed from English Jance + -er'.

## lancet
lancet n. small, sharp-pointed surgical knife. 1392 Jaun-
cet, later lancet (probably before 1425); borrowed from
Old French Jancette small lance, diminutive of lance
LANCE; for suffix see -ET.

## land
land n. Old English land, lond (about 725, in Beowulf);
cognate with Old Frisian Jand, lond land, Old Saxon
land, Middle Dutch and modern Dutch Jand, Old High
German Jant (modern German Land), Old Icelandic,
modern Scandinavian, and Gothic land, from Proto-
Germanic */andan. Outside Germanic cognates are
found in Old Irish Jand open space or area, Middle
Welsh Ilan enclosure, yard, French Jande moor, heath
(from Gaulish *Janda ), Old Prussian lindan (accusative)
valley, Old Slavic Jedina heath, desert, Byelorussian
lyada cleared land, and Czech (lada, lado fallow land,
from Indo-European */endh-/londh- (Pok.675).—v.
Probably about 1225 Jonden bring to land, set ashore,
in King Horn; later landen (probably before 1400, in
Morte Arthur ); from the noun.
The meaning of arrive at a place or position (as in
Fortune landed him in France or to land in bankrupt-
cy ) is first recorded in Jeremy Taylor’s works, in 1649,
and the more specific sense of to alight on the ground
after a leap, etc., is found in 1693. The informal sense
of get or obtain (as in to land a job) is first recorded in
1854, developed from the earlier meaning, in angling,
of bring (a fish) to land, to catch, net (1613).
—landed adj. owning land. About 1440 Jondid, in
Promptorium Parvulorum; formed from Middle
English Jond land + -ed?, possibly by influence of ear-
lier Old English gelandod landed, past participle of
*Jandian to have land. —landfall n. (1627, in Captain
John Smith’s The Seaman’s Grammar) —landing n.
Before 1420, disembarkation, in Lydgate’s Troy Book;
later, a landing place (about 1450). —landlady n.
(before 1536, in Tyndale’s writings) —landlord n. 1275,
as a surname; formed from Middle English /and + lord.
—landlubber n. Before 1700; formed from English land
+ lubber. —landmark n. About 1400 lJondes mark
‘boundary; formed from Middle English Jondes, geni-

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:607 COLUMN:2 -->
tive of Jond land + mark. —landowner n. (before 1733)
—landslide n. 1838, American English; the figurative
sense of an overwhelming electoral victory is first re-
corded in 1888, in the New York Times. —landsman n.
Probably before 1200 Jondesman; formed from Middle
English londes, genitive of Jond land + man. —land-
ward adv., adj. (probably about 1450).

## landau
landau (lan’d6) n. four-wheeled carriage with a top
made in two parts that can be folded back. 1743, from
Landau, a town in Germany, where this vehicle was
first made. The word was applied in English before
1934 to an automobile with a top similar to that of the
carriage.

## landscape
landscape n. 1603, a picture of natural inland scenery;
borrowed from Dutch landschap, from Middle Dutch
landscap region (land LAND + -scap -SHIP). The bor-
rowing of Middle Dutch Jandscap is a replacement and
cognate of Old English lJandscipe region (though no
such term appears in the record of Middle English).
The Middle Dutch is also a cognate of Old Saxon Jand-
scepi, Old High German Jlantscaf (modern German
Landschaft ), and Old Icelandic Jandskapr. The general
sense of inland natural scenery appeared in 1606, fol-
lowed by that of a view of inland scenery, in Milton’s
L’Allegro (1632). —v. arrange or embellish to form a
landscape. 1927, from the noun. An earlier meaning of
represent as a landscape, depict, appeared in Brown-
ing’s The Ring and the Book (1868).

## lane
lane n. Probably about 1300 Jane, in Sir Bevis of Ham-
toun; earlier, as a surname (1176); found in Old English
(971) Jane, lanu narrow, hedged-in road or way; cog-
nate with Old Frisian Jane, Jone lane, Middle Dutch
Jane (modern Dutch Jaan), and Old Icelandic Jon
oblong hayrick, row of houses; of unknown origin.
lang syne, or langsyne (lang’zin’) adv. Scottish. long
since, long ago. 1500-20, in William Dunbar’s Poems, a
compound of lang long and syne since, Scottish variants
of Middle English Jang LONG and sin, contraction of
sithen, sithens SINCE. —n. time long ago. 1788, in Auld
Lang Syne, a song written by Robert Burns.

## language
language n. About 1280 langage what is said, talk; later
language (about 1330); borrowed from Old French Jan-
gage, from Jangue tongue, language, from Latin lingua
TONGUE; for suffix see -AGE. The sense of speech of a
nation, tongue, is first found in Middle English about
1300. The form with u developed in English through
Anglo-French, from assimilation with French Jangue in
Middle English.

## languid
languid (lang’gwid) adj. drooping, weak, languishing.
1597, borrowed from Middle French Janguide, learned
borrowing from Latin, and borrowed directly from
Latin Janguidus faint, listless, from Janguére be weak or
faint; see LAX! loose.

## languish
languish (lang’gwish) v. become weak or weary, lose
energy, droop. Before 1325 Janguishen fail in strength,
weaken, in Cursor Mundi; borrowed from Old French
languiss-, stem of Janguir be listless, from Vulgar Latin
*Janguire, from Latin Janguére be weak or faint, see
LAX! loose; for suffix see -ISH?. The extended sense of
grow dull, slack, or less intense is first recorded in Ba-
con’s Sylva Sylvarum (1626).

## languor
languor (lang’gar) n. lack of energy, weakness, weari-
ness. Probably before 1300 Jangour sickness or misery,
in Sir Tristrem; later Janguor (about 1350); borrowed
from Old French Janguor, langour, from Latin languor
faintness, feebleness, lassitude, from /Janguére be weak

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:608 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: lank | lappet | 576 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:608 COLUMN:1 -->
or faint, see LAX! loose; for suffix see -OR!. The sense of
lack of energy, feebleness, was first recorded in English
in Blount’s Glossographia (1656). —languorous adj.
About 1475; borrowed from Middle French Janguer-
ous, from Old French Janguoreux, from Janguor; for
suffix see -OUS.

## lank
lank adj. long and thin, slender, lean. Probably about
1150 Jonke; later, in a surname Lank (1294); developed
from Old English (before 1000) hlanc, from Proto-Ger-
manic *Hlankaz. Old English hlanc is cognate with Old
High German hlanca loin, side, flank, Middle High Ger-
man Jenken to bend (modern German lenken to guide),
and Old Icelandic hlykkr bend, noose, loop, from Indo-
European *kleng-/klong- bend (Pok. 603). —lanky adj.
1670, (of hair) straight and flat; later, awkwardly tall
and thin (1818); formed from English Jank + -y!.

## lanolin
lanolin n. fat or grease obtained from wool. 1885, bor-
rowed from German Lanolin, from Latin Jana WOOL +
oleum OIL + -ina -in? (chemical suffix). The term was
coined by a German physician, Oscar Liebreich.

## lantern
lantern n. About 1250 Janterne lamp or lantern; bor-
rowed from Old French Janterne, from Latin Janterna,
from Greek lamptér, from l4mpein to shine; see LAMP.
The ending -erna in Latin Janterna (patterned after
lucerna lamp) may suggest an Etruscan intermediate
form or influence of such a form. The architectural
meaning of an upright structure on a roof or dome
(probably so called from its resemblance to a lantern)
is first recorded about 1406.

## lanthanum
lanthanum (lan’thanam) n. metallic chemical element.
1841, New Latin, from Greek Janthanein to lie hidden,
escape notice; so called because the element was found
concealed in oxide of cerium. The term was coined in
1839 by Carl Gustaf Mosander, a Swedish chemist who
discovered the element.

## lanyard or laniard
lanyard or laniard n. short rope or cord used on ships
to fasten rigging. 1626, in Captain John Smith’s writ-
ings, perhaps an alteration of Middle English Jainer
thong for fastening parts of armor or clothing (about
1330); later Janioure (1425); borrowed from Old French
laniere, lasniere, from lasne strap, thong. Old French
lasne was apparently an alteration (influenced by las
LACE) of *nasle lace, represented by dialectal French
(Walloon) nale ribbon, from Frankish (compare Old
High German and Old Saxon nestila lace, strap, band,
modern German Nestel ribbon, tape, Old Frisian nestla
lace, band, Middle Dutch and modern Dutch nestel,
from Proto-Germanic *nastila-, earlier *nat-st-ila-; re-
lated to Middle Dutch nette NET! fabric). The later
appearance (1626) may have been a reborrowing from
French rather than an alteration of Middle English
lanier. The new form Janyard differs greatly from the
Middle English and the Middle English form disap-
pears from the record from 1500 to 1626. The spelling
of English lanyard was influenced by YARD? a long
beam used to support a sail. Compare HALYARD. Lan-
yard in the sense of a short strap or thong to hold a
whistle, knife, etc. is first recorded in 1864.
lap} n. front part from the waist to the knees of a person
sitting down. Probably before 1300 Jappe lower part of
a shirt, in The Romance of Guy of Warwick, also, front
part from the waist to the knees of a person sitting
down; developed from Old English Jaeppa skirt or flap
on a garment, lappet (before 899, in Alfred’s translation
of St. Gregory’s Pastoral Care ). The Old English form
is cognate with Old Frisian Jappa flap, Old Saxon lappo

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:608 COLUMN:2 -->
end, rag, Middle Dutch Jappe (modern Dutch Jap rag,
patch), Old High German Jappa flap (modern German
Lappen rag, cloth), and Old Icelandic leppr, from
Proto-Germanic *Japp- (earlier */apn-). Outside Ger-
manic possible cognates are also found in Latin /abi to
slip, glide, fall, and Greek lobds pad, flap, from Indo-
European *lab-/lob-/lab- (Pok. 655).
The figurative sense of a place where anything rests
or is cared for (as in the Jap of luxury ) is first recorded
in Elyot’s The Boke Named the Governour (1531).
—lapboard n. (1840, American English) —lap dog
(1645) —lapful n. (1611)
lap? v. to lay (things) together, one partly over another.
Probably before 1325 Jappen to coil, fold, wrap, from
lappe flap, LAP!. The sense of overlap is first recorded
in 1607, in Markham’s writings. —n. 1673, something
coiled or wrapped up; from the verb. The meaning of
one of the number of turns around the track required
to complete the course is first recorded in 1861 (though
the verb sense is found as early as 1841 in American
English).
lap? v. lick or lift up with the tongue. Before 1325 lapen
to drink by lapping; developed from Old English (about
1000) Japian, from Proto-Germanic *Japdjanan. In the
Germanic languages Old English Japian is cognate with
Old High German Jaffan to lick, Old Swedish Japa and
Icelandic lepja to lap, Old Saxon Jepil spoon, Middle
Low German Jepel, Middle Dutch Jépel (modern
Dutch lepel), and Old High German J/effil (modern
German L6ffel ). Outside Germanic cognates are found
in Albanian lap I lap water, Latin Jambere to lick,
Greek /aptein to lap (with /élaphe he has lapped), and
laphyssein to swallow, gulp down, and Armenian Jap‘el
to lick, from Indo-European */ab-, */aph- (Pok.651).
The meaning of move with a lapping sound, splash
gently, is first recorded in Scott’s Peveril of the Peak
(1823). —n. 1567, something lapped; from the verb.
The meaning of act of lapping, a lick, smack, or taste,
is first recorded in 1820 (though a single instance of a
figurative use is found in a version of Piers Plowman in
1393).

## lapel
lapel n. part of the front of a coat folded back. 1789,
implied earlier in Japelled (1751, in Smollett’s The Ad-
ventures of Peregrine Pickle); formed from English
LAP! flap on-a garment + -el, diminutive suffix (ulti-
mately from Latin -ellus, -ella). Compare LAPPET.

## lapidary
lapidary (lap’oeder’é) n. About 1380 Japidarie treatise on
precious stones, in Chaucer’s House of Fame; also,
before 1382, person who cuts, polishes, or engraves
precious stones, in the Wycliffe Bible; borrowed, prob-
ably through Old French Japidaire, from Latin Japidari-
us stonecutter; originally, adjective, of or working with
stone, from Japis (genitive lapidis ) stone, probably cog-
nate with Greek Jépas bare rock, from Indo-European
*lep- (Pok.678).; for suffix see -ARY.
lapis lazuli (lap’is laz’yalé) deep-blue, opaque, semipre-
cious stone. Before 1425, in Trevisa’s translation of Bar-
tholomew’s De Proprietatibus Rerum; borrowed,
probably through Old French Japis Jazuli, from Medi-
eval Latin, a compound of Latin /Japis stone and Medi-
eval Latin Jazuli, genitive of lazulum lapis lazuli, from
Arabic lazuward azure, from Persian Jajward; compare
AZURE.

## lappet
lappet (lap’it) n. small flap, loose fold. Probably about
1425 Jappette lobe of the lungs or the liver, in a transla-
tion of Chauliac’s Grande Chirurgie; later, flap or fold

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:609 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: lapse | 577 | lark -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:609 COLUMN:1 -->
(1573); formed from Middle English lappe (modern
English Jap) lap’, flap on a garment + -et, diminutive
suffix.

## lapse
lapse n. slip of the memory, the tongue, the pen, etc.;
slight mistake. 1440 Japs an elapsing of time; later Japse
moral transgression, sin (before 1500), and slight mis-
take (before 1526); borrowed from Middle French laps
lapse, from Latin Japsus a slipping and falling, flight (of
time), a falling into error, from /abi to slip, glide, fall;
see LAP? front part. The legal sense of ending of a right
or privilege because of neglect is first recorded about
1447. —v. Probably before 1425 lapsen (of a humor) to
deviate from the normal, in a translation of Chauliac’s
Grande Chirurgie; later, (of time) to go by, pass (about
1443); borrowed from Latin Japsare lose one’s footing,
slip, related to Japsus a slipping and falling. The mean-
ing of fall into error, heresy, etc. is first recorded in
English in Shakespeare’s Cymbeline (1611).
As the first recorded meaning of the noun in English
refers to time (1440), and the verb sense referring to
time also occurs about the same time (1443), it is not
very likely that the noun in English developed from the
verb, though the verb appears earlier in the record of
English.

## lapwing
lapwing n. kind of crested plover, pewit. About 1350
lapwynge, alteration by folk etymology, which con-
nected the word with Jap’, v. and wing, n., of Old
English (about 1050) hléapewince (hléapan to LEAP +
-wince totter, waver, related to wincian to WINK); so
called from the irregular, flapping manner of the bird’s
flight.

## larboard
larboard (lar’bord) n. side of a ship to the left of a person
looking from the stern toward the bow; port. Perhaps
before 1583 lerbord, larborde, alteration of Middle
English (probably about 1380) ladde-borde the loading
side (laden to load, LADE + bord ship’s side, BOARD).
The alteration of ladde-borde to larborde and later Jar-
board was influenced by starboard. —adj. on the port
side of a ship. 1495, from the noun.

## larceny
larceny n. theft. Before 1475, in John Fortescue’s On
the Governance of the Kingdom of England; borrowed
through Anglo-French Jarcin with addition of the
English suffix -y°, signifying a condition, from Old
French Jarrecin theft, from Latin Jatrocinium robbery,
from Jatro (genitive /Jatronis ) hireling, mercenary, ban-
dit, from a lost Hellenistic */4tron mercenary, formed
from Greek J4tron pay, hire, wages; cognate with San-
skrit rati-s willing, generous, from Indo-European
*]é (i)-/la- provide, furnish (Pok.665). —larcenous adj.
1742, in Fielding’s Joseph Andrews; formed from
English Jarcen(y ) + -ous.

## larch
larch n. tree of the pine family. 1548, in larch tree;
borrowed from German Larche, from Middle High
German Jarche, lerche, from Latin Jarix (genitive Jari-
cis ), possibly from an Indo-European language spoken
in prehistoric times in the Alps, since the larch was
native to Alpine regions.

## lard
lard n. fat of pigs and hogs. 1231, as an English word in
a Latin context; borrowed from Old French larde
bacon fat, and directly from Latin Jardum, laridum
lard, possibly cognate with Greek Jarindés fattened, both
words being contractions of derivatives of an Indo-
European noun */4yos bacon, fat (root Jai, Pok.652).
—v. insert strips of bacon or salt pork in (meat) before
cooking. Before 1338 Jarden, in Mannyng’s Chronicle
of England; borrowed from Old French larder, from

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:609 COLUMN:2 -->
larde bacon fat. The figurative sense of intersperse or
garnish (speech or writing), interlard, is first recorded
in 1549.

## larder
larder n. pantry. About 1300, a supply of meat; later, a
place for storing meat (1380); borrowed through Anglo-
French Jarder a place for meats, corresponding to Old
French Jardier a tub for meats, from Medieval Latin
Jardarium a room for meats, from Latin Jardum LARD.

## large
large adj. Probably before 1200, abundant, ample,
roomy, in Ancrene Riwle; also, liberal or generous, lav-
ish; borrowing of Old French large, from Latin Jargus
abundant, copious, of uncertain origin, but possibly re-
lated to Jardum LARD. The sense of wide in range,
extensive, is first recorded before 1325, in Cursor Mun-
di; the general meaning of big, huge, is found in Chau-
cer’s Canterbury Tales (about 1385). —large intestine
(1869) —largely adv. Probably before 1200 Jargeliche;
formed from Middle English large + -liche -ly'.
—large-scale adj. (1887) —largish adj. (1787)

## largess or largesse
largess or largesse (larjes’ or lar’jis) n. generous giving.
Probably before 1200, quality of being generous; also,
liberal bestowal of gifts, in Ancrene Riwle; borrowed
from Old French Jargesse a bounty, from large LARGE.

## largo
largo (lar’g6) adj. Music. very slow and dignified, state-
ly. 1683, in notes to a work by Henry Purcell; borrow-
ing of Italian Jargo, literally, wide or broad; from Latin
Jargus abundant. —n. very slow, stately passage or
piece of music. 1724, from the adjective in English; also
possibly borrowed from Italian largo, from the adjec-
tive in Italian.

## lariat
lariat (lar’éot) n. lasso. 1832, American English; bor-
rowed from Spanish Ja reata the rope (Ja the, feminine
of el + reata rope, from reatar tie again, re- again +
atar to tie, from Latin aptare to join, from aptus joined;
see APT).
lark! n. small songbird. About 1275, as a surname
Larke; earlier, in the place name Lauerkesfeld (1184-
85), and laverche (probably about 1200); developed
from Old English lawerce (about 700); cognate with
Frisian Jiurk lark, Old Saxon Jewerka, Middle Low Ger-
man and Middle Dutch Jéwerke (modern Dutch
leeuwerik ), Old High German Jérihha (modern Ger-
man Lerche ), Old Icelandic Javirki, Swedish Jarka,
Danish and Norwegian lerke, from Proto-Germanic
*Jaiw(a)rikon. The designation is widespread in Ger-
manic but further connections are lacking. —larkspur
n. (1578)
lark? v. to frolic, sport, play tricks. 1813, possibly a
shortened form of skylark, skylarking to participate in
rough play, originally among sailors, and especially car-
ried on in the rigging of a ship (1809). The verb Jark was
probably also influenced by its earlier noun use. —n.
1811, possibly a shortened form of skylark, as in sky-
larking, vbl. n.
The meanings of Jark and skylark appear in the rec-
ord of English about the same time so that one deduc-
tion is as likely as another, but it is possible that Jark was
reinforced by northern British English Jake, a dialect
form of the verb meaning to play or sport, developed
from leyken, laiken to engage in sport or play (probably
before 1200, in The Ormulum ); borrowed from a Scan-
dinavian source (compare Old Icelandic /eika to play,
Swedish Jeka, Danish lege ); cognate with Middle High
German leichen to hop, Gothic Jaikan to hop, dance,
spring, and Old English /acan to swing, play, fight, from
Proto-Germanic *Jaikanan; cognate also with Old Irish

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:610 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: larrup | last | 578 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:610 COLUMN:1 -->
loig calf, and Sanskrit réjate hops, from Indo-European
*leig-/loig- (Pok.667).
A similar development is found in the noun lake,
developed from Jeyk, laik amusement, fun (probably
about 1200, in The Ormulum); probably borrowed
from a Scandinavian source. The correspondence of
both the noun and verb meanings of Jake and Jark add
some force to the suggestion of a connection between
the two words.
The OED explains the connection with Jake (found
also as Jairk ) through the shift in pronunciation with an
intrusive r-sound common to southern British English.

## larrup
larrup (lar’ap) v. Informal. beat, thrash. 1823, originally
dialectal; perhaps borrowed from Dutch Jarpen (pro-
nounced lar’apen) to slap, thrash, box the ears, from
larp rod, whip, of unknown origin.

## larva
larva (ldr’va) n., pl. larvae (lar’vé). Zoology. insect in the
early immature stage, grub. 1768, New Latin, special
use of Latin /arva, earlier /Jarua ghost, mask; related to
Lar (plural Larés ) tutelary god or spirit, probably of
Etruscan origin.
The word was applied to the immature form of the
insect by Linnaeus, because it masked or was a ghost of
the adult form (called by Linnaeus an imago).
The earliest recorded use of Jarva in English was in
the sense of a ghost or specter (1651); also borrowed
from Latin Jarva.
—larval adj. 1848, of a larva or grub; borrowed from
New Latin Jarvalis, from Latin larvalis of larvae or
ghosts, from Jarva ghost; for suffix see -AL!. The earlier
sense from Latin is recorded in English in 1656.

## laryngeal
laryngeal (larin’jéal) adj. of the larynx. 1795, formed in
English from New Latin laryngeus (from Greek Jarynx,
genitive /aryngos) + English -al!. —laryngitis n. in-
flammation of the larynx. 1822-34, New Latin; formed
from Greek Jarynx (genitive l4ryngos) + -itis inflam-
mation.

## larynx
larynx (lar’ingks) n. cavity at the upper end of the wind-
pipe. 1578, borrowed through Middle French larynx,
from New Latin, from Greek Jarynx genitive laryngos )
the upper windpipe, probably altered from Jaimés
throat, under the influence of pharynx throat, wind-
pipe. The only known relative of Greek laimés throat,
gullet, is laitma the gulf of the sea, the deep.

## lasagna or lasagne
lasagna or lasagne (lozin’ya) n. dish of wide, flat noo-
dles baked with cheese, tomato sauce, etc. 1846, bor-
rowing of Italian Jasagna, sing., or lasagne, pl., from
Vulgar Latin */asania, from Latin Jasanum cooking pot,
from Greek Jasanon, singular of J4sana trivet or stand
for a pot.

## lascar
lascar (las’kor) n. native sailor of the East Indies. 1625,
in Purchas’ Pilgrims; borrowed from Portuguese Jachar
(erroneously laschar ), probably from Hindi Jashkani sol-
dier, native sailor, from Jashkar army, camp, from Per-
sian Jaskar, from Arabic al-‘askar the army.

## lascivious
lascivious (lasiv’éas) adj. lustful, lecherous. About 1450,
perhaps borrowed through Middle French Jascivieux,
from Late Latin lascividsus, from Latin Jascivia lewd-
ness or playfulness, from Jascivus lewd or playful, see
LUST; for suffix see -OUS.
‘laser n. device which generates and amplifies light
waves of a pure color in a narrow and extremely in-
tense beam of light. 1960, acronym formed from J(ight )
a(mplification by) s(timulated) e(mission of) r(adia-
tion ), on the pattern of the earlier (1955) MASER. —lase

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:610 COLUMN:2 -->
v. to function or operate as a laser. 1962, back forma-
tion from LASER.
lash! n. part of a whip that is not the handle. Probably
before 1300 Jas a blow or stroke, in Arthour and Merlin;
later Jashe flexible part of a whip (about 1380, in Chau-
cer’s Parlement of Foules ), possibly of imitative origin.
—v. Probably before 1300 Jaisen to strike out, throw, or
move violently, in Arthour and Merlin; later lasschen to
whip or flog (before 1398, in Trevisa’s translation of
Bartholomew’s De Proprietatibus Rerum ); possibly of
imitative origin, as the noun.
lash? y. bind with a rope or cord. 1624, in Captain John
Smith’s The General Historie of Virginia; developed
from lasschyn to lace a garment (1440, in Promptorium
Parvulorum ); probably borrowed from Middle French
lachier, from Old French Jacier to LACE. —lashing n.
cord used for binding (1669).

## lass
lass n. About 1300 lasce, later las, lasse (about 1390);
possibly borrowed from a Scandinavian source (com-
pare Old Icelandic Joskr idle, weak, Old Swedish lask
kona unmarried woman, literally, one without a fixed
dwelling); cognate with West Frisian Jask light, thin,
and dialectal German Jasch slack or weak. —lassie n.
1725, formed from English lass + -ie.

## lassitude
lassitude n. lack of energy, weakness, weariness. Prob-
ably before 1425, in a translation of Chauliac’s Grande
Chirurgie; borrowed from Middle French lassitude,
from Latin Jassitado faintness or weariness, from lJassus
faint, tired, weary, see LET! to allow; for suffix see
-TUDE.

## lasso
lasso (las’6 or lasii’) n. long rope with a running noose
at one end; lariat. 1819, American English; borrowed
from Spanish Jazo, from Latin lagueum, accusative of
laqueus noose, snare; see the doublet LACE. —v. catch
with a lasso. 1831, American English. A single instance
of the verb is found earlier in a travel book on Argen-
tina (1807), but since its wider continuous appearance
does not occur until the 1830’s, it is probable that the
verb use is from the noun.
last! adj., adv. coming at the end. Probably before 1200
leaste, in Ancrene Riwle; also laste, latste (probably
about 1200, in The Ormulum ); developed from the
contraction of Old English Jatost (from Proto-Germanic
*Jatast-) and Old English, laetest (from Proto-Germanic
*Jatist-), found before 899, in Alfred’s translation of
Boethius’ De Consolatione Philosophiae. The Old
English forms are superlatives of Jaet, adj. and late, adv.
(see LATE) and correspond to Middle Dutch /aetst last
(modern Dutch Jaatst ), Old High German Jazzost, lez-
zist (modern German letzt ), and Old Icelandic Jatastr
slowest.
Though modern English Jatest is similar in form to
Old English Jztest, the superlative Jatest is a formation
from Middle English Jate + -est (probably before 1200)
and is not a resultant of the Old English form.
—n. one that is last. Probably before 1200 Jaste, in Laya-
mon’s Chronicle of Britain; from the adjective.
—last-ditch adj. 1951, back formation from earlier /ast-
ditcher one who fights to the last ditch (1909). —last
hurrah 1956, American English, from The Last Hurrah,
a novel by Edwin O’Connor, 1918-68, American novel-
ist. —lastly adv. About 1375, formed from Middle
English Jaste last + -/y!. —last straw (1848, in Dickens’
Dombey and Son) —last word (1563)
last? v. go on, hold out, endure. 1122 Jasten; later Jas-
ten (1137); developed from Old English /é@stan to con-

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:611 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: last | 579 | Latin -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:611 COLUMN:1 -->
tinue, endure (possibly about 750, in Cynewulf’s
Christ ); earlier, accomplish, carry out (about 725, in
Beowulf). Old English /éstan is cognate with Old Fri-
sian Jasta, lesta to fulfill, Old Saxon Jéstian to perform,
Old High German and modern German leisten to per-
form, carry out, and Gothic Jaistjan to follow, from
Proto-Germanic *Jaistjanan; all derived from the same
Germanic source as Old English /Jast track, footprint;
see LAST’. —lasting adj. Before 1333 (replacing earlier
lestind ); from the present participle of last? endure; for
suffix see -ING?.
last? n. shoemaker’s block shaped like a foot. Before
1300 Jeste; later laste (1395); developed from Old
English l#ste (about 1000, in A#lfric’s Glossary ), from
earlier Jast track, footprint, trace (about 725, in Beo-
wulf). The Old English forms are cognate with Middle
Dutch and modern Dutch Jeest form, model, last, Old
High German Jeist (modern German Leisten last), Old
Icelandic leistr trouser leg, sock, and Gothic laists foot-
print, from Proto-Germanic *laistaz, cognate with
Latin Jira furrow, from Indo-European *leis-/Jois-
(Pok.671). —v. form (shoes) on a last. 1880, from the
noun.

## latch
latch v. Probably before 1200 Jecchen catch, ensnare,
in Ancrene Riwle; later lacchen (about 1250), and Jatch-
en (before 1338); developed from Old English laeccan
to grasp or seize (about 950, in Lindisfarne Gospels ),
from Proto-Germanic *lJakkjanan (with stem *Jakk-
from earlier *Jagn-), cognate with Greek lazesthai
grasp (from earlier */Jagwje-) and labein seize, from
Indo-European *(s )lagw- (Pok.958). The sense of fasten
with a latch (from the noun) is first recorded in Promp-
torium Parvulorum (1440). —n. a catch for fastening a
door, etc. 1296-97 lacche (English word in Latin con-
text); later Jatche (about 1350); from Jacchen to catch.
—latchkey n. (1825) —latchstring n. (1791)

## late
late adj. Probably before 1200 Jet slow or sluggish; later
lat, late tardy, remiss (about 1225); developed from Old
English Jzt late, slow, sluggish (about 725, in Beowulf);
cognate with Old Frisian Jet late, Old Saxon Jat lazy,
Middle Low German Jat, Middle Dutch Jaet (modern
Dutch Jaat late), Old High German Jaz slow (modern
German Jass indolent, weary), Old Icelandic Jatr slug-
gish, lazy (Sw: dish, Norwegian Jat, Danish lad ), Gothic
lats, from Proto-Germanic ‘*latés, Indo-European
*lod6s, and related to Old English /#tan to allow, LET?.
—adv. Probably before 1200 Jate; found in Old English
late (about 750, in Cynewulf’s Juliana ); from lzt, adj.
—latecomer n. (1869) —lately adv. About 1340 Jatly,
formed from Middle English Jat late + -Jy!.

## lateen
lateen (latén’) adj. Nautical. having a triangular sail held
up by a long yard on a short mast. 1727-41, in Cham-
bers Cyclopzedia; borrowed from French Jatine in voile
latine Latin sail; so called from its use in the Mediter-
ranean. An earlier form Jatten (1540) with the same
sense is cited by Weekley in his Etymological Dic-
tionary of Modern English.

## latent
latent adj. present but not active, hidden. 1459, con-
cealed or secret; borrowed through Middle French l/a-
tent, and directly from Latin Jatentem (nominative
laténs ), present participle of Jatére to lie hidden, cog-
nate with Greek Jathein, lanthanein escape notice,
from Indo-European */4 (i )-/Ja-, la-dh-/la-dh- Pok.651);
for suffix see -ENT. The specialized meaning “(of a dis-
ease) dormant,” is first recorded in 1684. —latency n.
Before 1638; formed from English Jatent + -cy.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:611 COLUMN:2 -->

## lateral
lateral adj. of or at the side. Probably before 1425 Jate-
rale, in a translation of Chauliac’s Grande Chirurgie;
borrowed through Middle French Jatéral, and directly
from Latin lateralis belonging to the side, from Jatus
(genitive Jateris ) side; of uncertain origin. —n. lateral -
part or outgrowth. 1635, from the adjective.

## latex
latex (la’teks) n. milky liquid found in various plants.
1662, body fluid; borrowed from Latin latex (genitive
laticis ) liquid, fluid, probably from Greek Jdtax (geni-
tive /atagos) drops of wine in the bottom of a cup,
dregs; cognate with Old Icelandic lethja loam, and Mid-
dle Irish Jaith a liquid, from Indo-European */at- wet
(Pok.654). The sense of a milky liquid from plants is first
recorded in 1835, and from that the word’s application
to an emulsion of synthetic rubber is found in 1937.

## lath
lath n. thin, narrow strip of wood formerly used to
make a support for plaster or to make a lattice. 1281-82
lathe (English word in Latin context); later Jaththe
(before 1393); probably developed from Old English
*lzeththe, variant of lztt lath; cognate with Old Saxon
latta lath, Middle Dutch Jatte (modern Dutch Jat ), and
Old High German Jatta (modern German Latte ), ap-
parently from Proto-Germanic */aththo, whose double
th is otherwise unexampled. The relation of the Ger-
manic types is obscure. Other cognates are found in
Celtic: Old Irish slat rod, switch, Welsh Jlath rod, wand,
yard, and Breton Jaz, from Proto-Celtic *slatta. The
view of W.W. Skeat is still perhaps the best: that the
Middle English form was influenced by Welsh Jlath
(with er lath for his rod), The Indo-European root
would be *(s )Jat-. —v. cover or line with laths. 1439,
from the noun.

## lathe
lathe (laFH) n. machine for turning and shaping wood,
metal, etc. 1310, device used by coopers, perhaps a
turning lathe; probably borrowed from a Scandinavian
source (compare Danish -/Jad stand, supporting frame-
work, as in drejelad turning lathe, savelad saw bench,
veverlad loom, and Old Icelandic hladh layered pile or
pile regularly built up as from the shavings of a lathe,
related to hladha to load, LADE). The first particular
reference to a turning lathe is found in Cotgrave’s Dic-
tionary (1611).

## lather
lather n. 1583, probably redeveloped in modern
English from the Middle English verb. A noun is found
in Old English (about 1000) Jéathor washing soda, lath-
er; cognate with Old Icelandic Jaudhr foam, washing
soda, from Proto-Germanic *latithran, Greek Joutrén
(earlier Joetron ) bath, and ultimately with Latin Javere
to wash, from Indo-European *Jou-, Jowa- (Pok.692). No
developing form is recorded in Middle English, which
strongly suggests that the noun is the result of a func-
tional shift of the verb. —v. About 1450 Jatheren to
wash or soak clothes, alteration of earlier litheren, leth-
eren be bathed in, be covered with foam, sweat, etc.
(probably about 1200); developed from Old English
léthran, lythran to cover with lather (about 950, in Lin-
disfarne Gospels ); cognate with Old Icelandic leydhra
to clean, wash.

## Latin
Latin n. About 1275 Jatyn, possibly from the adjective,
and rarely found in Old English Jatin (about 950, in
Lindisfarne Gospels); borrowed from Latin Latinum.
The Old English form in general use was /#den (before
899, in Alfred’s translation of St. Gregory’s Pastoral
Care ), also found in Middle English, and altered from
earlier *laeden, from Vulgar Latin *Ladinum, a variant
of Latin Latinum, having arisen from a confusion with
léden, lyden, léoden language. The OED says the con-

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:612 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: Latino | launch | 580 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:612 COLUMN:1 -->
fusion originated with the compound béc-/léden book
language, which was formed by popular etymology as
a synonym for /@den. —adj. About 1391 Latin, in the
Prologue to Chaucer’s Treatise on the Astrolabe, found
in Old English Jatin (about 950, in Lindisfarne Gos-
pels ); borrowing of Latin Latinus belonging to Latium,
the part of Italy that included Rome.

## Latino
Latino (laté’nd) n., adj. Latin American. 1946, Ameri-
can English; borrowing of American Spanish Latino,
shortened form of Spanish Latinoamericano Latin-
American, (person) of or from Latin America.

## latitude
latitude n. distance north or south of the equator. About
1390, breadth, width, geographical latitude, in Chau-
cer’s Canterbury Tales; borrowed through Old French
latitude, and directly from Latin Jatitadd breadth,
width, extent, size, from /atus wide, earlier *stlatos,
cognate with Old Slavic po-stilati to spread out, from
Indo-European *stela-, stjtos (Pok.1018); for suffix see
-TUDE.
The figurative sense of an allowable degree or range
of variation is first recorded probably before 1425; that
of freedom from narrow restrictions, permitted variety
of action or opinion, is found in Bacon’s Of the Ad-
vancement of Learning (1605).
—latitudinal adj. 1392 lJatitudinel relating to breadth or
width; later Jatitudinal (probably before 1425); bor-
rowed from Old French Jatitudinel and from Medieval
Latin Jatitudinalis, from Latin Jatitudinis, genitive of
Jatitado latitude; for suffix see -AL!. Reference to geo-
graphical latitude is first recorded in 1778.

## latrine
latrine n. toilet in a camp, barracks, etc.; privy. 1297
laterin a privy, probably borrowed from Latin /atrina,
contraction of Javatrina washbasin, washroom (lavare
to wash, LAVE + -trina suffix added to a verb stem and
denoting a workplace). The word disappeared from the
record of English and is not found again until 1642 as
a new borrowing from French (usually in the plural
form Jatrines ), learned borrowing from Latin /atrina.

## latter
latter adj. About 1175 Jator, later; later lattre, adj. and
adv., less early, at a later time (probably about 1200);
developed from Old English Jztra, lator slower (about
1000). The Old English forms are the comparatives of
Old English Jaet LATE, and correspond to Old Frisian
letora latter, Middle High German Jazzer slower, and
Old Icelandic Jatari. The meaning of second of two is
first recorded in 1555.
Though modern English Jater is similar in form to
Old English Jaetra, the comparative Jater is a formation
in early modern English (1559 adj., 1548 adv.) from late
+ -er*, and is not a resultant of the Old English form.

## lattice
lattice n. 1304 Jattis; later Jatyce (probably about 1450);
borrowed from Old French Jatte lath, from Frankish
(compare Old High German Jatta LATH). —v. furnish
with a lattice or latticework. 1427-28 Jatisen; from the
noun.
laud vy. to praise. About 1378 Jauden, in a version of
Piers Plowman; borrowed from Old French Jauder and
from Latin Jaudare to praise, from lJaus (genitive laudis )
praise, fame, glory, from Indo-European */Jau-d-. The
Latin Jaus is probably cognate with Old English /éoth
song, poem, hymn, Middle Dutch Jiet (modern Dutch
lied ), Old High German liod (modern German Lied
song), Old Icelandic Jjédh strophe, stanza, from Proto-
Germanic *Jeuthan, Indo-European *J/éu-t-, root *léu-/
Jgu- a sound or cry (Pok.683). —n. praise. About 1375
laude praise or fame, in Chaucer’s Canterbury Tales;

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:612 COLUMN:2 -->
borrowed from Old French Jaude, learned borrowing
from Latin Jaudem, and probably borrowed directly
from Latin Jaudem (nominative Jaus) praise, glory,
fame.
The plural form /auds a morning church service with
psalms of praise to God (one of the canonical hours) is
first recorded as Jaudes, in Ayenbite of Inwyt (1340);
borrowed through Old French Jaudes and directly
from Medieval Latin, from Latin Jaudés, plural of Jaus
praise, glory, fame.
It is also possible that this plural use of the noun was
the immediate source of the generalized sense of
“praise,” as found above in Chaucer’s Canterbury
Tales, and that the noun, in some instances, influenced
the development of the verb in Middle English.
—laudable adj. praiseworthy. Probably before 1425,
borrowed from Old French Jaudable, and from Latin
laudabilis praiseworthy, from laudare to praise; for suf-
fix see -ABLE. —laudatory adj. expressing praise. 1555,
borrowed from Middle French Jaudatoire, and directly
from Late Latin Jaudatorius of praise, from Latin lauda-
tor praiser, from Jaudare to praise; for suffix see -ORY.

## laudanum
laudanum (l6’danom) n. solution of opium in alcohol.
1602-3, borrowed through Middle French Jaudanum,
and directly from New Latin Jaudanum, a word used by
Paracelsus as the name for an expensive concoction
used as a medicine which was supposed to contain opi-
um. The origin of the word is uncertain, though it may
have been confused with Jadanum, borrowed from
Latin Jadanum a gum resin, from Greek Jadanon, léda-
non, probably of Semitic origin.

## laugh
laugh v. Probably before 1200 Jahhen, in Ancrene
Riwle; later Jaughen (about 1375, in Chaucer’s Anelida
and Arcite); developed from Old English hlazhhan
(before 830, in the Vespasian Psalter ); earlier hlihhan
(before 725, in Genesis A ); cognate with Old Frisian
hlakkia to laugh, Old Saxon hlahhian, Middle Dutch
and modern Dutch lJachen, Old High German hlahhan,
lahhén (modern German lJachen ), Old Icelandic hlz#ja
(Swedish, Danish, and Norwegian le ), and Gothic hlah-
jan, from Proto-Germanic *HlaHjanan, cognate with
Greek kléssein cluck, from Indo-European *kl6k-/klak-:
(Pok.600), probably ultimately of imitative origin.
The original sound, as represented by gh in laugh,
cough, rough, etc., was like that of Scottish loch or
German ach. As the pronunciation shifted to the sound
of fin off, the spelling of some words also changed to
reflect this process, as in dwarf, draft (for draught),
etc.; but some spellings remained fixed.
The meaning of a cause of laughter, joke, is first re-
corded in 1895, in George Bernard Shaw’s writings.
—n. 1690, act of laughing, laughter; later, instance of
laughing (as in a hearty laugh; 1713, in Steele’s writ-
ings); from the verb.
—laughable adj. 1596, in Shakespeare’s Merchant of
Venice; formed from English laugh, v. +. -able.
—laughingstock n. (1533) —laughter n. Probably before
1200 Jahtre, in Ancrene Riwle; later laughter (about
1385, in Chaucer’s Troilus and Criseyde ); developed
from Old English hleahtor (about 725, in Beowulf). Old
English hleahtor corresponds to Old High German Jah-
tar laughter (modern German Gelachter ), Old Icelan-
dic hAlatr, and Danish, Norwegian latter, from
Proto-Germanic *HlaHtraz, and is derived from the
same Germanic source as Old English Alihhan,
hlzhhan to laugh.

## launch’
launch’ v. throw forward, propel. Probably before 1300

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:613 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: launch | lavish | 581 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:613 COLUMN:1 -->
launchen to leap, spring, rush, in Kyng Alisaunder;
later, to throw, hurl, as a weapon (about 1330); bor-
rowed from Old North French Jancher, lanchier, corre-
sponding to Old French Jancer, Jancier to fling, throw,
from Late Latin Janceare wield a lance, pierce with a
lance, from Latin Jancea light spear, LANCE.
The sense of put into the water, set afloat, is first
recorded probably before 1400, in Morte Arthur; the
meaning was extended to apply to any vehicle, such as
a rocket, by 1873. The figurative sense of start, set
going, set out (as in to Jaunch an enterprise ), is record-
ed in 1602. Doublet of LANCE, v.
—n. act of launching. 1440 Jaunche a leap or bound, in
Promptorium Parvulorum; from the verb. The applica-
tion to that of launching a vessel is first recorded in a
letter of Scott to Southey in 1814. —launching pad
(1951)
launch? n. small, open motorboat. 1697, largest boat
carried by a warship; borrowed from Spanish and Por-
tuguese Jancha barge or launch, apparently from Malay
lancharan, from lanchar quick, agile. The English spell-
ing was probably influenced by Jaunch!. The sense of
a small boat (later a motorboat) used for transporting
passengers from a large ship or as a pleasure craft, is
first recorded in 1865.

## Jaunder
Jaunder v. 1664, in Samuel Butler’s Hudibras; from the
noun Jaunder one who washes, especially linen (1440),
contraction of earlier lavender (about 1325), also found
as a surname Lavendre (1227); borrowed from Old
French Javandier male washer, lavandiere female
washer, laundress, from Medieval Latin Javandaria a
washer, from Latin Javanda (things) to be washed, from
Javare to wash, LAVE; for suffix see -ER'!. The modern
specialized meaning “(of money) make seem legiti-
mate, lawfully gained, or acceptable,” is first recorded
in 1970, from the idea of “cleansing” illegally obtained
(“dirty”) money. —laundress n. 1550, in Coverdale’s
writings; formed from English Jaunder + -ess. —laun-
dry n. Before 1450 Jawndre act of washing; earlier
lavendrye place for washing (about 1378, in a version
of Piers Plowman ); borrowed from Old French Javand-
erie, from lavandier, lavandiere washer; for suffix see
“RY.

## launderette
launderette n. = laundromat. 1949, American English,
formed from English Jaunder, v. + -ette.

## laundromat
laundromat (l6n’dramat) n. self-service laundry. 1943
Laundromat, American English (a trademark by the
Westinghouse Electric Company for an automatic
washing machine); formed from English Jaundr(y) +
-o- + -mat, as in automat.

## laureate
laureate adj. crowned with a laurel wreath as a mark of
honor. About 1375, in Chaucer’s Canterbury Tales;
borrowed from Latin Jaureatus, from Jaurea laurel
crown, laurel tree, from feminine of Jaureus of laurel,
from Jaurus LAUREL; for suffix see -ATE°.
The term poet Jaureate is first found in Lydgate’s
works in 1429, though Jaureat poete is to be found in
Chaucer’s Canterbury Tales. The first poet laureate of
England in the modern sense of a poet who receives a
stipend from the royal household was Ben Jonson, but
the title seems to have been first given officially to his
successor, Sir William Davenant, who was appointed in
1638.
—n. poet laureate. Before 1529, in Skelton’s Calliope;
from the adjective.

## laurel
laurel n. small evergreen tree. 1373 Jaureol, and before

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:613 COLUMN:2 -->
1375 Jorel; later laurel (about 1415); borrowed from
Latin Jaureola small laurel branch, from Jaurus laurel
tree, thought to be somehow from the same (apparent-
ly Mediterranean) source as Greek déphné laurel (with
dialectal variants datichna and dauchmés ).

## lava
lava (la’va) n. molten rock from a volcano. 1750, bor-
rowing of Italian Java, from dialectal Italian (Neapolitan
or Calabrian) Java, of uncertain origin (by traditional
etymology, from Latin Javare to wash, originally in Ital-
ian said to be from a rivulet caused by sudden down-
pour of rain, found in Florio, 1611). Italian etymologists
derive the word from Latin Jabés a fall, from /4bi to fall;
