see LAP!, n. Kluge-Gotze, however, consider it to be a
pre-Indo-European word for “‘stone,” similar to Ger-
man Lawine avalanche.
lavaliere, lavalier or lavalliere (lav’alir’) n. ornament
hanging from a chain around the neck. 1873 Lavalliere
a style of hat; later La Valiere a style of necktie, bor-
rowed from French Javalliére necktie with a large loose
knot, in allusion to the Duchesse de La Valliére (Fran-
coise Louise de La Baume Le Blanc, 1644-1710, mis-
tress of Louis XIV of France). The meaning of a small
microphone hung around the neck is first recorded in
1960 in American English.

## lavatory
lavatory n. washroom. Before 1382 lavatorie, lavatory
washbasin, in the Wycliffe Bible; borrowed from Latin
lavatorium place for washing, from lavare to wash,
LAVE; for suffix see -ORY. The meaning of a washroom
is first recorded in English in Blount’s Glossographia
(1656). Lavatory as a euphemism for bathroom or toilet
is found in 1845.

## lave
lave v. Archaic. to wash, bathe. Probably before 1200
laven to wash, bathe; formed in part by: 1) develop-
ment from Old English gelafian wash by pouring, pour,
as water, etc. (about 725, in Beowulf); possibly an early
borrowing from Latin Javare, lavere to wash, and corre-
sponding to Old Saxon Jabon, Middle Dutch Javen, and
Old High German Jabon (possibly only accidentally
similar in form because the continental Germanic
words, especially the Old High German, mean refresh,
and only at an early stage, if ever, meant to wash); and
2) by probable influence in form and meaning of Old
French Javer to wash, from Latin Javare, and perhaps
reinforced by Latin Javdare itself, which is cognate with
Greek lotiein to wash, Old Irish Juaith ashes (as a cleans-
ing agent), and Armenian Joganam I bathe, from Indo-
European *lou-/lowa- (Pok.692).

## lavender
lavender n. plant with pale-purple flowers. 1373 lavan-
dyr, borrowed through Anglo-French Javendre, from
Medieval Latin lavendula, livendula lavender, perhaps
derived from Latin lividus bluish, LIVID; probably later
associated with French Javande and Italian Javanda lav-
ender, from Javanda a washing (so called because of its
use in washing or its use to perfume distilled water)
from Javare, from Latin Javare, from the plant’s use as
a bath perfume. (The connection with washing is not
accepted by Bradley in the OED.) —adj. pale-purple.
1840, from the noun.

## lavish
lavish adj. giving or spending without stint; prodigal.
1469 laves outpouring, unrestrained, profuse, prodigal;
later lavas (1485); possibly developed as an adjective
use of earlier Javas, n., profusion, extravagant outpour-
ing (not recorded before 1483, in Caxton’s The Golden
Legend ); borrowed from Middle French Javasse, lav-
ache torrent (of rain), deluge, from Javer to wash, from
Latin lavare LAVE; for suffix see -ISH?. It is also possible

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:614 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: law | lay | 582 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:614 COLUMN:1 -->
that */auessh existed as a parallel form, implied in Jaues-
shenes lavishness (about 1477). —v. give or spend with-
out stint. 1542, in Udall’s translation of Erasmus’
Apothegms; from the adjective.

## law
law n. Probably about 1200 Jawe; developed from Old
English (before 1000) Jagu; borrowed from a Scan-
dinavian source (compare Old Icelandic Jog law, collec-
tive plural of Jag layer, measure, stroke; literally,
something laid down or fixed). The Scandinavian forms
correspond to -/Jag in Old Saxon gilag decree, fate, orlag
fate, war, and Old High German urlag fate, from Proto-
Germanic */agzan, Indo-European */Joghom, root *legh-
to lie (Pok.658). The semantic development from
“something laid down” to “decree, law” is not unique
to English but is also found in German Gesetz law, from
setzen to set down, and outside Germanic in Latin and
Greek.
The concept of international law, or the Jaw of na-
tions is first recorded in English before 1548, as wide-
spread trade, general commerce, and closer contact
among the nations of Europe necessitated the function
of envoys, ambassadors and other representatives of
government. Paralleling the function of such represen-
tatives in the Roman Empire, the men of affairs made
recourse to Latin jus gentium, which was already em-
bodied in part in the concept of the Jaw of nature, first
alluded to in English about 1225, from Latin Jex natu-
rae, lex naturalis, jus naturale, in Cicero, Seneca, and
other Roman jurists, but ultimately derived from Aris-
totle. This system of legal concepts was also developed
out of Old Testament law, first found in Old English in
A lfric’s commentaries (about 1000).
—lawbreaker n. (1440 lawe brekare, in Promptorium

giver n. Before 1382, in the Wycliffe Bible; formed

lawn! n. grassy ground. 1548 laune glade, open space

## layer

## lazar

## lazy
lazy adj. 1549 laysy disliking work, idle, slothful; origin
uncertain, possibly borrowed from Middle Low Ger-
man Jasich weak, feeble, tired; cognate with Middle
High German erleswen grow weak, Old Icelandic J/a-
sinn weak, slack, limp, Gothic Jasiws weak; also cognate
with Bulgarian Jos bad, wicked, and Tocharian A Jjask-
softness, weakness. The spelling with z is first recorded

The transferred sense of sluggish, dull, slow-moving (as
in a lazy mist, a lazy hour ), appeared before 1568, in
Roger Ascham’s The Schoolmaster.
It is tempting to construct a development through
possible forms such as */ase to Middle English laches,
lachesse soft, wanton, lazy (probably about 1425) and
lach, lache slack, negligent (probably about 1422);
loose, open (probably about 1300); and thence to Old
French Jasche, lache; however, the lack of phonological
connection and the persistent appearance of the older
forms in late Middle English, leave such a connection
wanting.
—v. be lazy, laze. 1612; from the adjective.
—n. act of lazing, idleness. 1862; from the verb.
—laze v. be lazy, idle. About 1588, in Robert Greene’s
The Comicall History of Alphonsus, King of Arragon;
back formation from LAZY. —lazily adv. (1587) —lazi-
ness n. (1580) —lazybones n. lazy person (1592).
-le! a suffix forming nouns found in the names of tools
and utensils, as in handle, thimble, kettle, and in the
names of articles worn to accomplish a purpose, as in
bridle, girdle. In words such as bundle the purpose of
-le and its relationship to the base form is unclear.

## The
The suffix had also a diminutive sense in Old English,
which is found in words such as nozzle and bramble,
but this has lost its force in modern English (compare
use as a frequentative form in Middle English and mod-
ern English -le’).
Modern English -le developed from Middle English
-el, -ele, and is also found in Middle English -/e, all of
which developed from or are found in Old English
noun suffixes -el, -ela, -ele, -le, -/. The Old English forms
‘are cognate with Old Frisian -le, Old Saxon and Old

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:615 COLUMN:2 -->
High German -al, -la (modern German -el ), Old Icelan-
dic -al, -i/] and Gothic -ils.
A number of words that have the appearance of be-
longing to this group are the same in form only by
influence of the similarity in pronunciation. Among
such words, usually borrowed from Old French are:
battle, bottle, castle, cattle, mantle, though riddle, by
confusion of s as a sign of the plural in Old English -els,
is in a separate category. The borrowings from Old
French -el, as in castle, derive from Latin -ellum a
diminutive suffix, or as in cattle froin Latin -ale neuter
singular; in battle the Old French form -aille is the
neuter plural of Latin -alis, in bottle the Old French
form -eille derives from the Latin diminutive suffix
-icula.
-le? a suffix forming adjectives with the meaning of
liable (to do something) or apt (to be something), as in
fickle and brittle, and usually having no obvious signifi-
cance as a particle because the root forms from Middle
and Old English are no longer recognizable.
Modern English -le developed from Middle English
-el, -ele, and is also found in Middle English -le, all of
which developed from Old English adjective suffixes
-ol, -ul, -el. The Old English forms are cognate with Old
Frisian -ol, -el, Old Saxon and Old High German -al, -il,
and Gothic -ils, -uls.
-le® a suffix forming verbs expressing repeated action
or movement (frequentative) as in sparkle, wriggle,
paddle, bubble and earlier sometimes apparently hav-
ing a diminutive sense. A few modern examples exist
from Old English, including nestle, twinkle, and wres-
tle, but most such words are of Middle and modern
English formation, such as the imitative words babble,
crackle, giggle, and mumble.
Modern English -le developed from Middle English
-elen, -len, both of which developed from Old English
-lian; cognate with Old Frisian -lia, Old Saxon and Old
High German -/én, and Old Icelandic -/a.

## This
This suffix is equivalent in sense to -er’, as in clatter,
jabber, putter.

mentation and raise dough. 1340 levain, in Ayenbite of
Inwyt; later leven (probably before 1425) and Jeaven
(1471); borrowed from Old French Jevain, from Latin
levamen alleviation, mitigation (literally, a lifting),
from levare to raise; see LEVER. —V. raise with a leaven;
make (dough) light or lighter. Before 1400 Jevainen, in
a translation of Lanfranc’s Science of Surgery; from the
noun.

## lecher
lecher n. lewd person. Probably before 1200 lecchur, in
Ancrene Riwle; later, in compounds lecher- (1280), and
the usual spelling lechour (from about 1300 to the
1600’s); borrowed from Old French Jechéor licker,
from lechier to lick, from Frankish (compare Old High
German leck6én to LICK). —lecherous adj. About 1300,
probably formed from Middle English Jecher- and lech-
erie lechery + -ous; but compare rare Old French le-
cheros, from lechéor licker as a possible alternative
source. —lechery n. Probably before 1200 Jeccherie, in
Ancrene Riwle; lecherie (probably about 1200); bor-
rowed from Old French J/echerie, from lechier to lick;
for suffix see -Y°.

## lecithin
lecithin n. fatty substance found in plant or animal tis-
sues. 1923, borrowed from French /écithine (Greek
lékithos egg yolk + French -ine -INE? chemical suffix).

## lectern
lectern n. reading desk or stand. Before 1425 lectryne;
also lectorne (1440); alterations (influenced by Medi-
eval Latin Jectrinum lectern) of earlier Jettorne (about
1390), Jetrune (before 1425); borrowed from Old
French Jetrin, leitrun. The Old French forms were
adaptations of Medieval Latin Jectrinum and Late
Latin Jectrum lectern, from Latin Jegere to read; see
LEGEND.

## lecture
lecture n. Probably before 1300, literature, written
works, in Kyng Alisaunder; later, reading, learning
from books (probably before 1387, in a version of Piers
Plowman ), and lectour reading aloud (about 1443);
borrowed through Old French J/ecture, and directly
from Medieval Latin Jectura a reading, lecture, from
Latin legere to read, see LEGEND; for suffix see -URE.
The sense of a planned talk or discourse, especially

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:618 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: ledge | leg | 586 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:618 COLUMN:1 -->
one given to a class, is first recorded in 1536, probably
borrowed from Middle French (1498). The sense of a
reprimand or scolding is found in Shakespeare’s As You
Like It (1600).
—v. give a lecture. About 1590, from the noun. The
sense of reprimand or scold is first recorded in 1706.
—lecturer n. 1583; formed from English Jecture + -er'.

## ledge
ledge n. narrow shelf. 1272-73 legge crossbar on a door;
later ledge (1452); perhaps formed from leggen to
place, LAY}. For a note on spelling see DRUDGE. The
sense of a narrow shelf appeared in 1558.

## ledger
ledger n. 1481, book that lies in a permanent place,
especially a large copy of a breviary; probably from
leggen to place, LAY! (perhaps in imitation of Dutch
ligger, legger one that lies down, a book kept for refer-
ence); for suffix see -ER'. The sense of a book of ac-
counts is first recorded in 1588, as a shortened form of
ledger-book a book containing records, book of ac-
counts (1553).

## lee
lee n. shelter, sheltered side. Probably about 1200
leohe; later le (before 1325, in Cursor Mundi ); devel-
oped from Old English (before 725) hléo shelter, pro-
tection. Old English h/éo is cognate with Old Frisian hii
shelter, protection, Old Saxon hleo, Middle Low Ger-
man /é, modern Dutch /ij lee side, Old Icelandic hlé lee
side, shelter (Swedish 14, Danish Jae, Norwegian Ie), also
hly warmth, and modern German Lee lee. The Ger-
manic forms are cognate with Sanskrit sara4d- autumn,
Lithuanian Si/ti; become warm, and Latin calére be hot,
from Indo-European *Kel-/KI-, kl-eu- (Pok.551). The
specialized sense of the sheltered side (of a ship, etc.)
appeared in Middle English probably about 1400.
—adj. sheltered from the wind. 1513; from the noun.
—leeward (lé’ ward; Nautical lii’ard) adj. 1666, situated
away from the wind; formed from English lee + -ward.
An earlier and obsolete sense of the adjective was “that
makes much leeway” (applied to a ship); it appeared
before 1618, in Raleigh’s writings. The adverb use is
first recorded in 1785. —leeway n. 1669, sideways drift
of a ship (away from the wind); formed from English Jee
+ way. The figurative sense of extra space is first re-
corded in Scott’s Journal (1827).
leech! n. bloodsucking worm. Probably about 1150
leche; developed from Old English l@ce (before 900),
Kentish /yce bloodsucking worm; cognate with Middle
Dutch lieke leech, of unknown origin. The form and
sense in Middle English were transferred to leche
physician, LEECH?, by early folk-etymology; however,
the meaning of physician eventually became obsolete,
leaving only the adopted sense of a bloodsucking
worm. The figurative sense of a person who is a para-
site, is first recorded in 1784.
leech? n. Archaic. physician. Probably before 1200
leche, developed from Old English (about 900) /#ce;
cognate with Old Frisian /étza physician, Old Saxon
laki, Old High German J/ahhi, Old Icelandic Jaknir
(Swedish /aka to heal, lakare physician, Danish lege,
Norwegian /ege (to heal, physician), and Gothic /ékeis
physician, from Proto-Germanic *l#kjaz one who
counsels, cognate with Greek Jégein say, and Latin
legere read, from Indo-European */eg- gather, pick
(Pok. 658).

## leek
leek n. onionlike vegetable. Before 1300 Jek, devel-
oped from Old English: Mercian (about 700) lc, -léc
(in compound garléc garlic), West Saxon (about 1000)
léac leek, onion, garlic; both Old English forms are

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:618 COLUMN:2 -->
cognate with Old Saxon lok leek, Middle Dutch looc
(modern Dutch Jook ), Old High German Jouh (modern
German Lauch ), and Old Icelandic Jaukr (Swedish Idk,
Danish lag, Norwegian lok, lauk), from Proto-Ger-
manic *Jauka-; related to Old English Jocc curl of hair,
LOCK?.

## leer
leer v. give a sly, sidelong look. 1530, in Palsgrave’s
Lesclarcissement, probably developed from (obsolete)
leer cheek, face, countenance; in turn developed from
Middle English Jer (probably before 1300); earlier leor
(probably before 1200). The Middle English forms de-
veloped from Old English (about 700) Aléor, originally,
area near the ear, from Proto-Germanic *Hleuzas, cog-
nate with Old Slavic sluchti hearing, from Indo-Euro-
pean *kleu-so-s (Pok.607). Old English hléor is also
cognate with Old Saxon hleor cheek, Middle Dutch
liere, Middle Low German l/er, and Old Icelandic Alyr.
—n. 1598, in Shakespeare’s Merry Wives of Windsor;
from the verb. —leery adj. 1718, alert, wide-awake;
formed from archaic English Jeer adj., looking slyly +
-y'. The sense of wary, doubtful, suspicious, appeared
in American English in George Ade’s Artie (1896).

## lees
lees n.pl. dregs, sediment. About 1380 lies, in Chaucer’s
House of Fame; borrowed from Old French lies, plural
of lie sediment, probably from Celtic (compare Old
Irish lige bed, cognate with Old English licgan to re-
cline, LIE?).

## left
left adj. Probably before 1200 Jift, luft, leoft, in Laya-
mon’s Chronicle of Britain; later left (Kentish dialect,
before 1333 and northern British dialects before 1325);
developed from Old English /yft- weak (not recorded
in Kentish dialect of Old English); cognate with Middle
Low German Jucht and Middle Dutch Jucht, Juft left,
from Indo-European *lup-t-, root *(s)/leup-/(s)lup-
(Pok.964). The Old English sense of ““weak” (as in lyft-
adl lameness, paralysis) apparently arises ultimately
from the fact that the left hand is generally the weaker
of the two hands. —adv. on or to the left side. Before
1325, in Cursor Mundi; from the adjective. —n. left side
or hand. Probably about 1200 Juft, later left (before
1325); from the adjective. Left, in the sense of the
members of a legislative body assigned to the left side
of the chamber is first recorded in Carlyle’s The
French Revolution (1837), probably a loan translation
of French la gauche (1791).
According to the OED, “This use originated in the
French National Assembly of 1789, in which the nobles
as a body took the position of honour on the President’s
right, and the Third Estate [persons not of the nobility
or clergy] sat on his left. The significance of these posi-
tions, which was at first ceremonial, soon became politi-
cal,” and the left side of a legislative chamber was
assigned by custom to those holding political views con-
sidered liberal in the 19th century. In the 20th century
Left is more broadly applied to include members as-
sociated with socialism and communism.
—leftist n. 1924 Leftist person with liberal or radical
political ideas; formed from English Left, n. + -ist;
perhaps modeled after French gauchiste. —left field
(1857, American English) —leftover n. (1891); adj.
(1897) —left wing (1884, in William James’ Will to Be-
lieve ) —left winger (1891) —lefty n. left-handed person
(1886); left winger in politics (1935).

## leg
leg n. Probably before 1300, in Kyng Alisaunder; bor-
rowed from a Scandinavian source (compare Old Ice-
landic leggr leg, bone, Norwegian legg, Danish leg,
and Swedish /agg ), from Proto-Germanic *lazjaz. The

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:619 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: legacy | 587 | legume -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:619 COLUMN:1 -->
Scandinavian forms are cognate with Old English lira
fleshy part of the body, Greek Jax, adv., with the heel
or foot, /aktizein to kick with the foot, and possibly with
Sanskrit rksala foot joint of a hoofed animal, from Indo-
European *Jek-/lok-/]k- (Pok.673). —leggings n.pl.
(1751) —leggy adj. (1787)

## legacy
legacy n. money or other property left by a will. About
1384, function or office of a deputy or legate, in the
Wycliffe Bible; borrowed from Old French legacie,
from Medieval Latin Jegatia, from Latin légare appoint
by a last will, bequeath, send as a LEGATE; for suffix see
-ACY. The sense of property left by a will appeared in
Scottish about 1460. —legatee n. one to whom a legacy
is left. 1679-88, formed from English legate, v. (1546,
borrowed from Latin /égatus, past participle of /égare
bequeath) + -ee.

## legal
legal adj. 1447, in Bokenham’s Legends of Holy
Women; borrowed from Middle French Jégal, learned
borrowing from Latin Jégalis legal, from /éx (genitive
légis ) law, possibly related to Jegere to gather, see LEG-
END; for suffix see -AL!. Doublet of LOYAL. —legality n.
1459 legalite; borrowed from Medieval Latin legalitas,
from Latin /égalis legal; for suffix see -1ITy. —legaliza-
tion n. 1805, formed from English legalize + -ation.
—legalize v. Before 1716, formed from English legal +
-ize. —legally adv. (1561) —legal aid (1890) —legal
tender (1740)

## legate
legate (leg’it) n. ambassador, representative. Before
1121, a representative of the Pope; borrowed through
Old French Jegat, and directly from Latin Jégatus,
originally, provided with a commission, past participle
of Jégare send as a deputy, send with a commission,
bequeath, from /éx (genitive Jégis ) contract, law, see
LEGAL; for suffix see -ATE®. —legatee n. See under
LEGACY. —legation n. Before 1400 Jegacyoun diplo-
matic mission; borrowed through Old French Jegation,
and directly from Latin /égationem (nominative léga-
tid), from Jégare send as a deputy, see LEGATE; for
suffix see -ATION.

## legato
legato (liga’t6) adj. Music. smooth and connected, with-
out breaks between successive tones. 1811, borrowed
from Italian Jegato bound, past participle of Jegare to
bind, from Latin Jigare to bind; see LIGAMENT.

## legend
legend n. Probably before 1325, story of the life of a
saint; borrowed from Old French legende, learned bor-
rowing from Medieval Latin, or borrowed directly
from Medieval Latin legenda legend, story; originally,
(things) to be read (on certain days in church, etc.),
from Latin, neuter plural gerundive of Jegere to read,
gather, select. Latin legere is cognate with Greek /é-
gein to speak, tell, say, gather, choose, /6gos word,
speech, account, reason.
The extended sense of a nonhistorical or mythical
story is first recorded in 1386. The sense of a writing or
inscription (from French but ultimately derived from
the Medieval Latin meaning of “things to be read”’) is
first recorded in Cotgrave’s Dictionary (1611).
—legendary adj. 1563-87 legendarie of the nature of a
legend, celebrated in legend; possibly through French;
but more likely borrowed directly from Medieval Latin
legendarius, from legenda (things) to be read; for suffix
see -ARY.

## legerdemain
legerdemain (lej ardaman’) n. sleight of hand, conjuring
tricks. Probably about 1430 legerdemeyn; borrowed
from Middle French Jéger de main quick of hand (/éger
light, from Vulgar Latin *Jeviarius, from Latin levis

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:619 COLUMN:2 -->
LIGHT? not heavy; de of, from, from Latin dé from; and
main hand, from Latin manus; see MANUAL).

## legible
legible adj. Probably before 1440; borrowed from Late
Latin Jegibilis that can be read, from Latin legere to
read, see LEGEND; for suffix see -IBLE. —legibility n.
1679, formed from English Jegible + -ity. —legibly
adv. 1586, formed from English legible + -ly.

## legion
legion n. body of soldiers, army. Probably before 1200
legiun Roman legion, in Layamon’s Chronicle of Brit-
ain; later legioun (about 1280); borrowed from Old
French Jegion, legiun, learned borrowing from Latin
legidnem (nominative legid ) a body of soldiers in the
Roman army, from legere to choose, gather (as for an
army), see LEGEND; for suffix see -ION.
The sense of a very large number is first recorded in
English about 1378, in a version of Piers Plowman. It
comes from the Biblical reference in Mark 5:9: “My
name is Legion, for we are many.” The military legion
suggests a host or great number, as the ancient Roman
legion consisting of between three and six thousand
soldiers.
—legionary adj. 1408, belonging to a legion, borrowed
from Latin legiénarius, from legidnem (nominative leg-
10 ); for suffix see -ARY.—n. member of a legion. 1598,
from the adjective, or borrowed from Middle French
légionnaire (1495, and found once in Old French,
1265). —legionnaire (léjanar’) n. member of a legion,
1818, in Shelley’s Letters, borrowed from French /é-
gionnaire, from Old French Jegion legion.

## legislator
legislator n. 1605, borrowed, probably from French
législateur, and directly from Latin Jégis lator proposer
of a law; Jégis, genitive of léx law (see LEGAL); lator
proposer, a form serving as agent noun of ferre to carry,
BEAR?; for suffix see -OR?. —legislate v. 1805, back for-
mation from Jegislator, legislation; for suffix see -ATE!.
—legislation n. Before 1655, probably borrowed from
French J/égislation, learned borrowing of Late Latin
législationem (nominative Jégislatid ) enactment of a
law or laws, from Latin Jégis (genitive of Jéx law) + Jatio
a bringing, a form serving as abstract noun of ferre to
carry, bring, BEAR?; for suffix see -TION. It is also possi-
ble that in some instances legislation was formed after
English Jegisla(tor) + -tion; compare LEGISLATIVE.
—legislative adj. About 1641, formed (probably
through influence of French Jégislatif) from English
legislat(or ) + -ive. —legislature n. Before 1676, legisla-
tive body, formed from English legislat(or ) + -ure.

## legitimate
legitimate adj. rightful, lawful. Before 1464 Jegitimat
lawfully begotten; later, lawful (1638); borrowed from
past participle of Middle French Jegitimer (from Medi-
eval Latin Jegitimare) and directly from Medieval
Latin legitimatus, past participle of legitimare make
lawful, from Latin Jégitimus lawful; originally, in line
with the law, from Jéx (genitive /égis ) law; see LEGAL;
for suffix see -ATE®. —legitimacy n. 1691, formed froin
English legitimate, adj. + -cy. —legitimize v. 1848,
formed in English from Latin lJégitimus lawful +
English -ize.

## legume
legume (leg’yiim) n. plant having a number of seeds in
a pod, such as beans, peas, etc. 1676, borrowing of
French /égume, learned borrowing from Latin Jegu-
men, of uncertain origin.
According to the ancient Roman scholar Varro, legu-
men derives from legere to gather, in allusion to the
fact that the plant’s fruit may be gathered by hand.
Ernout and Meillet suggest that the word is of non-

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:620 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: lei | lenticular | 588 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:620 COLUMN:1 -->
Indo-European origin, but provided with a Latin end-
ing.
—leguminous adj. 1656, in Blount’s Glossographia,
probably borrowed from French /égumineux, from
Latin legiimen (genitive Jegaminis) + French -eux
-ous. Leguminous also appeared in Middle English
(probably before 1425, in a translation of Chauliac’s
Grande Chirurgie) in the sense of “containing meal
made from the seeds of legumes.”

## lei
lei (1a) n. garland of flowers, shells, etc. 1843, inJ. Jarves’
History of the Hawaiian or Sandwich Islands; borrowed
from Hawaiian, in which the word means any orna-
ment worn about the neck or around the head, usually
one given as a symbol of affection.

## leisure
leisure n. Probably before 1300 Jeiser time free from
work or duties, in Kyng Alisaunder; borrowed from Old
French leisir permission, leisure, from Jeisir, v., be per-
mitted, from Latin licére be permitted; see LICENSE.
The spelling /eisure appeared in English in the 1500’s
and was used by Shakespeare. It was probably in-
fluenced in form by words ending in -ure, such as
measure. —leisurely adv. (1486); adj. (1604)

## leitmotif or leitmotiv
leitmotif or leitmotiv (lit’motéf’) n. recurring musical
theme associated with a particular person, situation,
etc. 1876, borrowing of German Leitmotiy, literally,
leading motive (Jeiten to guide, LEAD! + Motiv motive,
from French motif MOTIF). The extended sense of any
recurring theme, as in a novel or a conversation, is first
recorded in Havelock Ellis’ writings, in 1896.

## lemma
lemma (lem’a) n. theme, subject, glossed word. 1570,
subsidiary proposition in mathematics; later, heading
or theme (1601, in Ben Jonson’s The Poetaster ); bor-
rowing of Latin Jémma a theme, from Greek /émma
anything received or taken, see DILEMMA. The sense of
a word or phrase glossed (as in a glossary) appeared in
1896. —lemmatize v. group together all inflected or
various forms of a word. 1967, formed from English
Jemmata, pl. (from Greek /émmata, plural of Iémma )
+ -ize. —lemmatization n. (1967)

## lemming
lemming n. small, mouselike arctic animal. 1713, bor-
rowing of Norwegian lemming, lemende, related to
Old Icelandic /Jomundr, laemingi, laemingr lemming, of
uncertain origin (possibly the barker; cognate with
Latin Jatrare, Old Slavic Jajati, Lithuanian /6ti to bark).

## lemon
lemon n. About 1400 /ymon, in Maundeville’s Travels;
borrowed from Old French Jimon (probably influenced
by Old Provengal limon, or Italian limone ), from Ara-
bic liman, from Persian Jimt (n ). The shift in spelling
to e that was a natural development in late Middle
English and early modern English did not occur until
the mid-1600’s in lemon. The slang sense of a worthless
person or thing is first recorded in 1906 in American
English. —lemonade n. 1663, borrowed from French
limonade, from Old French Jimon lemon; for suffix see
-ADE.

## lemur
lemur (lé’mor) n. animal somewhat like a monkey.
1795, New Latin Jemures, a name given by Linnaeus
from Latin Jemurés, pl., specters, ghosts; so called be-
cause of the animal’s nocturnal habits and ghostlike
appearance. Latin Jemurés is of uncertain origin, per-
haps cognate with Greek Jamyros greedy, gluttonous,
or with J4mia monster.

## lend
lend v. Probably about 1375 lenden, alteration of ear-
lier Jenen (probably before 1200, in Layamon’s Chroni-
cle of Britain ); developed from Old English (before 725
lznan to lend, from /@n LOAN.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:620 COLUMN:2 -->
According to the OED, the substitution of lend- for
len-, which began early in Middle English, was due to
the influence of the past tense /Jende and to association
with many words in -end, such as bend, rend, send,
wend.

## length
length n. 1122 Jengthe; developed from Old English
(about 893) Jengthu; cognate with Old Frisian lengethe
length, Middle Low German and Middle Dutch Jen-
gede, and Old Icelandic lengd, from Proto-Germanic
*Jangitho; derived from the Germanic root that was the
source of Old English Jang LONG!, adj. —lengthen v.
About 1450 Jenthenen, formed from Middle English
lengthe length + -enen -en!. —lengthwise adv. (about
1580); adj. (1871) —lengthy adj. 1689, American
English; formed from length+ -y!.

## lenient
lenient adj. 1652, softening, soothing, relaxing; bor-
rowed from Middle French Jenient, from Latin /énien-
tem (nominative /éniéns ), present participle of /énire
soften, from /énis mild; for suffix see -ENT. The Latin
lénis was probably an altered form (under the influence
of ségnis sluggish or mollis soft) of earlier */énos, cog-
nate with Lithuanian /énas quiet, tame, slow, Greek
lédein be tired, and Gothic Jétan permit, from Indo-
European */é (i )- leave, relax (Pok.666).
The sense of mild, gentle, merciful is first recorded
in English in 1787, probably influenced by the mean-
ing of Jenity mildness, gentleness. —lenience n. 1796,
formed from English lenient + -ence. —leniency n.
1780, formed from English lenient + -cy.
While lenient, lenience, etc. are not always exact
synonyms for Jenitive, lenity, etc., the former group of
words has generally replaced the words in English de-
veloped around Jenity, except in ecology and phonetics
where lenis, lenitic, and lenition have developed spe-
cialized meanings.

## lenity
lenity (len’até) n. mildness, gentleness, mercifulness.
1548 lenitie, borrowed from Middle French Jénité,
learned borrowing from Latin /énitatem (nominative
lénitas ), from Jénis mild, see LENIENT; for suffix see
-ITY. In Middle English (probably before 1425, in a
translation of Chauliac’s Grande Chirurgie ) the word
was used in medicine with form Jenite and the sense of
“softness.” The figurative use of 1548 was probably a
reborrowing of the Middle French word.

## lens
lens n. 1693, New Latin Jens a shaped piece of glass for
focusing rays of light, from Latin /éns (genitive Jentis )
LENTIL (in reference to its seeds which have a double-
convex shape similar to an optical lens).

## Lent
Lent n. the forty days before Easter. Before 1387 Jente,
in Trevisa’s translation of Higden’s Polychronicon, a
shortened form of earlier Jenten spring, lent (1123);
developed from Old English (about 700) Jencten
spring. The Old English form is cognate with Old Saxon
and Middle Dutch /Jentin spring (modern Dutch J/ente ),
and Old High German lengizin, lenzin, Jenzo (modern
German, poetic Lenz), all probably derived from a
Proto-Germanic compound */anga-tinaz, made up of
the root that was the source of Old English lang LONG!
and that of Gothic -teins (in sinteins daily), cognate with
Lithuanian diena day, Old Slavic dini, Sanskrit dina-m,
and Latin diés (see DEITY). The probable reference is
to the lengthening of the days as characterizing the
season of spring. Only in English did the ecclesiastical
meaning of Lent develop; among the other Germanic
languages the meaning remained confined to spring.

## lenticular
lenticular (lentik’yalor) adj. having the form of a lens.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:621 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: lentil | less | 589 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:621 COLUMN:1 -->
Probably before 1425, shaped like a lentil, in a transla-
tion of Chauliac’s Grande Chirurgie; borrowed from
Middle French Jenticulaire, and from Latin lenticularis
having the shape of a lentil, from Jenticula LENTIL; for
suffix see -AR.

## lentil
lentil n. a plant whose pods contain seeds shaped like
a double-convex lens. About 1250, in Genesis and Ex-
odus; borrowed from Old French lentille, from Vulgar
Latin *Jenticula, from Latin lenticula, diminutive of
léns (genitive Jentis ) lentil, possibly from the same un-
known source as Old High German Jinsin (modern Ger-
man Linse ), and Old Slavic lesta, both meaning lentil.

## lento
lento (len’t6) adj., adv. Music. slow, slowly. 1724, bor-
rowing of Italian Jento slow, from Latin Jentus slow,
lasting, flexible; see LITHE.

## Yenvoi or l’envoy
Yenvoi or l’envoy (len’voi) n. short concluding passage;
postscript, especially to a book or poem. Probably
before 1439 Jenvoie, in Lydgate’s Falls of Princes; bor-
rowed from Middle French /’envoy dedication, post-
script; literally, the message (/’, contraction of Je the;
envoy message; see ENVOY? a separate borrowing, but
a parallel form, found about 1380, in Chaucer’s writ-
ings).

## leonine
leonine (lé’anin) adj. of or like a lion. About 1375, in
Chaucer’s Canterbury Tales; borrowed from Old
French leonin, from Latin Jedninus belonging to a lion,
from Jeo (genitive lednis ) LION; for suffix see -INE?.

## leopard
leopard n. Probably before 1300 Jeuparz, lipard; bor-
rowed from Old French Jeupart, leupard, lipard,
learned borrowing from Late Latin leopardus, from
Greek ledpardos (lé6n LION + pardos male panther,
PARD!; the leopard originally being thought a hybrid
animal). The spelling leopard appeared in Middle
English about 1330, apparently borrowed from Late
Latin.
The English pronunciation (lep’ard) reflects that of
Old French Jeupart, leupard. The modern French
léopard has been refashioned on the basis of Latin and
is pronounced (la6par’).

## leotard
leotard (lé’atard) n. tight-fitting one-piece garment.
1920, in allusion to Jules Léotard, 1830-1870, a French
trapeze artist who performed in Paris and London
wearing such a garment.

## leper
leper n. Before 1398 Jepre person who has leprosy, in
Trevisa’s translation of Bartholomew’s De _ Pro-
prietatibus Rerum, perhaps developed from /eprous or,
more likely from attributive use of earlier Jepre leprosy
(about 1250, in Genesis and Exodus ), borrowed from:
1) Old French liepre, lepre leprosy, learned borrowing
from Late Latin Jepra, and 2) probably directly from
Late Latin Jepra (in Latin, only Jeprae, pl.), from Greek
lépra leprosy, formed from the feminine of Jeprés, adj.,
scaly, from /épos a scale, which is related to /épein to
peel, lopds a peel, cognate with Lithuanian /apas leaf,
from Indo-European *lep-/lop- (Pok.678). —leprosy n.
1535, in the Coverdale Bible; developed from earlier
lepruse (probably before 1450), from /eprus, variant of
LEPROUS; for suffix see -y°. Middle English lepruse re-
placed the @arlier /Jepre leprosy (about 1250); see LEP-
ER. —leprous adj. Probably before 1200 Jeprus in
Ancrene Riwle; later leprous (about 1280); borrowed
from Old French lepros and Late Latin Jeprosus, from
lepra leprosy, see LEPER; for suffix see -OUS.

## lepidopterous
lepidopterous (lep’adop’taras) adj. belonging to the
order of insects with scaly wings, including butterflies
and moths. 1797, formed in English from New Latin

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:621 COLUMN:2 -->
Lepidoptera, pl., the order name (Greek lepis, genitive
lepidos , fish scale, related to Jépein to peel; see LEPER
+ pterén wing, FEATHER) + English -ous.

## leprechaun
leprechaun (lep’rakon) n. in Irish folklore, a sprite or
goblin resembling a little old man. 1604 Jubrican; bor-
rowed from Irish Jupracan, alteration of Old Irish Ju-
chorpan (lu little + corpan, diminutive of corp body,
from Latin corpus; see CORPSE). The spelling lepre-
chaun appeared in 1860. The Irish word has several
variant forms, the one closest to leprechaun being lei-
preachan.

## lepton
lepton n. Physics. any of a class of light, weakly interact-
ing elementary particles. 1948, any elementary parti-
cle of small mass, formed in English from Greek Jeptés
small, thin, delicate; literally, peeled (related to /épein
to peel; see LEPER) + English suffix -on. The current
meaning appeared about 1969 to distinguish the group
of leptons from hadrons.

## lesbian
lesbian adj. 1601 Lesbian of or relating to the Greek
island of Lesbos (in the northeastern Aegean sea); later
Lesbian of or relating to homosexual relations between
women (1890); borrowed from Latin Lesbius of Lesbos,
from Greek Lésbios, from Lésbos Lesbos. The second
(and now common) meaning developed because of the
reputed homosexuality of Sappho, the Greek lyric
woman poet of Lesbos. The lower-case form lesbian is
first recorded in the 1960’s, though certain derived
forms, such as Jesbie have been recorded in lower-case
since the 1920’s. —n. homosexual woman. 1925 Lesbi-
an, in Aldous Huxley’s Letters; from the adjective.
—lesbianism n. female homosexuality. 1870 Lesbian-
ism, formed from English Lesbian of Lesbos + -ism.

## lese-majesty
lese-majesty (léz’maj’asté) n. crime against the sover-
eign power, treason. 1536, borrowing of Middle
French lése-majesté, learned borrowing from Latin
crimen laesae majestatis charge of insulted sovereignty
(laesa, feminine past participle of laedere to damage,
see LESION; majestatis, genitive of majestas MAJESTY).
The form in Latin appears about one hundred years
earlier in Lydgate’s Falls of Princes (probably before
1439).

## lesion
lesion (lé’zhan) n. injury, damage. Probably before
1425 lesioun bodily injury, in a translation of Chauliac’s
Grande Chirurgie; borrowed from Middle French le-
sion, from Latin Jaesionem (nominative Jaesio ) injury,
from Jaedere to strike, hurt, damage, of uncertain ori-
gin; for suffix see -SION. —v. cause a lesion in. 1972,
from the noun.

## less
less adj. About 1125 Izsse the younger or smaller (in
importance); later lesse, lasse (about 1150). The forms
in Middle English developed from a fusion of Old
English I@s, adv. (before 725), and la@ssa, adj. (about
725, in Beowulf) comparative of las (from Proto-Ger-
manic *Jaisiz), which is cognate with Old Frisian and
Old Saxon Jés less, Middle High German, Middle Low
German, and Middle Dutch lise soft or gentle, modern
German leise soft, gentle, slight. Outside Germanic the
word is cognate with Lithuanian Jjesas thin, and Greek
liards mild or gentle, loisthos last, from Indo-European
*Jeis-/lois-/lis- (Pok.662). —adv. Probably about 1175
lesse, lasse, developed from Old English Jés. —n. Prob-
ably about 1175 Jesse, developed from a fusion of Old
English Izésse (about 1000, from Jéssa, adj.) and les
(about 725, in Beowulf, from the adv.). —lessen v. Prob-
ably about 1380 Jesnen make less; later lessenen (prob-
ably before 1400), from earlier Jessen (probably about

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:622 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: -less | leuco- | 590 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:622 COLUMN:1 -->
1200), formed from Jesse, adj. + -en!. —lesser adj. (as
in the lesser evil). About 1225, comparative of Jess,
formed from Middle English lesse + -er?. —adv. less.
1594, in Shakespeare’s Richard III, now generally ar-
chaic except, since about 1960, in Jesser-known (for less
well-known ), formed by analogy with better-known.
-less a suffix meaning without a , that has no
, as in childless, homeless; that does not
, as in tireless; that cannot be ed, as in
countless. Middle English -lesse, developed from Old
English -Jéas, from Jéas free from, without. The Old
English forms are cognate with Old Saxon /ds loose,
Middle Dutch and modern Dutch Jos, Old High Ger-
man 16s (modern German los, lose ), Old Icelandic lauss,
and Gothic Jaus empty, from Proto-Germanic *Jausaz,
Indo-European *lou-so-s (Pok.682).

## lesson
lesson n. something learned. Probably before 1200 les-
ceun, in Ancrene Riwle; later lessoun (about 1300); bor-
rowed from Old French lecon, from Latin /éctionem
(nominative /éctid ) a reading, from Jegere read; see
LEGEND.
The earliest recorded meaning of lesson in Middle
English was a portion from the Bible or other sacred
writing read aloud to the congregation. This was fol-
lowed by the meanings of something designed to be
read or listened to (probably before 1300) and some-
thing set to be learned by a student, a lesson for formal
study (before 1300).

## lest
lest conj. for fear that. Probably before 1200 Jeste, in
Layamon’s Chronicle of Britain, contraction of the
phrase Jes te less that, developed from Old English
(about 1000) thy l@s the whereby less that (thy, instru-
mental case of thaet THAT; Is LESS; the, relative parti-
cle, Old English thé, the, a worn-down form of
Proto-Germanic demonstrative stem *tha- ).
let! v. allow, permit. 1106 Jeten, developed from Old
English (before 725) /#tan, /étan to allow, let, let go,
rent. The Old English forms are cognate with Old Fri-
sian Jéta to let, Old Saxon Jatan, Middle Dutch, modern
Dutch, and Middle Low German Jaten, Old High Ger-
man /azzan (modern German lassen), Old Icelandic
lata, and Gothic /étan, from Proto-Germanic */€tanan.
Cognates outside Germanic are found in Latin lassus
weary, Albanian /’oth I tire, and Lithuanian /éisti to let,
from Indo-European */éid-/léd-/lad- (Pok. 666).
The shortening of the vowel from Old English /étan
and Jétan (which through the Proto-Germanic root
*lz@t- developed from */éd- and is related to *Jat- the
Proto-Germanic root of English Jate ) has not been ac-
counted for.
let? v. Archaic. prevent, hinder. Before 1121 Jztten;
later letten (probably before 1200); developed from
Old English Jettan hinder or delay (before 889, in Al-
fred’s translation of Boethius’ De Consolatione Philoso-
phiae ). Old English Jettan is cognate with Old Saxon
lettian to hinder, Middle Dutch Jetten, Old High Ger-
man Jezzen to delay or hurt (modern German verletz-
en to hurt), Old Icelandic Jetja hold back, and Gothic
latjan, from Proto-Germanic *Jatjanan; all derived from
the Proto-Germanic root that was the source of Old
English Jaet LATE. —n. prevention, hindrance. Prob-
ably before 1200 Jette; from the verb. The sense of
interference with the ball in tennis and similar games
is first recorded in 1871, though now many amateurs at
tennis in America call a let ball, a net ball.
-let a suffix meaning: little, as in booklet, leaflet; thing

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:622 COLUMN:2 -->
worn as a band on, as in anklet. Middle English -let;
borrowed from Old French -elet, a compound formed
of -e/ (from Latin -ellus, diminutive suffix, or -a/e, neu-
ter of -alis -AL!) + -et -ET. The suffix -let was not com-
mon in English before the 1700’s.

## lethal
lethal adj. causing death, deadly. 1583, borrowed from
Late Latin /éthalis, an alteration with th of Latin /étalis,
from /étum death, of uncertain origin (perhaps from an
Indo-European */é-to-m a slackening, root */éi-, Pok.
666); or with Etruscan connection (compare Etruscan
leine he is dead, Leinth goddess of the underworld); for
suffix see -AL!. The development of the Late Latin
form with th came by association with Latin Léthé,
name in classical mythology for a river in Hades, the
waters of which when drunk caused forgetfulness of
the past. The Romans borrowed Léthé from Greek
Jéthé forgetfulness, along with the mythology associat-
ed with Léthés hydér the name of the river in Greek
mythology (literally, water of Lethe). —lethality n.
1656, formed from English Jethal + -ity.

## lethargy
lethargy n. drowsy dullness, sluggishness. 1373 litarge,
also litargie (about 1380), and letargye (about 1410);
borrowed from Old French litargie, letargie, or direct-
ly from Medieval Latin litargia, from Late Latin
léthargia, from Greek Jéthargia, from léthargos forget-
ful; originally, inactive through forgetfulness (Jéthé for-
getfulness, related to Janthanein escape notice + argos
idle, from a- without + érgon woRK); for suffix see
- Y°.The spelling Jethargy (with th) is first recorded
about 1593, influenced by the Latin and Greek forms.
—lethargic adj. Before 1398 Jitargik, in Trevisa’s trans-
lation of Bartholomew’s De Proprietatibus Rerum; bor-
rowed from Old French litargique, lethargique, from
Latin J/éthargicus, from Greek Jéthargikds, from
léthargia \ethargy; for suffix see -IC.
The difference in the Old French forms Jitargie, le-
targie for the noun and Jethargique (litargique a one-
time occurrence) for the adjective demonstrates the
vagaries of tracing forms. Surely with only 25 years
between the recording of the noun and the adjective
in Middle English, both forms (in -it- and -eth- must
have existed side-by-side in Old French, though the
record is incomplete on this point.

## letter
letter n. Probably about 1150 Jettre knowledge of read-
ing and writing, book learning; later alphabetic sign,
written message (probably before 1200, in Ancrene
Riwle ); borrowing of Old French Jettre, from Latin
littera, earlier litera (spelled leitera ) letter of the alpha-
bet, litterae, pl., epistle, written documents, literature,
probably related to linere smear, rub out; see LINI-
MENT. It has been suggested (especially by Hesychius,
who was notorious for his improved words and asser-
tions) that Latin littera was borrowed (through Etrus-
can) from Greek diphthéra tablet, since the Latin
alphabet was adopted from the Greek. However, this
theory has everything against it: the development of 1
from d (in spite of such examples as Odysseus; Ulixes )
and the earlier Latin -eit- for expected -ipt-.
—v. 1668, mark with letters; from the noun.
—letterhead n. (before 1887) —letter-perfect adj. (1845)

## lettuce
lettuce n. About 1300 Jetuse; borrowed from Old
French Jaitués, plural of laitué, from Latin Jactuca let-
tuce, from Jac (genitive Jactis ) milk; so called from the
milky juice of the plant; see GALAXY. The slang sense
of paper money (from the green color) was first record-
ed in 1929 in American English.
leuco- or leuko- a combining form meaning white, col-

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:623 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: leucocyte | lexicology | 591 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:623 COLUMN:1 -->
orless, or slightly colored, as in leucocyte, leukemia.
Also spelled leuc- or leuk- before vowels. Borrowed
from Latin Jeuco-, from Greek Jeuko-, combining form
of leukés clear, white; see LIGHT! radiant energy.

## leucocyte
leucocyte n. white blood cell. 1870 (probably in-
fluenced by French leucocyte and German Leukocyt );
formed from English Jeuco- + -cyte.

## leukemia
leukemia n. disease characterized by a large excess of
white blood cells. 1855; formed in English from Jeuk-
white + -emia blood, after earlier German Leukamie
(1848). Another form Jeucocythzmia occurred earlier
(1852), but disappeared from the record of English in
the early 1900’s.

## Levantine
Levantine (lovan’ten) adj. of or belonging to the Le-
vant, the countries of the eastern part of the Mediter-
ranean. 1649, formed from Middle English Jevant the
Levant (1497) + -ine!. Middle English levant was a
borrowing of Middle French Jevant the Levant, the
Fast, the Orient, from Jevant, present participle of
lever to rise, from Latin Jevare to raise, from levis
LIGHT? in weight; so called because of the Levant’s
position relative to the rising sun. The capitalized form
Levant is first recorded in English in 1558. Attributive
use of Levant is recorded as early as 1503-04 in English.
—n. 1706, native of the Levant; from the adjective. The
special use of levantine (lower-case) in the sense of a
sturdy twilled silk cloth is first recorded in English in
1831 as a borrowing from French, from Middle French
levant in reference to the Levant, where this kind of
cloth was originally made and exported.
levee! (lev’é) n. bank built to keep a river from over-
flowing. 1719 levée a French word used in a descrip-
tion of New Orleans, in Justin Winsor’s Narrative and
Critical History of America; originally, feminine past
participle of Jever to raise, from Old French, from
Latin levare, from levis LIGHT? in weight. The sense of
a landing place for boats, dock, was first recorded in
1813, in American English.
levee? (lev’é) n. reception. 1672, in Dryden’s Marriage-
a-la-Mode; borrowed from French lever a rising from
bed, reception held while rising, noun use of the verb
lever to rise, raise; see LEVEE!. French kings used to
hold levees in the morning while they were getting up
and dressing.

## level
level n. 1340, device for showing whether a surface is
horizontal, flat, or even, in Ayenbite of Inwyt; bor-
rowed from Old French livel, from Vulgar Latin *Jibel-
lum, from Latin Jibella a balance, level, diminutive of
libra balance, scale, unit of weight; of uncertain origin.
The sense of a horizontal condition or position (as in
the level of the lake ) appeared in Middle English prob-
ably before 1400. The figurative sense of a position or
standard on a certain scale, degree of something (as in
level of intellect ) is found in 1609.
—v. About 1450, to make even or level; from the noun.
—adj. 1431, having an even surface, horizontal, flat;
from the noun. —level-headed adj. (1879)

## lever
lever n. About 1300 Jevour bar used for prying or dis-
lodging something; later lever (1408); borrowed from
Old French Jevier a lifter or lever (Old French leveor
with a different suffix is also sometimes cited), from
lever to raise, from Latin levare to raise, from levis
LIGHT? in weight; for suffix see -ER!. —v. move with a
lever. 1856; from the noun. —leverage n. 1724, action
of a lever; formed from English lever, n. + -age. The
figurative sense of advantage for accomplishing a pur-

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:623 COLUMN:2 -->
pose, power, influence, appeared in 1858, in Glad-
stone’s writings.

## leviathan
leviathan (lovi’athan) n. Before 1382, a huge sea animal
in the Bible; also, the Devil, in the Wycliffe Bible; bor-
rowed from Late Latin leviathan, from Hebrew livya-
than dragon, serpent, huge animal of the sea, probably
from the root of lavah he twisted, wound. The figura-
tive sense of a great and powerful person or thing is
first recorded in 1607.

## Levi's
Levi's (lé’viz) n.pl. trademark for heavy blue denim
trousers; blue jeans. 1926, American English, from the
name of Levi Strauss and Company, the original
American manufacturer of such trousers. The forms
Levis (1926) and levis (1944) are frequent alterations of
the trademark form.

## levitate
levitate v. rise or cause to rise in the air. 1673, in An-
drew Marvell’s The Rehearsal Transposed; formed in
English from Latin levitas lightness (see LEVITY) +
English -ate!, patterned on earlier gravitate. It is also
possible that Jevitate is a back formation from levita-
tion. —levitation n. 1668, in Henry More’s Divine Dia-
logues, formed in English from Latin levitas lightness
+ English -ation, patterned on earlier gravitation.

## levity
levity n. lack of seriousness, frivolity. 1564, borrowed
from Latin Jevitas (genitive Jevitatis ) lightness, frivoli-
ty, from Jevis LIGHT? in weight; for suffix see -ITY.
levo- (lev’a-) a combining form in chemistry and phys-
ics meaning toward the left, as in Jevorotatory (turning
the plane of polarized light to the left), or meaning
levorotatory, as in Jevoglucose. Borrowed from French
lévo-, from Latin laevus left, cognate with Greek Jaids
and Old Slavic /évi, from Indo-European *Jaiwés (Pok.
652).

## levy
levy n. imposition or collection of a tax, etc. 1416 leve
act of raising taxes, etc.; borrowed through Anglo-
French Jeve, from Old French Jevée act of raising, levy,
from feminine past participle of Old French Jever to
raise; see LEVER. The term is found in Anglo-French
context as early as 1227. —v. impose or collect (a tax,
etc.). 1436-37 Jeveyen; from the noun.

## lewd
lewd adj. Before 1121 lewed nonclerical, lay, unedu-
cated; developed from Old English /l#@wede (before
899, in Alfred’s translation of Bede’s Ecclesiastical His-
tory ); of uncertain origin. The sense of wicked, un-
chaste, lustful, is recorded probably about 1378 in
Wycliffe’s treatise De Officio Pastorale.

## lexeme
lexeme (lek’sém) n. Linguistics. minimal meaningful
element in the vocabulary of a language. 1940, in
Whorf’s Language, Thought, and Reality; formed in
English from Greek Jéxis word + English -eme, as in
morpheme, phoneme; see LEXICON.

## lexicographer
lexicographer (lek’sakog’rafar) n. compiler of dic-
tionaries. 1658, formed in English from French Jexico-
graphe lexicographer (1578) + English suffix -er'. The
French word was borrowed from Greek Jexikographos
(lexikén wordbook, LEXICON + graéphein to write; see
CARVE). It is also possible that lexicographer was
formed from English lexicon + -grapher, on the pat-
tern of geographer. —lexicography n. compilation of
dictionaries. 1680, formed from English lexicon +
-graphy, or from Jexicographer, on the pattern of such
pairs as geographer, geography.

## lexicology
lexicology n. study of words. 1828, borrowed from
French Jexicologie, from Greek lexikén wordbook +
French -logie -logy.

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:624 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: lexicon | liberty | 592 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:624 COLUMN:1 -->

## lexicon
lexicon (lek’sakon) n. wordbook, dictionary. 1603, bor-
rowed probably through Middle French Jexicon from
Greek lexikon (biblion ) wordbook, from neuter of lex-
ikés pertaining to words, from Jéxis word, from Jégein
say; see LEGEND. The sense of vocabulary of a language
or subject is first recorded in 1647. —lexical adj. of
words or vocabulary. 1836, formed from English lexi-
con + -al’.

## liable
liable adj. 1450, bound by law, legally subject; probably
formed with the English ending -able from Old French
lier to bind, from Latin ligare; see LIGAMENT. The
sense of likely to suffer from (something unpleasant) is
first recorded in 1593; that of subject to the possibility,
likely, in 1682. —liability n. 1794-1809; formed from
English liable + -ity.

## liaison
liaison (lé’azon or 1éa’zon) n. Before 1648, act of thick-
ening a sauce; borrowed from French Jiaison a union,
entanglement, a binding together, from Latin ligatio-
nem (nominative /igatio ) a binding, from ligare to bind;
see LIGAMENT; for suffix see -SION. The sense of a close
relation or connection between persons or groups is
first recorded in 1809, followed by that of an illicit
connection or intimacy between a man and a woman,
in Byron’s Don Juan (1821). —liaise (léaz’) v. form a
liaison. 1928 (military use); back formation from Jiaison.

## liar
liar n. before 1225 liar, lier; developed from Old
English /égere (about 950, in the gloss of the Lindis-
farne Gospels); later léogere (before 1023, in Wulf
stan ); from Anglian légan, and West Saxon léogan be
untruthful, LIE?.
The form in -ar is a common variant of -er! found in
northern dialect forms of England in such words as
syngar singer, and in such modern words as beggar,
pedlar, probably in imitation of the refashioned forms
such as scholar for scoler and pillar for piler.

## lib or Lib
lib or Lib n. 1970, American English, shortened form of
liberation (originally in Women’s Lib, short for
Women’s Liberation ). —libber n. Informal. one who
favors a liberation cause. 1971, American English,
formed from Jib + -er'.

## libation
libation n. a pouring out of wine, etc., as an offering to
a god. About 1384 libacioun, in the Wycliffe Bible; bor-
rowed from Latin Jibatidnem (nominative /ibatio),
from /ibare pour out (an offering), earlier *loibaye-,
formed from a lost *Joiba, cognate with Greek Joibé
libation, related to Jeibein to pour, from Indo-Euro-
pean *leibh-/loibh- (Walde-Pokorny II,393); for suffix
see -ATION. The sense of any liquid poured out to be
drunk is first recorded in 1751.

## libel
libel n. About 1300, formal written statement; later,
little book (about 1382, in the Wycliffe Bible); bor-
rowed through Old French Jibel, libelle and directly
from Latin libellus a little book, pamphlet, note, peti-
tion, lampoon, diminutive of liber book; see LIBRARY.
The meaning of a plaintiff's statement of charges is
first recorded in Ayenbite of Inwyt (1340); this usage
evolved into the sense of any published or written
statement that is likely to harm the reputation of a
person, as first recorded in 1521.
—vV. write or print a libel about. 1570, from the noun.
—libelous adj. 1619, formed from English libel, n. +
-OuS.

## liberal
liberal adj. Probably before 1350, befitting free men,
noble, generous; borrowed from Old French liberal,
learned borrowing from Latin liberalis noble, gener-
ous, from liber free; for suffix see -AL’. Cognates of

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:624 COLUMN:2 -->
Latin /iber are found in Greek eleutheros free (original-
ly) belonging to the people, of genuine tribal stock, Old
High German /Jiut people (modern German Leute ),
Old English /éod, Russian Ijudi people, from Indo-Euro-
pean *Jeudh- to grow (Pok.684).
The term Jiberal arts, referring originally to the
seven arts (the trivium and quadrivium ) that were con-
sidered “‘worthy of or befitting free men” in the Middle
Ages, appeared in Middle English before 1398 (in
Trevisa’s translation of Bartholomew’s De _ Pro-
prietatibus Rerum ) and was a translation of Medieval
Latin artes liberales. The sense of free from prejudice,
tolerant, is first recorded in Gibbon’s Decline and Fall
of the Roman Empire (1776-88), followed by the politi-
cal sense of favoring constitutional change and legal
reforms in 1801. The latter was probably borrowed into
English from French J/ibéral, attested in 1750 with the
sense of favorable to individual political freedoms.
—n. 1820, member of a liberal political party; later,
person who holds liberal views, especially in theology
(1887); from the adjective.
—liberalism n. 1819, formed from English /iberal, adj.
+ -ism. —liberality n. Probably about 1350 liberalite
generosity; borrowed from Old French liberalité, from
Latin liberalitatem (nominative liberalitas ), from liber-
alis liberal; for suffix see -ITy. —liberalization n. 1835,
in De Quincey’s writings; formed from English liberal-
ize + -ation. —liberalize v. 1774, in Burke’s writings;
formed from English liberal + -1ze.

## liberate
liberate v. set free. 1623, in Cockeram’s Dictionary;
borrowed from Latin /iberatus, past participle of libe-
rare, from liber free, see LIBERAL; for suffix see -ATE!.
In some instances, liberate is probably a back formation
from earlier Jiberation. —liberation n. Probably before
1425 liberacion, in a translation of Higden’s Poly-
chronicon; borrowed (perhaps in some _ instances
through Middle French /ibération ) and directly from
Latin /iberatidnem (nominative liberatio ), from Iibe-
rare set free; for suffix see -ATION. —liberator n. 1650,
formed from English liberate + -or?.

## liberationist
liberationist n. person advocating freedom from social
biases or restrictions. 1970, American English, abstract-
ed from Women’s Liberationist; formed from English
liberation + -ist.
An earlier use of this term (1869) was restricted to a
member of the “Liberation Society” of Great Britain,
which advocated disestablishment (withdrawal of state
support from the established church). The current |
form is a redevelopment in English.

## libertarian
libertarian n. 1789, one who holds the doctrine of free
will; later, person advocating liberty in thought and
conduct (1878); formed from English liberty + -arian, .
as in Unitarian.

## libertine
libertine n. dissolute or licentious person. About 1384,
emancipated slave, freedman, in the Wycliffe Bible;
borrowed from Latin Jibertinus member of the class of
freedmen, from /ibertus one’s freedman, from liber
free, see LIBERAL; for suffix see -INE!. The sense of a
freethinker is first recorded in an edition of Foxe’s
Book of Martyrs (1563-83), evidently influenced by the
word liberty, and the sense of a dissolute or licentious
person is found in 1593. —adj. 1577, freethinking;
later, dissolute, in Bacon’s Of the Advancement of
Learning (1605); from the noun.

## liberty
liberty n. About 1375 Jibertee, in Chaucer’s Canterbury
Tales; borrowed from Old French liberté freedom,
learned borrowing from Latin libertatem (nominative

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:625 -->
<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: libido | lie | 593 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:625 COLUMN:1 -->
libertas ), from liber free, see LIBERAL; for suffix see
=v:

## libido
libido (labé’d6) n. sexual desire or instinct. 1909, in A.A.
Brill’s translation of Freud’s Selected Papers on Hys-
teria; borrowed from Latin libido desire or lust, from
libére be pleasing, please; see LOVE. —libidinal, adj. of
the libido. 1922, formed from English libido + -al'.
—libidinous adj. lustful. 1447, borrowed probably
through Middle French libidineux (feminine libidi-
neuse ), from Latin libidindsus, from libido (genitive
libidinis ) desire or lust; for suffix see -OUS.

## library
library n. About 1380 librarye place containing books,
in Chaucer’s translation of Boethius’ De Consolatione
Philosophiae; later librarie collection of books, in the
Wycliffe Bible (before 1382); borrowed through Anglo-
French Jibrarie, from Old French Iibrairie collection of
books, and directly from Latin Jibrarium chest for
books, from liber (genitive libri) book, paper, parch-
ment, inner bark of a tree (used in early times for writ-
ing), earlier */uber, from Indo-European */ubhros; see
LEAF.
The Romance languages now use the word to mean
bookstore, derived from that sense in Late Latin, as
formed in French librairie, Italian Jibreria, Spanish Ii-
breria, Portuguese livraria, etc.; library in the English
sense is rendered bibliothéque in French, etc.
—librarian n. 1670, scribe; later, custodian of a library
(1713, in Steele’s writings); formed from English library
+ -an.

## libretto
libretto (lobret’6) n. words of an opera or other long
musical composition. 1740, in Richardson’s Pamela;
borrowing of Italian Jibretto, diminutive of libro book,
from Latin liber (genitive /ibri ); see LIBRARY. —libret-
tist n. 1862, probably borrowed from French Jibrettiste
(1846), from libretto (from Italian) + -iste -ist.

## license
license n. Before 1376 licence permission given by law
to do something, in Piers Plowman; borrowed from Old
French licence, learned borrowing from Latin licentia,
from licentum (nominative licéns ), present participle
of licére be allowed, be lawful, cognate with Oscan
likitud let it be allowed, and with Lettish Jikt to come
to terms (of sale), from Indo-European *leik-/lik-
(Pok.669). —v. give a license to, permit by law. Prob-
ably before 1400 licencen; from the noun. —licensee n.
1868, formed from English license + -ee.

## licentious
licentious (lisen’shas) adj. lawless, immoral. 1535, law-
less; later, lewd or lustful (1555); borrowed from Latin
licentidsus full of license, unrestrained, from licentia
LICENSE; for suffix see -OUS.
The later meaning “lewd” may have come from Mid-
die French licencieux (1537), appearing in a translation
of Castiglione’s I] Cortegiano (The Courtier).
An earlier example of licentious is found in Middle
English about 1425 in the sense of freely, with permis-
sion (adjective used as an adverb).

## lichen
lichen (li’kon) n. organism consisting of a fungus and
alga growing together. 1601, liverwort (formerly in-
cluded in the same group with the lichens), in Holland’s
translation of Pliny’s Natural History; borrowed from
Latin lichén, from Greek Jeichén, (originally) what eats
around itself, probably from Jeichein to LICK. The cur-
rent meaning of lichen is first recorded in 1715.

## licit
licit adj. lawful, permitted. 1483, in Caxton’s translation
of Cato’s writings; borrowed from Middle French licite,
learned borrowing from Latin Jicitus lawful; and bor-

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:625 COLUMN:2 -->
rowed directly from Latin Jicitus, from licére be al-
lowed, be lawful; see LICENSE.

## lick
lick v. Probably about 1200 licken; developed from Old
English liccian (830, in the Vespasian Psalter). Old
English liccian is cognate with Old Saxon likkén to lick,
modern Dutch likken, Old High German leckén (mod-
ern German lecken ), Old Icelandic sleikja, and Gothic
bilaigon; cognates are also found outside Germanic in
Latin lingere to lick, ligurrire to lick, lick up, Old Irish
ligim I lick, Greek Jeichein to lick, Lithuanian liéSti,
Old Slavic lizati, Armenian lizum I lick, and Vedic San-
skrit Jédhi, rédhi (he) licks, Classical Sanskrit Jihati,
from Indo-European *(s)leigh-/loigh-/léigh-/(s)lig¢h-
(Pok.668).
The sense of beat or thrash is first recorded in 1535;
the extended sense of overcome or defeat is found in
1800.
—n. stroke of the tongue over something. 1603, from
the verb. —licking n. a beating or thrashing (1756).

## lickety-split
lickety-split adv. Informal. at full speed. 1859, in Bart-
lett’s Dictionary of Americanisms; American English,
formed from earlier (1817) lickitie very fast (irregular
formation from lick, n., used dialectally in the sense of
“fast”) + split, n. Lickety-split was one of a group of
formations that included lickety cut (1831), lickety-
click (1847), and lickety-switch (1858).

## licorice
licorice (lik’aris or lik’arish) n. sweet, gummy extract of
a root, used as flavoring. Probably before 1200 licoriz,
in Layamon’s Chronicle of Britain; borrowed through
Anglo-French lycorys, Old French licorice, licorece,
from Late Latin Jiquiritia, alteration of Latin glycyrrhi-
za, from Greek glykyrrhiza, a compound of glykys
sweet + rhiza root. The development of Late Latin
liquiritia was in part influenced by Latin Jiquére
become fluid, in reference to the process of treating
the root to obtain its extract.

## lid
lid n. Before 1250 lid eyelid, in Bestiary; later, covering
or cover (about 1300); developed from Old English
(about 1000) hlid lid, cover, opening, gate. Old English
hlid is cognate with Old Frisian hlid lid, Middle Low
German lit, Middle Dutch Jit (modern Dutch lid ), Old
High German Jit, hlit (modern German Lid and Au-
genlid eyelid), Old Icelandic hlidh gate, from Proto-
Germanic *Hlidan, cognate with Sanskrit Srita-m, neu-
ter of sritd-s leaning, lying, and Greek klinein lean,
from Indo-European *klei-/kli- (Pok.601).
lie! vy. speak falsely. Probably about 1175 lien; later
ligen (probably before 1200) and legen (before 1250);
developed from Old English /égan, ligan (before 830, in
the Vespasian Psalter ), and earlier Jéogan (before 725).
The Old English forms are cognate with Old Frisian
liaga to lie, Old Saxon liogan, Middle Dutch lieghen
(modern Dutch liegen), Old High German liogan
(modern German ltigen ), Old Icelandic ljaga (Swedish
Jjuga, Danish lyve ), and Gothic liugan, from Proto-Ger-
manic */euzanan; also cognate outside Germanic with
Old Slavic /igati to lie, and Lithuanian /agoti to re-
quest, from Indo-European */eugh-/lugh- (Pok.686).
—n. false statement. About 1175 lyge; later lye (about
1385); developed from Old English (about 900) lyge lie;
cognate with Old High German Jugi (modern German
Liige ), and Old Icelandic lygi, from Proto-Germanic
*luzin, from the root */uz-/leuz- that is the source of
Old English Jéogan to lie.
lie? v. rest horizontally. 1137 lien; later liggen (prob-
ably before 1200); developed from Old English licgan

<!-- PAGE_MARGIN: lieder | light | 594 -->
<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:626 COLUMN:1 -->
to lie (about 725, in Beowulf); cognate with Old Frisian
liga, lidzia to lie, Old Saxon liggian, Middle Dutch
ligghen, modern Dutch liggen, (from Proto-Germanic
*lezjanan), Old High German Jigen (modern German
liegen ), Old Icelandic liggja (Swedish ligga, Danish and
Norwegian ligge ), and Gothic ligan. Outside Germanic
cognates are found in Gaulish Jegasit he put, laid, Old
Irish lige bed, grave, laigid lies, Latin lectus bed, Greek
léchos bed, léchesthai lie down, Old Slavic leZati to lie,
Tocharian A Jake and Tocharian B leke bed, and Hittite
lagari he lies, from Indo-European *legh-/logh-
(Pok.658).
Middle English liggen represents a regular phonetic
development from Old English licgan. The form lien,
from which modern English Jie developed, was a new
formation based upon Old English lig-, stem of the
second and third person singular.
—n. way in which something lies. 1697, from the verb.

## lieder
lieder (lé’doar) n.pl. of lied, used principally in reference
to German songs of Schubert and Schumann. 1852,
borrowed from German Lieder, plural of Lied song;
see LAUD.

## lief
lief (lef) adv. About 1300 leve, adv., willingly, gladly;
later lef (before 1376, in Piers Plowman ); from the
adjective leve, leove dear, beloved (before 1121); de-
veloped from Old English /éof dear, beloved (about
725, in Beowulf). The Old English adjective is cognate
with Old Frisian liaf dear, Old Saxon liof, Middle Dutch
and modern Dutch Jief, Old High German liob (mod-
ern German Jieb ), Old Icelandic /jafr, and Gothic liufs;
related to Old English Jufu LOVE. Compare LIVELONG.

## liege
liege (léj) adj. entitled to feudal allegiance and service.
Probably before 1300 liege, in Kyng Alisaunder, also
lige (about 1300); later lege (probably about 1390); bor-
rowed through Anglo-French lege, and directly from
Old French liege, lige, from Late Latin Jaeticus cul-
tivated by serfs, from Jaetus serf, probably from a Ger-
manic source (compare Old English /#t half-freedman,
serf, Old Frisian /ét, Old High German Jaz, Middle Low
German /at, and Gothic fra-Jéts forgiveness; all prob-
ably derived from the Proto-Germanic root that is the
source of Gothic /étan and Old English /#tan to allow,
LET'). —n. lord entitled to feudal allegiance. Probably
about 1375 lige vassal, in Chaucer’s Canterbury Tales;
and lege feudal lord (about 1380); from the adjective.

## lien
lien (lén) n. legal claim on the property of another for
payment of a debt. 1531, borrowing of Middle French
lien a band or tie, from Latin ligamen bond, from ligare
to bind; see LIGAMENT.

## lieu
lieu (li) n. place, stead. 1534 in (the ) lieu of in place of,
instead of (possibly also about 1300, in a single use re-
corded in OED); borrowed from Middle French lieu
place, Old French Jeu, from Latin Jocum (nominative
locus ) place; see LOCATE.

## lieutenant
lieutenant (liiten’ant; British leften’ant) n. About 1378
lieutenant, civil or military officer who acts for a superi-
or, in a version of Piers Plowman, and leeftenaunt one
who acts for another (before 1387, in Trevisa’s transla-
tion of Higden’s Polychronicon ); borrowed from Old
French /uetenant substitute; literally, placeholder (/ieu
place, LIEU + tenant, present participle of tenir to
hold, from Latin tenére; see TENANT). The origin of the
British pronunciation, represented before 1387 in such
spellings as lJeeftenaunt, remains uncertain.

## life
life n. Before 1121 life, in Peterborough Chronicle;
developed from Old English life, dative of lif (about

<!-- SOURCE_PAGE:626 COLUMN:2 -->
725, in Beowulf); cognate with Old Frisian Jif life, per-
son, body, Old Saxon lif life, person, Middle Dutch and
modern Dutch lif body, Old High German Jib life
(modern German Leib body), and Old Icelandic Jif life
(Swedish lif, Danish and Norwegian liv life, body), from
Proto-Germanic *liba-; related to Old English Jifian,
libban to have life, LI1VE!. —lifeblood n. (1590, in Spen-
ser’s Faerie Queene ) —lifeboat n. (1801) —lifeguard n.
(1896, American English) —life insurance (about 1809,
American English) —lifeless adj. Before 1200 lifleas;
developed from Old English /ifléas (lif life + -léas -less).
—lifelong adj. (1855; earlier, 1757, as a substitute for
livelong ) —lifetime n. (before 1250 lif time ) —lifework
n. (1871)

## lift
lift v. Probably about 1200 liften, in The Ormulum;
borrowed from a Scandinavian source (compare Old
Icelandic lypta to raise). Old Icelandic lypta is cognate
with Middle Low German liichten to raise, lift, Middle
Dutch luchten (modern Dutch lichten ), Middle High
German I/tiften, from Proto-Germanic *Juftjanan; all
derived from the Proto-Germanic root that is the
source of Old English /yft heaven, air; see LOFT —n. act
of lifting. 1485, in Malory’s Morte d’Arthur; from the
verb.
The figurative sense of act of helping, helping hand
is first recorded in 1633, and that of help given by
offering a ride in a vehicle, in Swift’s Journal to Stella
(1712). Lift meaning an elevator (now only in British
usage) is found in 1851 in the specific sense of a dumb-
waiter and in 1861 as a passenger elevator.
—liftoff n. takeoff of a rocket or aircraft. (1956, in Dr.
Woodford Heflin’s The U.S. Air Force Dictionary,
American English).

## ligament
ligament n. 1392, band of strong tissues; borrowed from
Latin ligamentum band, tie, ligature, from ligare to
bind, tie; for suffix see -MENT. Latin ligare is cognate
with Middle Low German /ik band, Middle High Ger-
man geleich, joint, limb, Albanian lJith I bind, and
Ukrainian nalyhaty to bridle, fetter, from Indo-Euro-
pean *Jeig-/lig-, also *leig-/lig- (Pok.668).

## ligature
ligature (lig’achur or lig’achoar) n. anything used to bind
or tie up. Before 1400, in a translation of Lanfranc’s
Science of Surgery, borrowed through Old French liga-
ture, and directly from Late Latin ligatuira, from Latin
ligare to bind, see LIGAMENT; for suffix see -URE.
The sense in music of a method indicating notes to
be sung to one syllable is first recorded in 1597. The
sense of two or more letters joined in writing and print-
ing is first recorded in 1693, possibly taken from
French (1680).
—v. bind or tie up with a ligature. 1716-20; from the
noun.
light! n. radiant energy. About 1175 Jiht; later light
(before 1325, in Genesis and Exodus, and 1317, as a
surname); developed from Old English Jéht (before
830, in the Vespasian Psalter ); earlier leoht (about 725,
in Beowulf). The Old English forms are cognate with
Old Frisian liacht light, Old Saxon lioht, Middle Dutch
and modern Dutch licht, Old High German Jioht (mod-
ern German Licht), Old Icelandic Ijés, and Gothic li-
uhath. The word is represented outside Germanic by
Old Irish Juchair luster, Latin liix (genitive Jicis ) light,
lGcére to shine, Greek leukos white or light, Lithuanian
latkas pale, Old Slavic Juéa ray or beam, Armenian Jois
light, Sanskrit rdcate (it) shines, Tocharian A and To-
charian B Juk-, and Hittite Juk-, Jukk- to shine, from
Indo-European *leuk-/louk-/luk- (Pok.687).
